en: Now begins the ninth chapter.
I shall declare the eternal laws concerning the union and separation of a man and a woman who abide in the path of righteousness. 9.1.

Following the section on adultery (*strīsaṃgrahaṇa*), there is the indication of the legal topics (*vivādapada*) concerning "the duties of husband and wife and partition" (*strīpuṃdharmo vibhāgaś ca*, MDh 8.7). That is now being stated. When a husband is excessively afflicted by passion (*kāma*) and oppresses her in any way whatsoever, she may, if necessary, litigate against him before the king. This applies only when he follows the path of justice and is not possessed of hatred, envy, or similar vices; for it is said that toward such a husband, the wife should behave accordingly. However, this does not imply that she possesses authority over the husband. Her "service" (*upacāra*) consists of obedience like a servant, massaging his feet, and so forth. Although the words *strī* (woman) and *puruṣa* (man) denote the human species as qualified by specific genders, here they refer to the relationship of wife and husband. In the verse, "Women must be kept dependent by their own men day and night" (MDh 9.2), the use of the word "own" (*svaiḥ*) indicates this specific relationship. The purpose of the present promise is as follows: I shall describe the conduct regarding the union of husband and wife—their cohabitation when together in one place—and likewise their separation when traveling abroad, as well as their mutual duties, such as personal adornment and the protection of the body. The inclusion of the word "eternal" (*śāśvata*) is for the sake of praise. "On the lawful path" (*dharmye vartmani*) is a restatement; it refers to the proper course established by the scriptures and traditional practice. (9.1)
Women must be kept under control by their own men day and night; even when they are becoming attached to sensual objects, they must be established under one's own authority. 9.2.

Women must not be permitted to act according to their own will in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma. Whatever wealth is to be employed for dharma and other such purposes, their own male guardians—the husband and others—must be consulted according to their respective ages. These "own male guardians" are those authorized to protect them, as specified in the passage beginning, "The father protects [her]" (MDh 9.3). For when they become attached to sense-objects such as singing and the like, or indulge in them, they must be brought under their own control and restrained from such activities. Although the loss of independence regarding all actions has already been taught by the statement that women are "not independent," the repeated mention of turning away from sense-objects is intended to ensure they are avoided with special effort. It should not be understood that they are to be restrained only from contact with other men and the like, while remaining addicted to drinking liquor and so forth even while staying at home.

By the word *ca* (and), this duty has first been stated for men. It follows that independence should not be granted to women; by implication, it is stated that they too must not be independent. And thus, in the verse "Of the man and of the woman indeed" (MDh 9.1), those duties which pertain to both the woman and the man in relation to one another are what are expressed by the word *ca*, and not sacrifices and the like; such is the logical connection. || 9.2 ||
The father protects her in childhood; the husband protects her in youth; the sons protect her in old age. A woman does not deserve independence. 9.3

Protection (*rakṣā*) is the warding off of misfortune (*anartha*). Misfortune, however, consists of humiliation through the transgression of improper conduct, through failing to engage in [proper duties], or through the unjust seizure of wealth and so forth. Its warding off is its prevention; this must be performed by the father and others. The form *rakṣati* is used here in the sense of the optative (*liṅ*) due to Vedic usage; hence, the suffix of the optative is applied in the injunction *rakṣet*. The mention of the divisions of age is for the purpose of indicating that the fault [of non-protection] is greater [in those stages]. However, all [relatives] are always authorized for the sake of protection. The mention of "childhood" (*kaumāra*) is intended to indicate the period prior to marriage. Similarly, "youth" (*yauvana*) is an illustration for a woman whose husband is living. Therefore, this is merely a restatement of a constant rule: whenever she is under the authority of someone, at that time she must necessarily be protected by him. Thus, even while the husband is living, the father and the son have their respective authorities. This has been shown in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "All these [relatives] should always perform her protection. To elaborate on this would result in excessive prolixity of the text.

But is this not already stated by the passage, “by a girl, or by a young woman” (MDh 5.145)? Not so; for lack of independence (*asvātantrya*) is one thing, and protection (*rakṣā*) is another. In that [other] context, lack of independence was taught, whereas here, protection is being discussed. Even for a woman who is under the control of another, misfortune can be averted. But is it not also recited here that “a woman does not deserve independence”?

It is said: By this [verse], it is not intended to enjoin a lack of independence regarding all actions. What then? It means that one who is not independent and whose mind is distracted is not capable of protecting oneself, due to a natural deficiency in power. However, the statement in the fifth [chapter] is for the sake of [establishing] non-independence, because a different meaning has been stated there. (9.3)
A father who does not give [a daughter] in marriage at the proper time is censurable; a husband who does not approach his wife is censurable;
and when the husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother is censurable. (9.4)

If, when the time for giving has arrived, the father does not give [the daughter], who indeed is the time for the giving of a maiden? It is recorded in the Smṛti: "From the eighth year onwards, prior to puberty" (GDh 18.21). Here too there is an indicative mark [in the text]: *anupayan*, meaning not approaching, not having intercourse, not sporting with his wives, being dependent. Regarding the time for approaching, it is stated that the fertile period (*ṛtu*) is the time, excluding the forbidden days (MDh 3.45). 9.4.
Women must be guarded especially against even the slightest of attachments;
for if they are not protected, they will bring sorrow upon two families. (9.5)

"Prasaṅga" means improper association. This refers to such things as being occasionally in the company of someone whose character is unknown, or a child, or the sight of a man in bright attire standing at the door of the house, and so forth. By implication, these lead to the agitation of the mind and must be guarded against. Indeed, these are not themselves directly of the nature of faults; for direct contact with women is not itself a fault in women [but rather the agitation they cause]. Because of this subtlety, they must be protected—that is, prevented. It is established that she must be guarded with special effort by all those of her own family, such as brothers, paternal uncles, brothers-in-law, and others. Therein, no [other] protection is required. (9.5)
For seeing this supreme dharma common to all castes, even weak husbands strive to protect their wives. (9.6)

This is the highest [duty] for the four castes... seeing and knowing this, even those who are weak should strive and exert effort to protect their wives. [The suffix] *liṅ* is used here in the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*). ... Regarding the protection of property and oneself, it has been stated that there, the body of the bride—surrounded by jewels, appearing outwardly radiant, and born of noble lineage—should be protected from the day and night of passion through some restraint, such as by taking refuge in the royal palace which possesses great splendor. 9.6.
For by protecting his wife with diligence, he indeed protects his offspring, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma. (9.7)

The protection of women must not be performed solely on account of the instructions of the scriptures; rather, there are many other purposes for it. "Offspring" refers to progeny characterized by sons and daughters; the meaning is that no *saṃkara* (mixture of castes) occurs. "Conduct" refers to the customary behavior of the cultured (*śiṣṭa*). "Family" has been explained previously. For any noble family, when the wife’s character is corrupted, the fault attaches to the entire lineage, as it is said: "Virtuous women are not [the property] of these [men]. Alternatively, because of the absence of purity in the lineage of fathers, grandfathers, and so forth, the funeral rites (*aurdhvadaihika*) would not be accomplished; therefore, protection is necessary. [He protects] himself: it is well known that he is inevitably killed by a paramour or even by his own wife through poison and the like. And [he protects] his own dharma, because a woman who is unchaste is ineligible for religious duties. Therefore, one who protects his wife protects all of this. (9.7)
The husband, having entered his wife and become an embryo, is born here; for that indeed is the "wifehood" (jāyātva) of the wife, because he is born again from her. 9.8.

This is a figurative statement (*arthavāda*). For there is no observation of the husband entering the wife’s womb. Therefore, this "entry" is spoken of figuratively by way of the semen, which is the essence of the body. "The self, indeed, is named the son" (ŚB 14.9.4.26)—this very fact is the basis for the application of the word *jāyā* in the sense of "wife," because the husband is born from her. When the word *jāyā* is used in the sense of the birth of offspring, even the paramour is called the "wife" (*jāyā*) [of the child]. 9.8.
For whatever kind of man a woman associates with, she gives birth to a son of that same kind;
therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, one should guard women with great effort. (9.9)

He demonstrates what was stated in the verse, "her own offspring" (MDh 9.7). One should not think that she gives birth to a son of such a caste as the second man whom she serves; nor is similarity of qualities intended here. For [otherwise], one born from a Śūdra or other [low caste] would possess the status of a Caṇḍāla or similar [outcaste]. Furthermore, even for one born of a woman of the same caste, there would be no belonging to that same caste, because of the statement: "among wives whose wombs are unconsecrated" (MDh 10.5). Even if similarity of qualities were meant, it would follow that a woman whose husband is of poor character or destitute would be permitted to approach a superior man. However, when this is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), then the phrase "of such a kind" is understood to mean "in accordance with her family. (9.9)
No one is able to guard women by force;
however, they can be guarded by the application of these means. 9.10

This verse is intended to praise the means that will be explained hereafter. Women cannot be protected by force—that is, by physical compulsion such as confining them within the inner apartments (*śuddhānta*) or by expelling other men from them; rather, they can be protected through these applications of skillful means. "Applications" (*yoga*) refers to methods of practice; the meaning is: "by means of these methods being employed. (9.10)
He should employ her in the collection of wealth and in its expenditure, as well as in cleanliness, religious duties, the cooking of food, and the supervision of household utensils.

*Artha* means wealth. Its *saṃgraha* (accumulation) consists of setting it aside in the house after determining its quantity by counting and so forth, for the purpose of protection—storing it by securing it with ropes, iron chains, and the like, or marking it with seals, and so on. *Vyaya* (expenditure) is the spending of that very same wealth: "This much is for food, this is for soup, and this much is for vegetables. *Śauca* (cleanliness) is the purification of the ladles, pots, and other utensils, as well as the smearing of the floor and so forth. *Dharma* (duty) is the giving of water for ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) and the offering of libations (*tarpaṇa*), and the worship of the gods with offerings of food, flowers, and various articles in the women’s quarters, the inner chambers, and so on. *Annapakti* (cooking of food) is well known. *Pāriṇāhya* refers to items such as stools and couches; she should be appointed to supervise these. (9.11)
Those women who, though confined at home and guarded by trustworthy men, protect themselves by their own efforts—they are truly well-protected. (9.12)

Those who act appropriately at the right time are called "attentive" (*avadhānavant*); these are the chamberlains (*kañcukin*) who serve in the inner apartments (*śuddhānta*). When women are confined in their own homes by them and deprived of independence—being guarded by the prohibition against moving about as they please—they are not truly protected. Rather, they protect themselves by means of themselves. How do they protect themselves? By being employed in these tasks. This is a praise of the aforementioned method, not a prohibition of other methods. (9.12)

Drinking, association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about, sleeping [independently], and dwelling in another's house—these six are the causes of a woman’s corruption. 9.13.

Wandering through marketplaces for the purpose of buying food, vegetables, and the like; staying for many days in the families of kinsmen or living in the houses of others; and the seduction of women—these are the causes of mental agitation for women, for they cast aside the fear of their fathers-in-law and others, as well as the fear of public scandal. (9.13)
They do not examine his form, nor is there any consideration of his age; whether he be handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply because he is a man. 9.14

One should not harbor this conceit: "I am fortunate, handsome, and young; how could she desire another after rejecting me? For these women do not consider whether he is attractive or of heroic appearance; they perceive him merely as "a man" and, for that reason alone, they enjoy him and unite with him. (9.14)

"Due to their proclivity for men, their fickle-mindedness, and their natural lack of affection, these women act perversely toward their husbands even when guarded with great effort in this world. (9.15)

When any man whatsoever is seen, the agitation of women’s minds—thinking, "How might I be united with him?"—is *pauṃścalya* (unchastity). Furthermore, there is instability even regarding other matters such as dharma and so forth, due to their fickle-mindedness; for instance, they desire with lustful intent that very person who is hateful, such as a brother or a son, simply because he has been seen. They possess affection (*sneha*), passion (*rāga*), and thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) toward their husbands, sons, and others, their hearts being bound by pride. Through union with these defects, they become corrupted and undergo transformation toward their husbands. (9.15)
Therefore,
having thus understood their nature as born from the creation of Prajāpati,
a man should exert the utmost effort toward their protection. 9.16.
Prajāpati is Hiraṇyagarbha. He was born at the time of his own manifestation, that is, at the time of creation. The rest is clear. 9.16.
Manu ordained for women beds and seats, ornaments, lust, anger, ignobility, a malicious disposition, and bad conduct. (9.17)

*Śayyā* (bed) means the habit of lying down and sleeping. *Āsana* (seating) means the habit of not rising [to greet]. *Alaṃkāra* (ornament) is the decoration of the body. *Kāma* (lust) is the longing for the enjoyment of men. *Krodha* (anger) is hatred. *Anāryatā* (ignobility) is affection toward one who is hateful and hatred toward one who is dear; it is the concealment of outward appearance and a lack of righteousness. It is a treacherous disposition. *Drogdhr̥tva* (treachery) refers to the nature of one's husband, father, and so forth, being unrighteous due to their susceptibility to the vices of men. The compound is formed with the noun *drogdhr̥tva* (from the root *duh*, "to harm," with the suffix *tṛc*) joined with the word *bhāva*. *Kucaryā* (bad conduct) is the service of base men. This is the innate nature of women, ordained by Manu at the beginning of creation. Bed, seating, and ornament are presented as examples for treachery and bad conduct; just as these things are inherent and unchangeable, so too are bad conduct and the rest. (9.17)
"There is no ritual efficacy for women through mantras; such is the established rule in the Dharma.
For women are devoid of spiritual faculties and lack mantras; they are falsehood—this is the settled conclusion. (9.18)

Some argue as follows: "Even if there is infidelity on the part of women, they will attain purity through Vedic recitation (*japa*), secret penances (*rahasya-prāyaścitta*), and so forth; therefore, there is no fault. This is not correct. For women have neither ritual action nor even *japa* performed with mantras, by which they might—should their conduct deviate and the matter remain unpublicized—attain purity through their own learning alone. Therefore, this [verse] is merely a supplement to the rule: "They must be protected with great effort" (MDh 9.15).

Therefore, some explain that this is a general prohibition of mantras; and considering it to be such a prohibition, they maintain that whatever rite connected with women is performed by anyone—whether women are involved as the agents, as in the evening *bali* offering and so forth, or as those to be consecrated, as in the *cūḍā*-ceremony and so forth, or as the recipients, as in the *śrāddha* and so forth—in all such cases, because of the prohibition of mantras, rites such as the *śrāddha* for women must be performed without mantras.

Those [who hold this view] speak incorrectly, because this [text] is intended for another purpose. Since it is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), this must be explained with reference to the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the *cūḍā*, which involve mantras prescribed and prohibited according to the principle of having that [subject] as their objective support (*ālambana*). Furthermore, due to the absence of formal study (*adhyayana*), there is an absence of the recitation of mantras for atonement (*prāyaścitta*), as one should consider.

They are without sense-faculties (*nirindriyāḥ*). "Sense-faculty" (*indriya*) refers to vigor, steadfastness, wisdom, power, and so forth; these women lack them. Therefore, even when they do not wish it, they are sometimes overcome by force through evil conduct. Consequently, it is proper to protect them. Women are called "untruthful" (*anṛtam*); this is a censure based on their untruthfulness due to the instability of their moral character and affection. (9.18)
And likewise, many Vedic verses have been sung even in the Nigamas;
listen to their expiations for the purpose of examining their specific characteristics. 9.19.

He cites Vedic sentences in the form of *mantra* and *arthavāda* as witnesses for the point that women are by nature impure-hearted. And so it is: just as I have stated, "Women are falsehood," even so there are *śruti*s in the *nigamas*, that is, the Vedas. The word *nigama* is a synonym for *veda* and its usage is well-attested; for example, [in Pāṇini’s rule]: "In the *nigama*, [the forms] *babhūtha*, *ātatantha*, etc. [Pāṇ 7.2.64]. It also has the sense of being a limb (*aṅga*) for the exposition of the meaning of the Veda, as in: "The *nirukta*, *nigama*, and *vyākaraṇa* are the limbs. Indeed, there is a usage in the *Nirukta*: "These are the *nigamas*" [Nir 1.1]. However, since the term *śruti* is used here, or because of the examples to be cited later, that [usage of the word *nigama* as a specific limb] is impossible in this context. Therefore, the word *nigama* is taken here to mean the Veda. And the relationship of container and contained exists due to the distinction between the whole and its parts. Within those *nigamas*, the *śruti*s—being constituent parts—are "chanted" (*nigīta*), which means they are studied, proclaimed, and recited. Furthermore, the *Nirukta* explains that because the Veda is eternally active, there is no division of time and so forth.

There is an alternative reading, “*nigadāḥ*” [63]. *Nigadas* are specific types of mantras; *śrutis* are sentences from the Brāhmaṇas. In both the mantras and the Brāhmaṇas, this meaning is shown: that women are untruthful. In the view that there are many such [statements], the word [“many”] is to be supplied. Listen to those among those *śrutis* which take the form of expiations (*niṣkṛti*) for transgression, serving as penances for infidelity. If it is asked for what purpose they are cited, it is for the sake of examining their own characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*). Their own characteristic is an inherent nature that is eternally present; the purpose is to demonstrate that. This “own characteristic,” meaning their inherent nature, is distinct from characteristics such as armlets or earrings [which are external]; the meaning is that their own characteristic consists of infidelity itself. This is their own characteristic, namely, that which is of the nature of transgression. (9.19)
"Whatever my mother, wandering about unfaithful to her husband, lusted for—that seed let my father take up"; this is the illustration of that. (9.20)

By the three quarters ending with *itikāraṇāt*, a portion of the mantra is imitated: “Whatever [sin] my mother, who was unfaithful (*apativrata*), [committed]—she whose vow (*vrata*) and discipline (*niyama*) were such that she had no desire for another man even in her mind; the opposite of that is ‘unfaithful’ (*apativrata*). Wandering about, going to the houses of others, having seen there a person in splendid attire, she became lusting (*pralulubhe*). She conceived a longing (*lobha*), a desire, directed toward another man. May that sin, which belongs to my father through my birth—that seed (*retaḥ*), the semen (*śukra*)—remove (*vṛṅktām*) it! By that seed, may that fault be wiped away. The nominative case is used by transposition (*vyatyaya*) in place of the genitive in the word *pitā*. Alternatively, the seed itself is figuratively conceived as the father (*pitṛtvena parikalpyate*). Without abandoning its own grammatical gender, it enters into a coreferential construction (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word ‘seed’: just as in the Vedic passage, “The sky is my father” (*dyaur me pitā*, RV 2.3.20). Or else, the seed of the mother is also called ‘seed’ (*retaḥ*). That seed, the father—the progenitor—may remove (*vṛṅktām*) it, i.e., purify it. The meaning is: “By the power of the seed born of the father, may the fault of the mother be removed. This is the illustration (*nidarśana*) and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for this act consisting of infidelity. All those performing the recitation (*japa*) utter this mantra. And if all women were of a corrupt nature, then the constant application (*nityavat prayoga*) of the mantra would be appropriate; otherwise, it would be merely occasional (*pākṣika*). This mantra is employed in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices and in the consecration of the water for washing the feet (*pādya-anumantraṇa*) at a Śrāddha ceremony. (9.20)
Whatever undesirable thing she contemplates in her mind for her husband, this is rightly called the concealment of that transgression. (9.21)

The "grasper of the hand" (pāṇigrāha) is the husband. Whatever undesirable or unpleasant thing a woman thinks of in her mind—such as contact with another man—the concealment or purification of that mental transgression is declared by this mantra when it is employed in the ritual. Although the purpose of the mantra used in a rite is simply its contribution to the efficacy of that rite, nevertheless, because it is also applied in practices such as silent recitation (japa), its purpose is stated here as being for the cessation of mental transgression. (9.21)
Whatever the qualities of the husband with whom a woman is united according to the prescribed rule, such qualities she acquires, just as a river does when it joins the ocean. 9.22

One who desires to protect his wife must protect himself from immorality; yet not by this alone. For the wife of one who is immoral becomes likewise [immoral], while the wife of one who possesses virtue remains virtuous. Just as a river, though its water be sweet, becomes salt-water when it joins with the ocean. (9.22)
Akṣamālā, though born of a low womb, attained venerable status through her union with Vasiṣṭha; and Śāraṅgī reached the same state of honor through Mandapāla. || 9.23 ||

Even Akṣamālā, though of low birth, attained a state of great honor through her union with Vasiṣṭha; likewise, Śāraṅgī, though of the animal species, was honored in the same way when united with the sage Mandapāla. Therefore, women of lower birth, even if younger, are to be honored even more than their husbands. Thus it has been said: "Women [are respected] according to age. (9.23)
These and other women in this world, though born of lowly origin, have attained eminence through their own respective auspicious qualities as wives. (9.24)

Those whose birth or origin (*prasūti*) is low or base are "those of low birth" (*avakṛṣṭaprasūtayaḥ*). There are others as well, such as Gaṅgā, Kālī, and so forth. Because two [categories] are under discussion, the plural form "these" (*etāḥ*) implies a third by means of the word "and" (*ca*); or else, there is a reduplication: "these and [others]" (*ete ca*). (9.24)
Thus has been declared the auspicious conduct for men and women in this world, which yields happy results both in this life and after death; now learn the duties concerning progeny.

The journey of the world (*loka-yātrā*), the conduct of the world (*loka-vṛtta*), and the practice of the world (*loka-ācāra*)—this is established by worldly consensus. This matter is not defined by scriptural injunction (*vidhi-lakṣaṇa*) such that it can be protected in this way and not otherwise. Furthermore, if these [women] are not protected, defects such as those regarding procreation arise. Now, learn the laws concerning progeny: does the offspring belong to the sower of the seed or to the owner of the field? "Udarka" refers to the future time; they are those for whom that [future] is happy. For all things indeed come to an end at their conclusion, but these do not; thus is the praise [of them]. (9.25)

But what is the resulting happiness of the duty of procreation? For offspring depend upon women, and since women are shrouded in many faults, they ought to be abandoned. Why then did [the sage] say, "Who indeed should support all within the home"? [He said]: "For the sake of procreation, these fortunate ones are worthy of honor and are the lights of the household;
there is no difference whatsoever between women and the goddesses of fortune (*śrī*) within homes. (9.26)

They are worthy of honor because their faults can be remedied. This detailed exposition of their faults is not intended for the sake of contempt or for the sake of avoidance, like one would avoid those who are accursed or fallen. Rather, it is for the purpose of protection against those very faults. For one does not refrain from placing a pot on the fire simply because there are beggars, nor does one refrain from sowing barley because there are wild animals. By "procreation" (*prajana*), what is intended is the entire process beginning from conception up to the nurturing of the offspring; as he will state later: "The procreation of offspring and the protection of those already born" (MDh 9.27). It is like lamps in a house. For it is well known that no service whatsoever exists in a house without women. Even when one possesses wealth and prosperity, if a wife is absent, householders are unable to win over friends, kinsmen, and others who have arrived by providing them with food and other comforts, person by person. Just as there is no power in a poor man, therefore there is no difference between a woman and prosperity in households. (9.26)
The procreation of offspring, the nurturing of those born, and the constant maintenance of worldly life—woman is the manifest foundation for these. (9.27)

The woman is the binding cause (*nimitta*). This is evident in matters such as the procreation of offspring. Social intercourse (*lokayātrā*) consists of winning over those who have come to one's home by giving food and other gifts, as well as invitations and formal requests. In every single matter of this [social intercourse], the woman is the binding cause. The reading is *pratyaham* ("daily"). The word *pratyakṣa* here expresses that which is internal (*antaraṅga*); the meaning is "internal. (9.27)
Offspring, religious duties, service, and supreme delight—these depend upon the wife; likewise, heaven for one's ancestors and for oneself depends upon her. (9.28)
The meaning of this verse has already been shown previously. || 9.28 ||
She who does not deceive her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body, attains the worlds of her husband and is called "virtuous" by the righteous. (9.29)
But through infidelity to her husband, a woman incurs reproach in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases. (9.30)
Both verses in the fifth [chapter] have been explained (cf. MDh 5.162–63). 9.29–30.
Listen to this meritorious discourse, beneficial to all people, which has been proclaimed by the virtuous and by the great seers of old concerning a son. (9.31)

An *upanyāsa* is the introduction of a subject to be examined, or the examination itself; listen to that. It was spoken (*uditam*) concerning a son (*putraṃ prati*), by the virtuous, the learned, and the great seers (*maharṣibhiḥ*). It is beneficial to all people (*viśvajanyam*) and auspicious (*puṇyam*). Because of the intervening praise of women, this introduction is made once again for the sake of showing respect for the meaning of the phrase "listen to the duty regarding progeny" (*prajādharmaṃ nibodhata*): "Listen to the introduction" (*upanyāsaṃ nibodhata*). 9.31.
They recognize the son as belonging to the husband; however, there is a conflict in the sacred texts regarding the progenitor.
Some say he is the one who produces him, while others know him to be the owner of the field.

The *bhartṛ* is the husband, the one who has wedded her. All learned men recognize and accept as his son that child born of a woman who was consecrated by him through the sacrament of marriage (*vivāhasaṃskāra*). There is no disagreement on this point; this is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). However, regarding the case of the mere progenitor, there is a conflict of scriptural authority (*śrutidvaidha*). When the man is merely the progenitor—having fathered a child in the field of another without being her husband—there is a conflict of scripture, meaning a difference of opinion. He demonstrates this: some say the child belongs to the progenitor, while others say it belongs to the owner of the field, that is, the one whose wife she is, even though he did not procreate it. Having thus presented the doubt arising from the disagreement among teachers, he supports that very point by stating the reason. (9.32)
The woman is considered to be the field, and the man is considered to be the seed; from the union of the field and the seed, there is the birth of all embodied beings. 9.33

A woman is like a field; a "field" is a portion of land that serves as the place of origin for rice and other crops, and a woman is similar to that. Just as seed sown in a field grows when it is held there, so too is the semen infused in a woman. The man is the very essence of the seed. Here too, the word *bhūta* (being/essence) is used in a figurative sense (*upamā*). His semen is the seed, not the man himself directly; however, because it has him as its substratum, he is designated as such. "Union" (*samāyoga*) is the relationship characterized by the container and the contained. From that comes the "origination" (*saṃbhava*), the birth of all embodied beings (*sarvadehin*), that is, of the fourfold collection of living beings. Even for those born from sweat, space is the field and the sweat is the seed. Therefore, doubt is appropriate, since origination is impossible without both. Both are active in the production of offspring. Since there is no reason for a definitive determination (*vinigamanā*) as to whose [the child] it is—whether of both or of one of the two—there is this uncertainty. And this is the meaning of the entire section: the relationship between offspring and progenitor is not to be determined through inference. As we shall state in the verse on the division [of inheritance]: 9.33 ||
In some cases the seed is superior, while in others it is the female womb;
but where both are equal, that offspring is highly praised. (9.34)

The superiority of the seed has been observed by great sages such as Vyāsa and Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, in the case of sons born from the wombs of women—such as Dhṛtarāṣṭra and others—who, though born from a Brāhmaṇa, were of the Kṣatriya caste because they followed the mother's lineage. However, when both [seed and womb] are equal—meaning they belong to the same master and are of the same caste—that procreation is praised because there is no conflict of status. As it has been said: "They recognize the son as belonging to the husband" (MDh 9.32). 9.34.
Between the seed and the womb, the seed is said to be superior;
for the procreation of all beings is indeed characterized by the nature of the seed. (9.35)

When doubt has been thus raised, he first adopts the position that the seed is primary. Because of its primacy, offspring belongs to the one whose seed it is. Its primacy is established because, although a substance such as rice has many causes like soil and so forth, it is observed to conform to the qualities of that [seed]. Consequently, since offspring clearly conforms to the unseen seed and is thus an effect, it is logical to accept that it follows the qualities of the seed, just as in the case of rice and other grains. For in this way, the uniformity of form in every effect is not abandoned. Thus, he demonstrates the primacy of the seed: "For it is the source of all beings. The source—that is, the birth or production—of all beings is characterized by the seed; it is marked or defined by whatever characteristics the seed possesses, such as its form, color, and configuration; in other words, it conforms to the nature of the seed. (9.35)
Whatever kind of seed is sown in a field prepared at the proper time, such a crop grows from it, manifested with its own inherent qualities. (9.36)

This verse is provided by the author as an expansion of the meaning of the immediately preceding [verse], demonstrating the connection [between them]. He will explain the meaning of the word *yādṛś* ("of such a kind") with the passage beginning, "rice, śāli grain," and so forth (MDh 9.39). When prepared at the proper time—that is, when the sowing season, such as the rainy season, has arrived and the ground has been refined by plowing, leveling, and other such means—it grows, that is, it is produced. It manifests a visible form characterized by its own qualities, such as color, configuration, taste, and potency. (9.36)
For this ground is called the eternal womb of all beings;
yet the seed does not nourish any qualities of the womb during its growth. (9.37)

The persistence of the qualities of the seed (*bīja*) has been stated previously; by this [verse], the absence of the qualities of the field (*kṣetra*) is expressed. This ground is called the womb (*yoni*) or the field (*kṣetra*) of beings—of stationary things such as herbs, grasses, shrubs, and creepers. Yet, none of its qualities are seen in those beings. Neither the soil nor the dust is perceived there. The seed "thrives" (*puṣyati*) in its nourishments (*puṣṭi*). Here, the word "seed" refers to rice and the like once they have emerged as sprouts, not to the root itself; for even that, when sown from what remains after consumption, certainly becomes a seed again in the following year. That [the field] does not thrive or persist [in its qualities]. The verb *puṣ* is used in the sense of "persisting" (*anuvṛtti*) which constitutes a part of "thriving" (*puṣṭi*). Its transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) is the cause for the second case ending (*dvitīyā*). Or, it "attains" (*prāpnoti*) or "partakes of" (*bhajate*) the qualities of the womb. It does not thrive or persist on account of those parts which constitute its nourishment. If the persistence of the factors of thriving were already expressed by the verb, then the phrase "in the nourishments" (*puṣṭiṣu*) would be redundant. Therefore, since roots have multiple meanings, only the other meaning [here] is to be explained by the verb.

Or [the term] "in nourishments" (*puṣṭiṣu*) may be for the sake of completing the verse; in some way, the tautology must be avoided. Alternatively, the connection should be stated by way of the relationship between the general and the particular, as in the expression "he has nourished his own nourishment. (9.37)
Even in a single field on the earth, seeds sown at the proper time by farmers arise in various forms here according to their own nature. (9.38)

The meaning just stated is explained by means of an illustration [100]: "In a single field" (*ekakedāre*). The word "even" (*api*) is to be supplied here. The sense is that even in a single field—that is, of the soil—at whatever specific time a particular seed is sown by farmers, seeds of different forms arise, because they conform to their own inherent natures (*svabhāva*). For if the field were the predominant factor, then because the field is one, all the seeds would be of a single form. || 9.38 ||
Rice, śāli grain, mung beans, sesame, beans, and likewise barley, as well as garlic and sugarcanes, sprout according to their respective seeds. (9.39)

He shows those seeds as being of various forms, according to the nature of each seed, by way of the predominance of the seed's own essence. In all cases, the plural number is used when referring to a genus. 9.39
That one thing is sown and another is produced—this is not tenable;
for whatever seed is sown, that very same thing sprouts forth. 9.40

This very same point is concluded by means of different words: [102] "When mung beans are sown, rice grows"—this does not exist. The restatement, by way of affirmation, of what was previously stated by way of negation is expressed as follows: "For whatever is the seed... (9.40).
Therefore, a wise and disciplined man, who understands both theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom and desires long life, must never sow his seed in the wife of another. 9.41

Thus, having stated the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). By this [verse], the primacy of the field (*kṣetraprādhānya*) is expressed. But surely, there is no word here that explicitly denotes the primacy of the field; rather, only a prohibition against approaching another’s field is heard: "One must never sow in the wife of another. The meaning of this is simply that the emission of seed (*bījaniṣeka*) into another's wife must not be performed. It does not, however, mean what is stated by the principle "the offspring belongs to the owner of the field" (*yasya kṣetraṃ tasyāpatyam*).

True. Because this [prohibition] forms a single syntactical unit with the statement, "In the same way, a seed sown in another's field perishes" (MDh 9.43), this prohibition is caused by the visible defect characterized by the loss of offspring; it is not a prohibition of sexual intercourse for the sake of some unseen spiritual result (*adṛṣṭa*). For that [latter] has already been refuted in the fourth book by such passages as, "Indeed, there is nothing so detrimental to longevity... (MDh 4.134). Therefore, since the scriptural prohibition is subordinate to something else and forms a single syntactical unit with what follows immediately, it lacks independence; thus, it is logical that its purpose is to establish the primacy of the field (*kṣetra*).

"With a wise person" means with one possessing innate wisdom (*sahajā prajñā*). "Disciplined" means instructed by his father and others. "One who knows knowledge and realization" (*jñānavijñānavedin*): here the words *jñāna* and *vijñāna* function as instrumental nouns. *Jñāna* refers to the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas (*vedāṅga-śāstra*); *vijñāna* refers to the domain of logic (*tarka*) and the arts (*kalā*), and so forth. This is what is meant: he who possesses some degree of intelligence should not act in this manner, for such is the established rule in all the scriptures. As for the fool who resembles an animal, he is simply not qualified for this matter; thus, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*). The phrase "by one desiring long life" is intended to re-identify the prohibition mentioned in the fourth chapter. Consequently, any suspicion that this might be a separate, independent prohibition is dispelled. (9.41)
In this regard, those who know the past recite verses sung by Vāyu:
"Just as a seed should not be sown by a man in what belongs to another. (9.42)

The word *gāthā* denotes a specific type of metrical composition. As Piṅgala has stated: "In this [system], the *gāthā* is that which is not established [by fixed rules]" (*PiṅS* 8.1). Furthermore, verses handed down through tradition that are not subject to dispute are also called *gāthās*. Having said, "Therefore, this sacrificial *gāthā* is sung," *gāthās* are recited later in the Veda as *ślokas*: "That which was his before, that is his after" (*AitB* 14.5). "Proclaimed by Vāyu" means sung or recited by Vāyu. "Those who know the past" refers to those who understand the ancient *kalpas* and other [scriptures]. "In the possession of another" means in the field of another. (9.42)
Just as an arrow, once shot, vanishes from the sight of one who continues to pierce the air where it was struck, so too does seed sown in another's possession quickly perish. 9.43

He now shows these verses: "The arrow, the shaft—it perishes. When one shoots at a deer already pierced by another archer, the ownership of the first shooter [of that animal] ceases here. Or, when an arrow is discharged into the open space of the sky, it perishes—that is, becomes fruitless—without reaching its mark, even for one who shoots at what has already been pierced. In the same way, the seed deposited in the wife of another belongs to that progenitor; the offspring belongs to the owner of the field. (9.43)
Those who know the past understand that even this earth was the wife of Pṛthu;
they say that a field belongs to him who clears away the stumps, and a deer to him who possesses the arrow.

Such is this relationship between husband and wife established by the ancient seers, in that even though they are distinct, they appear as if united. For instance, the Earth, despite having been joined in marriage with him for many thousands of years, is designated by his very name as "Pṛthivī. Therefore, even if a son is born to another man from the wife of someone else, he belongs to that father.

They say that a field belongs to one who has cleared away the stumps, because there is no other relationship [between them]. The genitive case expresses the relationship between owner and owned. A "stump-clearer" (sthāṇuccheda) is one who cuts down where stumps—grown thick with shrubs, bushes, creepers, and so forth—are located. That field belongs to him by whom the ground was made into a field after cutting away the grown shrubs, creepers, and climbing plants. In that case, the fruit arising from plowing and sowing belongs to him alone.

The phrase "they say [the deer belongs to] the one with the arrowhead" is understood to follow here. Among many who are pursuing a deer for the sake of hunting, they say that the deer belongs to him whose arrow-head is seen in the animal. And it has been stated in the verse "the arrow is lost" (MDh 9.43) that he also belongs to the first shooter. 9.44.
"The person is only this much: wife, self, and offspring—so the wise have said; likewise, he who is the husband is remembered as the woman. (9.45)

And it is logical that the offspring belongs to him whose wife she is, because there is indeed oneness between the wife and the husband; for progeny is truly one's own self. How could the self of one person belong to another? Such is the case observed in this world. Even those Brahmins who are learned in the scriptures have spoken in this very way. (9.45)
A wife is not released from her husband by means of sale or abandonment;
thus we know the law established of old by Prajāpati. (9.46)

Now, one might think: "By purchasing them through the gift of wealth and so forth, the wives of others will be made one's own; consequently, when the other's ownership has ceased, the son born of her becomes the son of the biological father."

This is not so; because it is impossible to bring another’s woman into the state of one’s own property even for a thousand gold coins (*niṣka*). Nor does she, having been abandoned by her husband, become the property of the recipient simply by virtue of being relinquished. For, based on the grammatical indication of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the rule “he shall marry” (*udvaheta*, MDh 3.4)—which signifies that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent—a woman consecrated by one man cannot become the wife of another. Just as the *Āhavanīya* and other sacrificial fires do not acquire the designation of *Āhavanīya* through the ritual acts of someone other than their installer. "Sale" (*niṣkrama*) means selling, bartering, or giving away; "relinquishment" (*visarga*) means abandonment. By these two, she is not released [from her status], nor does her status as a wife depart from her. (9.46)
A share of inheritance falls but once; a daughter is given away but once;
one says "I give" but once—these three things happen only once among the virtuous. (9.47)

This has been explained in the eighth section on the rules for latent dispositions (*anuśaya-vidhi*, MDh 8.227). For at the time of partition, those entitled to equal or unequal shares must carry out the division after determining the equal or unequal portions. This [verse] is intended to prohibit anyone who might act in opposition once that division has been made. Even in that case, if one should declare at the outset that some portion was not correctly determined, then there should indeed be a re-partition. However, if after a long time one should claim that the division was improperly performed—by which time the others may have made additions to their respective shares, such as repairs to dilapidated structures, or consumed items such as clothing and gold—then he is empowered only to establish equality, but not to effect a total redistribution of the entire estate.

Others, however, state that the purpose of the rule regarding "once-only" distribution is this: for those such as eunuchs who were previously ineligible for a share, once it is subsequently discovered that they possess eunuchhood or other such conditions which preclude their receiving a share, there is no retroactive withdrawal of the share already given.

Likewise, if those entitled to two, three, or four shares should by chance agree among themselves to an equal division, they would not—should they later regret it—be permitted to withdraw from and overturn that prior arrangement. However, in the case of one who has fallen (patita), I shall explain the forfeiture of the share even if it has already been received.

"A maiden is given only once. Although by this [rule] the ownership of the husband is stated even before the marriage following the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*), nevertheless, upon considering such passages as "one may take back even a maiden who has been given" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.65) and "the completion of those [rites] should be known by the wise to occur at the seventh step" (Manu Smṛti 8.227), it is restricted to a specific case, and that has already been explained. He says, "I give [her] only once. For cows and other such things pass to another in the very same form in which they were one's own property; but a maiden, being one's own as a daughter, is given as a wife while her own relationship [to her father] remains unceased—thus she is mentioned separately.

But surely, as long as the father’s own connection [to the girl] does not cease, how can the giving of the maiden be accomplished? For this is the nature of a gift: that the connection of one ceases while the connection of another arises.

This is not a fault. For here there are two types of relationship: that of offspring and progenitor, and that of owner and owned. Of these, the relationship of offspring and progenitor does not cease, whereas the other does cease. Thus, by stating "in childhood she shall remain under the control of her father" (MDh 5.146), he indicates the non-cessation of the father's ownership here, and by stating "of the one who took her hand" (MDh 5.146), he indicates the arising of that [ownership] for the husband. || 9.47 ||

Just as one who fathers offspring upon cows, mares, camels, female slaves, buffaloes, goats, or sheep does not share in the ownership of those offspring, so it is likewise with the wives of others. 9.48
Those who possess seeds but have no field, who sow them in another's field, never obtain any fruit of the crop that has grown there. (9.49)

This is indeed well known: those who possess the seed but do not own the field—the owners of seeds such as rice—do not obtain the fruit of the crop produced, such as mung beans or black gram, if its growth occurs in another's field. (9.48–49)
If a bull were to sire a hundred calves upon the cows of others, those calves belong only to the owners of the cows; the bull's seed was spent in vain. (9.50)

By the preceding verse, the law regarding stationary things (plants) was declared as well-known or established. By this [verse], it is illustrated in the case of domesticated animals such as cows and the like. Even if another’s bull were to sire many calves upon other cows, the owner of the bull would not receive even a single calf; all those calves belong to the owners of the cows, the *gomin*s. The *ārṣabha*—that which pertains to the bull—is the discharged semen (*skandita*), which is in vain, useless, and fruitless. (9.50)
In the same way, those who possess no field but sow their seed in another's field benefit the owner of the field; the owner of the seed does not obtain the fruit. (9.51)

This is an instruction regarding the former [case]: just as they do with cattle and other such things, and likewise with stationary objects, so too do they act among humans; they accomplish the purpose, the need, and the work of the seed for the owners of the field. (9.51)

But when no agreement regarding the fruit has been made between the owner of the field and the sower, the benefit clearly belongs to the owner of the field; for the womb is more powerful than the seed. (9.52)

It was stated without qualification that the fruit belongs to the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*) and not to the owner of the seed (*bījin*). He states that this refers to a remaining case by the words "without prior agreement" (*anabhisaṃdhāya*). "Agreement" (*abhisaṃdhāna*) is the establishment of a mutual understanding between the owner of the seed and the owner of the field, like the proverb of the lost horse and the burnt chariot: "Let the fruit belong to both of us. Where such a verbal arrangement does not exist, the manifest result—the certain fruit—belongs to the owner of the field alone. By the word "manifest" (*pratyakṣa*), he expresses its indisputable nature. For the womb is more powerful than the seed; the field possesses superior strength. (9.52)
But when there is an agreement,
since the undertaking of the labor is accepted, that which is given for the sake of the seed—
of that, both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field are seen here as sharers. (9.53)

It has been stated that when there is no intention regarding the owner of the field, [the fruit belongs to the owner of the seed]. But when there is such an intention, does it belong to the owner of the seed, or to both? There is this doubt. He says: "To both. The "undertaking of the action" (*kriyāyā abhyupagama*) means its acceptance—namely, the certainty characterized by the conviction, "This is exactly so. Having caused that undertaking to be accepted, whatever is given for the sake of the seed—that is, for the purpose of producing the fruit which is the effect of the seed—it is understood by implication that this refers to the seed. In this case, both are sharers in the result. (9.53)
If seed carried by the force of a flood sprouts in someone's field, that seed belongs to the owner of the field alone; the owner of the seed does not receive the fruit. (9.54)

It has been stated that when seed is sown in another's field, the loss falls upon the sower. In this regard, one might think: "Due to the fault of the man, his taking [the crop] is indeed appropriate; surely he desires to seize the field. Otherwise, why would he sow in another's field? But what is the fault of one who has sown in his own field, if by flood or wind it is carried elsewhere, and he thus loses his own property? To address this, he says: "Seed carried by flood or wind"—*ogha* means a downpour of water; whatever grows in whose field after being carried or led there by that [flood] or by the wind, belongs to him alone. This being already established, the statement "the owner of the seed does not receive the fruit" is for the sake of clarity. The meaning is that in all cases, the field is predominant. (8.54)
This law regarding the offspring of cows, horses, female slaves, camels, goats, sheep, birds, and buffaloes should be understood. (9.55)

Because the context concerns offspring, one might think that this rule applies only to them; therefore, the mention of "cows, horses, and so forth" is made to prevent such a restriction. Alternatively, since the common usage of the terms "seed" and "fruit" is more widely established as referring to crops and the like, he says [the following] to exclude that: "This law applies everywhere—to bipeds, quadrupeds, birds, and immovable things. By the word "this," two things are referred back: when there is no prior agreement, the fruit belongs to the owner of the field; but when there is an agreement, it belongs to both. Furthermore, because the mention of cows, horses, and so forth is intended merely as an illustration, this same principle applies even to dogs, cats, and other such animals.

In that case, for what purpose is it said, "if among other cows" (MDh 9.50)? This is a restatement of a well-known fact: generally, cows belong to men, whereas birds and the like do not. "Dāsīs" refers to those obtained through the seven sources of slaves. "Prasava" means physical birth; the meaning is "with respect to that [birth], in that [place]. (9.55)
Thus has been proclaimed to you the essential and the worthless nature of seed and womb;
hereafter I shall declare the duty of women in times of distress.

"Sāra" means the essential or primary; "phalgu" means the non-essential. "Upasaṃhāra" is the conclusion of the preceding section. The latter half [of the verse] indicates what is to be explained hereafter. "Āpad" refers to the absence of food and clothing that serve as the causes for maintaining life, as well as the interruption of one's lineage. (9.56)
The wife of an elder brother is the teacher’s wife for the younger;
but the wife of the younger brother is considered the daughter-in-law of the elder. (9.57)

With two verses, he restates the established rule regarding ordinary circumstances in order to prescribe *niyoga* (authorization for levirate) in times of distress: "The elder (*jyeṣṭha*) is one born first; the younger (*anuja*) is one born later; the youngest (*kanīyān*) or junior (*yavīyān*) is indeed the younger brother. (9.57)

The elder brother who approaches the wife of the younger, or the younger brother who approaches the wife of the elder—even if they are authorized [to do so]—become outcasts, unless there be a time of distress. (9.58)

In the case of approaching each other's wives, there is loss of caste for the elder and the younger brother respectively when no distress exists, even though a formal authorization (niyoga) may have been granted. (9.58)
When the lineage is on the verge of extinction, a woman who has been duly authorized by her husband or by a sapinda relative may obtain the desired offspring. (9.59)

By this [verse], an injunction distinguished by all its particulars is prescribed: that when the lineage is on the verge of extinction, a woman who has been duly authorized must properly procreate offspring from a brother-in-law or others. What was stated as "the duty of women in times of distress" (MDh 9.56)—this very "distress" refers to the extinction of the lineage. By the word "lineage" (*saṃtāna*), a son is meant, as well as a daughter who is an appointed daughter (*putrikā*); for she alone continues the father's line, and no other. Its "extinction" means non-production, the loss of one already born, or the failure to appoint an appointed daughter. For we shall explain that a woman alone has no authority over an appointed daughter or any other substitute for a son. "Authorized" means permitted by her elders; she should procreate [offspring].

How much more so, then, for "elders" (*gurubhiḥ*)? This is because of the illustration provided by another *smṛti* text; or else, it follows from the word "commission" (*niyoga*) itself. For in common usage, "commission" is said to be connected with elders (*guru*). Indeed, one does not say that a person is teaching "because he has been commissioned by a student. Rather, one says that a person "acts or recites because he has been commissioned by his teacher" (*ācārya*). Furthermore, "elders" should be understood as those belonging to the husband’s lineage, such as the mother-in-law, father-in-law, brother-in-law, and so forth, and not [one's own] father and others. By this, they are called "those who possess offspring" through that offspring, and they are those to whom the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) performed by that offspring provide benefit.

If this is so, then since the maternal grandfather also has a benefit derived from the daughter’s son, it would follow that the father should appoint his daughter [to another man]. It has been stated [in response]: "He by whom they are called 'those who possess offspring' [is the one to appoint]. By the mention of the *devara* (husband's younger brother) and the *sapiṇḍa*, those belonging to the same lineage (*gotra*) come to mind. Furthermore, in various places in the *Mahābhārata*, the status of the appointing authority is shown to belong exclusively to those on the husband's side. For this very reason, when a brother's son exists, the practice of *niyoga* (appointment) must not be performed.

For those who are appointed, it is only their own continuum that is benefited. When affection is produced toward a son, they are authorized while seeking the benefit of the offspring; there is no authorization for one who is dead. How then is he designated as "his offspring"?

In some way, he benefits [the deceased] through the offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*). We say this "by virtue of the word" (*vacanāt*); for although the injunction "one must produce offspring" was not performed by him, nevertheless, the meaning of the scripture is that the offering of the *piṇḍa* and so forth must be performed by one born through the injunction of *niyoga* upon his field (*kṣetra*). Thus, it is understood that he is a benefactor. We shall explain how this is so in detail further on.

The *devara* is the husband’s brother. A *sapiṇḍa* is one belonging to the husband’s lineage; that same [rule applies] to the woman as well. By the statement in another *Smṛti*, "and from [a man] of the same caste," it is implied. The word "properly" (*samyak*) reiterates the rule to be mentioned later regarding being smeared with ghee and so forth. In the injunction, the suffix *-kṛtya* indicates that the desired offspring (*īpsitā prajā*) is to be obtained. By the word "desired" (*īpsita*), he expresses fitness for the task. Therefore, if a daughter is born, or if [the son] is blind, deaf, or otherwise [deficient], the *niyoga* (authorization for procreation) must be performed again. 9.59.
But one appointed to a widow, being anointed with clarified butter and remaining silent, may procreate a single son during the night; he must by no means procreate a second.

The mention of a "widow" (*vidhavā*) is not restrictive. This same rule applies even when the husband is living, provided he is impotent (*klība*) or otherwise incapable; for the author will state later: "Those two who, having been appointed [to procreate], deviate from the rule" (MDh 9.63). This is precisely its purpose. Here, the restriction concerns the objects [of the act], not the rules themselves; otherwise, if it were understood differently, these would apply only to the widow, as they are not the subject under discussion. This is intended to exclude the use of lamps and other such light sources at night, since intercourse during the day is prohibited by another scriptural injunction.

But others say: "That prohibition concerns the purpose of man, whereas this [rule] concerns the purpose of the ritual act. Therefore, by traveling during the day, one may procreate a son born in the field; one may procreate one son, but not a second. (9.60)
The counter-exception to this is as follows:

"Some who know the truth regarding women consider a second procreation [permissible], seeing that the purpose of the *niyoga* (levirate union) between those two has not yet been fulfilled according to the law. (9.61)

The opinion of some is that there should be a second son. Those who know this—those who understand the rules for the procreation of a *kṣetraja* son—perceive that the purpose of the appointment (*niyoga*) has not been fulfilled. They consider that the injunction "a child must be procreated by the appointed woman" is not fully accomplished by the procreation of only one [son]. They hold that the singular number [in the injunction] is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). What is their intention? They hold that the singular number is not intended to be significant because the action is primarily concerned with the substance [the offspring], and thus the singular number is subordinate (*guṇabhāva*), just like the singularity of the cup (*graha*) in the ritual.

But surely, even when there is an instruction regarding something not [otherwise] acquired (*anupāttopadeśa*), and although the predominance of the substance is understood through the accusative case, the intention to express a specific number and so forth remains established. For instance, in the injunction regarding offspring, "A twice-born man should marry a wife" (*udvaheta dvijo bhāryām*, MDh 3.4), there is a departure from the singular number due to the gender [of the word *bhāryām*], as in "Place ten sons in her" (*daśāsyāṃ putrān ādhehi*, RV 9.10.7).

If this were so, there would not be a restriction to exactly two [sons]. It is precisely with this doubt in mind that the word "second" is used for the purpose of excluding others. Its meaningfulness also has this intention: in the case of the *aurasa* (legitimate son), the indicative mark is found in the section on marriage due to the recitation of the mantra; however, here there is a departure from the number one, based on the traditional saying of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) that "one who has no son is one who has only one son. Alternatively, it may be understood as a praise of the second son according to this very Smṛti. This is by virtue of Dharma and the conduct of the learned. (9.61)
But when the purpose of the appointment regarding the widow has been fulfilled according to the rule, the two should behave toward each other like a father-in-law and a daughter-in-law. (9.62)

But here, the subject of the injunction is that to which one is enjoined; and that [act], characterized by approaching [the woman], culminates in sexual union and physical contact. When that has ceased, the previous conduct applies: as toward a teacher, so toward a daughter-in-law. Regarding the wife of an elder brother, it is as toward a teacher for the younger; regarding the younger brother's wife, it is as toward a daughter-in-law for the elder. Because of the mutual reference, a woman should behave toward an elder man as toward a daughter-in-law, and a man toward an elder brother’s wife as toward a teacher. (9.62)

If those two, being appointed, should act according to their own will by disregarding the prescribed rule, both would become outcasts, like one who violates his daughter-in-law or one who violates the bed of his teacher. 9.63.

The rule [is] beginning with "anointed with clarified butter" (MDh 9.60). In the transgression of that, there is loss of caste. The elder brother who is appointed, the man who has intercourse with his daughter-in-law, and the younger brother who has intercourse with his elder's wife [are all] violators of the Guru’s bed. 9.63.
A widow must not be appointed to another [husband] by the twice-born;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal dharma. (9.64)
This is a prohibition of the appointment (niyoga) previously ordained.

Regarding this, some maintain that because of the mention of the "widow," the prohibition applies to one whose husband is dead; however, since there is an injunction stating that she "should be appointed by a husband who is impotent," they conclude that the injunction and the prohibition have distinct scopes.

Others, however, argue that since the injunction for the rite mentions the cessation of the lineage as its cause, and such cessation can occur even when a man is impotent, diseased, or deceased; thus, the prohibition is no different from the injunction. A woman whose connection with her husband has departed is called a "widow" (*vidhavā*); this condition is identical in both cases.

This must necessarily be understood in this way; otherwise, even the rule regarding being anointed with ghee and so forth would not apply to a woman who is appointed by a eunuch. For they likewise prescribe in that case: "And one appointed to a widow shall be anointed with ghee" (MDh 9.60). Therefore, since there is no distinction in what is enjoined, the prohibition is also without distinction. Consequently, when the scope of both injunction and prohibition is equal, there is an option (*vikalpa*). And this mandatory injunction for procreating offspring is indeed subject to option, like the taking or not taking of the *Soma* cup.

But when there is an injunction for the production of a result, such as "one conquers through a son" (MDh 9.137), then, since in the absence of offspring there is no performance of that duty—the benefit pertaining to the afterlife—how could there be an option between two distinct results? An injunction and a prohibition are optionally combined when they have the same scope and refer to a single purpose; as some say, this is the case regarding the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśī* cup.

It has been stated that when there is an abundance of auxiliary factors (*aṅga*), there is an abundance of the result; however, regarding the accomplishment of the primary purpose (*pradhānakārya*), there is no distinction. Therefore, according to this view, he states the absence of benefit to the son. If one engages in this [rite] for the sake of a specific benefit, then by transgressing the prohibition, it is equivalent to the Śyena sacrifice.

This, however, must be examined here: why does he who is appointed proceed [to act]? For there is no injunction for him stating, "One who is appointed must go. But for the woman, such an injunction exists: "By a woman who has been properly appointed" (MDh 9.59). Nor can it be said that the meaning is that the fulfillment of the *niyoga* occurs when the brother-in-law and others proceed [to act], because their own engagement is due to passion (*rāga*), as it is stated: "The son born of the field (*kṣetraja*) is desired through that injunction" (referring to the husband's appointment). If it is argued that the prescription of rules such as being smeared with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) would be purposeless since the engagement arises from passion, we say: it is not purposeless; for when [the son] is produced according to those specific rules, he receives the designation of *kṣetraja*, and not otherwise.

Furthermore, as for those who say that the injunction "one must do what the teacher says" is the basis for engaging in action: if this were so, it would follow that one might engage in drinking liquor and similar acts simply by the teacher's desire. And such a person is not a true teacher who incites one to what ought not to be done, for even a teacher may be arrogant and ignorant of what is right and what is wrong.
The abandonment of one who has set out upon a wrong path is ordained.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti; and "abandonment" means desisting from the duties of one's teacher.

By this, the following is also refuted: the statement regarding the fall from caste (*pātitya*) due to the violation of a rule implies that he is authorized to live according to the rule, namely, "those two would both be fallen" (MDh 9.63). Otherwise, if one were to incur fall from caste in every manner of intercourse, then a specific fall from caste would be untenable; for that [fall] is not heard of for the man alone, but rather for the woman. And for her, who desires a son, *niyoga* is ordained. It is with reference to that [act of *niyoga*] that the statement of falling occurs upon transgression: "those two would both be fallen" (MDh 9.63). In the absence of transgression, the man alone is fallen; but upon transgression, both are so—it is thus clearly established by the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Therefore, it must be explained how activity characterized by the injunctions regarding the divine king and so forth [is possible].

It is said: Just as there is an expectation of the elders' formal authorization (*guruniyoga*) for the sapindas when offering the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to a deceased relative—as seen in the case of Vyāsa and others—so too, there is an expectation of such authorization for the production of a *kṣetraja* son. Therefore, it must be understood that there is no lapse (*cyuti*) in approaching [the brother-in-law] under those circumstances. Indeed, it is not reasonable to admit that great souls engage in action characterized by passion (*rāga*). As for the argument that the scriptural statement regarding one’s fallen status (*patitatva*) upon violating a rule serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*), that is incorrect; for if the man were fallen, he would lack the qualification to procreate, and thus the act of producing a son would be purposeless. Therefore, this is merely a semblance (*ābhāsa*) of the injunction concerning the brother-in-law and others. (9.64)
Nowhere in the mantras pertaining to marriage is the practice of *niyoga* (appointment) mentioned;
nor is the remarriage of a widow prescribed in the rules for wedding ceremonies. (9.65)

The rite of marriage (*udvāhana-karma*) involves the recitation of mantras such as: “The maidens have worshipped the god Aryaman and Agni” (ĀśG 1.7.13), as well as other related ones like “With me as husband, may you reach old age” (RV 10.85.36) and “With me as husband, may you be blessed with offspring” (AV 14.1.52). Regarding these, they say that in every case the child belongs to the one who carries her away, the suitor. It is nowhere heard there [in the marriage rites] that “wherever you are appointed by me, from there procreate. By mentioning the mantras, he shows this; even the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) of the mantras are not of such a nature. He demonstrates this even more clearly: “The remarriage of a widow is not mentioned in the rules for marriage. Here, “remarriage” (*āvedana*) is intended to mean “approaching” (*gamana*). Now, if she were joined in marriage itself—such that the brother-in-law would marry the wife of his brother—then this appointment (*niyoga*) would indeed be prescribed by the marriage rite. But here, there is no marriage rite at all. This explanatory passage is a supplement to what preceded. (9.65)
This practice, condemned as the law of beasts by the ignorant twice-born, was declared even for human beings while Vena was ruling the kingdom. (9.66)

This too is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) supplementary to the prohibition of the injunction. Those who are ignorant and do not correctly understand the scripture—those practitioners who do not recognize that the injunctive suffixes (*liṅga*) and so forth have another purpose—they [performed] that which is the "beastly practice" (*paśudharma*), which is utterly censured even for humans; they proclaimed and set it in motion. That [practice] is of recent origin, not beginningless; it occurred while King Vena was ruling and protecting the kingdom. But has it not been stated that there are no such indicative marks (*liṅga*) at all?

This is not so; for it has been stated that [such practices] do not exist in the marriage mantras (*udvāhaka-mantra*). However, they are seen elsewhere, as in: “Who, like a widow, makes you two her co-habiting companions in the bed, as a woman makes a mortal her husband? (RV 10.40.2), and so forth. Just as a widow makes a brother-in-law her husband and shares the same bed with him, who makes the two [deities] mindful so that they do not depart? What is the distinction regarding the marriage mantras? The intention is that they indeed follow the sequence of the rules for the procreation of offspring.

Other scholars read "by others" (*anyaiḥ*). It is said to be censured by men; this practice called "approaching the wife of a brother" is the law for animals, and it prevailed in the kingdom of Vena. (9.66)
In former times, while ruling over the entire earth, that most excellent of royal sages,
his mind overwhelmed by desire, brought about the intermixture of the social orders.

"Eating" means protecting. But how can he, while causing the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), be considered the foremost of royal sages (*rājarṣi*)? It has been said [in verse 176]: "He who enjoys the entire earth does so by virtue of being a great king (*mahārāja*). He is one whose consciousness—the stability of the mind—is afflicted and destroyed by desire, characterized by passion and the like. (9.67)
From that time forward, the virtuous censure any man who, out of delusion, employs a woman whose husband has died for the sake of offspring. (9.68)
The explanatory passage (arthavāda) has a clear meaning. || 9.68 ||
If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made true,
her own brother-in-law shall wed her according to this procedure.

Because it takes the form of a formal commission (*niyoga*), this practice is said to pertain to a maiden. When the verbal betrothal has been made true—that is, when the verbal gift has been completed, she has been given by one man and accepted by the other—her own brother-in-law (*devara*) shall, according to the procedure to be described hereafter, take her for himself; that is, he shall marry her. (9.69)
Having approached her according to the rule—she who is clad in white garments and pure in her vows—he shall enjoy her in private once at each menstrual period until she gives birth. (9.70)

"In accordance with the rule and the scripture": he should marry her according to the rite for marriage (*vaivāhya vidhi*). This marriage is based solely on verbal declaration (*vācanika*); thus she is called a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman). Or rather, even though she has been wedded, she does not become a wife; the verbal marriage performed for her sake is merely for the benefit of another. And so it is shown: "Having given a daughter to one man, she is not to be given again to another" (MDh 9.71). The meaning is that she is not to be given to the husband's brother (*devara*). How indeed could she, being ungiven and not his own property, become a wife? [The verse continues: "She who wears white garments"—this is the rule regarding sexual intercourse; this same duty is intended even in the case of another form of appointment (*niyoga*). (9.70)
A wise man, having given his daughter to one, should not give her again to another;
for by giving her once more after she has been given, he incurs the sin of lying regarding a human being. 9.71.

"Their marriage is to be understood by the wise as finalized at the seventh step" (MDh 8.227). This is a prohibition against the apprehension that even a woman who has been given [in marriage] might be given again if the groom dies before the wedding; however, this specific statement is made regarding a particular case, for such a woman is called a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman). One should not give her to another after having already given her to one man; doing so incurs the sin of falsehood regarding a person—the same sin that exists in the abduction of a human being falls upon him. (9.71)
Even after accepting her according to the prescribed rites, one may abandon a bride who is blameworthy, diseased, corrupted, or one who was presented through deception. (9.72)

*Vidhi* is the sacred scripture (*śāstra*); that which is worthy of it is *vidhivat*. Such is the rule prescribed by the scripture: "For the foremost of the twice-born, [the marriage] is with water alone" (MDh 3.35). And regarding this, some record in their tradition (*smṛti*) that there is an authorization for water in the case of a maiden. Therefore, even after having accepted her, one may abandon the maiden before the wedding. One should abandon her if she is censured, possessed of ill-omens, or if she was previously accepted but remains a virgin (*akṣatayoni*); likewise, one should abandon her if she is shameless, speaks excessively to many men, is diseased—specifically afflicted by consumption (*kṣaya*), or is corrupted (*vipraduṣṭā*), meaning she is designated as being sickly and so forth, and whose affection is fixed on another.

Others explain [the term] *kṣatayoni* as "one who is corrupted. They do not think correctly. If a woman who has not been enjoyed by a man is a maiden (*kanyā*) and remains unaltered, then she is certainly not corrupted. But if she has been united with a man, then she is no longer a maiden at all. In that case, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "one should abandon the maiden" would be untenable; yet her abandonment has indeed been stated. Furthermore: "She who is presented through deception, or one who has deficient or redundant limbs, or one who was assigned for a specific purpose—even if she has already accepted the groom, she must be abandoned if even minor defects were not disclosed. (9.72)
