But if one should bestow a daughter who has defects without having disclosed them, he shall render void that gift of the evil-minded giver of the girl. (9.73)

The defects of a maiden have been described. If one gives her away—that is, bestows her—without having declared or mentioned them, that gift shall be rendered void and fruitless by her being returned. This very point, already stated, has been made perfectly clear by the preceding verse. (9.73)
A man who has business abroad should depart after providing for his wife's maintenance;
for a woman, even one of steadfast character, may fall into corruption when distressed by a lack of livelihood. (9.74)

When he is about to go abroad, he should provide for his wife’s maintenance before departing; this is how the injunction “having provided” (*vidhāya*) is to be understood: “While going abroad, he should provide for his wife’s maintenance. He should act in such a way that she has maintenance for as long as his absence lasts—namely, food, clothing, household utensils, and so forth, which are the means for sustaining the body. Having provided that, he may depart from his own country to another land. He should be motivated by a purpose (*kāryavān*), whether that purpose pertains to human goals seen in this world or unseen in the next; the unseen is *dharma*, while the seen consists of wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*). As he will state later: “One who has gone abroad for the sake of religious duty,” etc. (MDh 9.76). Apart from these specific causes, traveling abroad while abandoning one’s wife is forbidden. The statement that she would be “emaciated by lack of maintenance” is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) intended to demonstrate the visible fault. Emaciated and afflicted by poverty due to lack of resources, she might become corrupt through contact with other men and the like. Even if she possesses stability—that is, if she is endowed with the conduct of her family—she might, when distressed by hunger, incur blame by taking up residence with another husband; this is what is being considered here. The optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of possibility. 9.74.
If her husband has gone abroad after providing for her maintenance, she should live adhering to her prescribed rules;
but if he has gone abroad without providing for her, she should live by means of irreproachable crafts.

The rule is as follows: just as when the husband is present there is a prohibition against traveling abroad or leaving the household, so too when he has gone away on a journey, she remains steadfast and maintains her composure. However, if he has gone away and she cannot maintain herself [by his means], she may live by crafts such as spinning or making nets. "Despised articles" refers to fans and the like. This indeed is the means of livelihood for widows and others, produced by their own labor. (9.75)
A man who has gone abroad for the sake of dharma should be waited for eight years;
if for the sake of learning or fame, six years; but if for the sake of pleasure, three years. (9.76)

Regarding what was stated, "One who has business may travel abroad" (MDh 9.74), he now demonstrates those specific duties; for it is by their particular nature that the distinctions in the duration of waiting are determined. However, it was not explicitly stated there that "after this [period], she must do this.
On this point, some say: based on the context, it refers to "she shall live by blameless means" (MDh 9.75).

That is incorrect. Why should she die before this time [of her husband's death] "without reproach"? For suicide is not permitted for her, as it is forbidden for women just as it is for men. Therefore, even before this rule regarding waiting, she who cannot subsist by blameless crafts may live by reprehensible ones. Others, however, maintain that this refers to adultery; and thus it is said in another Smṛti: "When the husband has disappeared, died, renounced the world, is impotent, or has become an outcast..."
In five calamities, another husband is ordained for women. (NSm 12.97)

Others also say: her religious studenthood (*brahmacarya*) can never be taken away. For even Manu has ordained that among the duties of women this is prescribed for her: "But when her husband is dead, she should not even utter the name of another" (MDh 5.155). When the husband is dead, there is no transgression; how much less so when he is merely away on a journey? Indeed, the word *pati* is based on the act of protecting, as in "lord of the village" or "lord of the army. Therefore, by this statement, she would not be dependent upon her husband; rather, for the sake of her own livelihood, she might resort to another through such work as serving as a *sairandhrī*. And when she has been supported for six months or a year by someone who has taken her in, if the husband should arrive and be able to bring her under his control, saying, "Leave your wife," then until the time is complete, she belongs to the husband alone; the rest has been chewed over in the fifth [chapter].
Others also state this point;

however, the ancients maintain that there is remarriage (*punarbhū-vṛtta*). A woman who has been abandoned by her husband, or whose husband does not return for such a long time because his livelihood was withheld, is considered as good as abandoned by him. Consequently, if she were married to another according to the law of remarriage, then when the [original] husband returns, he should say nothing such as, "This is the wife of my remarried brother-in-law.
That is incorrect. We shall demonstrate the meaningfulness of that verse [from Manu]: "Not by sale or abandonment" (MDh 9.46).
Dharma and its effect constitute "dharmakārya" (the business of dharma). Since that is the purpose or objective of the journey, it is "for the sake of dharmakārya."

Why? Because for a householder, a long-term journey is not consistent with his religious duties (*dharma*). For he must necessarily tend to the sacred fires (*agni*) and perform the five great sacrifices (*pāñcayajñika*). How could he go away when it is prescribed that "one should sacrifice with the *Jyotiṣṭoma* every spring"? Even ritual baths at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and other such acts prescribed by the *Smṛtis* must be performed provided they do not conflict with the *Śruti*. Nor does the rule apply to one who has made arrangements before departing, as it is said: "Even having made arrangements, one may travel until the next full-moon festival (*parvan*)," and "One should personally offer the oblation on the *parvan*, or [arrange for] the priests to do so at one of the two times. Although the five sacrifices are equal to the pilgrimage in being *smārta* duties for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), since it is appropriate for him to go accompanied by his wife, it is not proper to go to a sacred ford by abandoning her.

It is said: by the word of a teacher—that which one is sent by teachers for the sake of dharma, whether to serve a king or for one's own business, is travel for the sake of dharma; or it is expiation through wandering in regions such as penance groves.
Alternatively, it is intended for the sake of performing a religious duty even while seeking wealth, thinking: "I am poor; I shall acquire wealth from somewhere. Or it is for the sake of learning.

But surely, the acquisition of a wife occurs after one has bathed, and the bath occurs after one has completed one's studies. In that case, how can there be a desire for knowledge on the part of one who has already married?
This has already been shown: one who has slightly understood the meaning of the Vedas is qualified for marriage, while the bath and other rites are performed once [the meaning] is ascertained.
This is not correct; for the bath occurs when the inquiry into Dharma is completed, and that inquiry results in an ascertained meaning through the removal of doubt preceded by investigation.

True. This is not an injunction for the sake of seeking knowledge. For if that were the case, it would already be understood by the phrase "for the sake of performing dharma. Even when the understanding necessary for one's qualification has arisen, this [study] is for the sake of excellence in practice and for the sake of distinction in other branches of knowledge; for the sake of quickly proclaiming valor and fame; and for the sake of proclaiming one's status as a distinguished scholar abroad. Traveling to another country is a cause for fame.

For the sake of desire, one may follow the practice of those who live by their beauty in order to marry a more desirable wife. Regarding the timing, a difference in period is recorded in another Smṛti according to the number of children born: likewise Viṣṇu states, "Eight for a Brāhmaṇa, six for a Kṣatriya, four for a Vaiśya, and double that for one who has borne [children]. "There should be no fixed rule regarding time for a Śūdra woman; some say it is one year. (9.76)
A husband should wait for one year for a wife who hates him;
but after a year has passed, he may take back her property and no longer cohabit with her. (9.77)

"She who hates her husband" refers to one who is hostile toward him; however, on this account, he should not carry out her expulsion. This is because the accusative case in the word *enām* is incompatible with the verb *vas* preceded by the prefix *sam-*, which would require the form *vāsayet*—meaning he should "restrain" or "threaten" her. Even in the case of a grave sin (*pātaka*), there is no expulsion for her, according to the injunction: "He should confine her in a single room" (MDh 11.175). Even when this cause necessitates penance, the "removal" intended is for the purpose of instilling discipline; it is not a total and absolute deprivation of everything. (9.77)
She who transgresses against one who is negligent, intoxicated, or afflicted by disease shall be abandoned for three months, deprived of her ornaments and belongings.

Transgression consists in showing contempt for her service and a lack of devotion toward what is beneficial, such as medicine and the like; it does not consist in consorting with another man. Furthermore, there must be an abandonment of sexual union for three months for the very same reason stated previously. She should be deprived of ornaments such as necklaces and bracelets, as well as of her personal belongings, such as household vessels and utensils, or even her male and female servants. (9.78)

There is no abandonment of one who is insane, fallen [from caste], impotent, seedless, or afflicted by a foul disease; nor is there any revocation of the inheritance for a wife who shows hostility. 9.79

The words *klība* (impotent) and *abīja* (seedless) denote a neuter person (*napuṃsaka*). However, there is a distinction: one is one whose semen is wind-like (*vātaretas*), while the other is one whose organs are inactive. There is no punishment for one who hates such a person, as previously stated. "Substitution" (*apavartana*) means taking away; [the consumption of] food brought by one who is away on a journey or one who is forbidden, and so forth, are prohibited by other Smṛti texts. 9.79.
A woman who drinks liquor, is untruthful in conduct, or is repulsive; one who is diseased, or who is violent and always wasteful of wealth—such a woman may indeed be superseded. 9.80.

A woman who drinks liquor is one who delights in drinking intoxicants; because she is incapable of performing the duties of the household, such as cooking and maintaining the domestic order, she deserves to be superseded by another wife. However, for her whose drinking of liquor has been forbidden by her elders, the author will prescribe a punishment in the verse: "If she should drink [liquor] despite the prohibition" (MDh 9.84). In the case of one who violates a self-imposed vow, it is appropriate that she be restored through penance—just as in the case of violating a vow imposed by another—and there may also be a second marriage. Thus, the grounds for supersession are enumerated as being caused by the impairment of religious duties, the failure to produce offspring, and the neglect of household affairs, in the words: "one who is hostile, diseased, or wasteful" (MDh 9.79). As for a Brāhmaṇa woman who is prohibited from drinking liquor by the scriptures, there is merely the penance for drinking it if she does so again after desisting; however, there is no loss of caste (*pātitya*) for drinking liquor, because the loss of caste is specifically enumerated in the rule: "A woman falls [from her caste] by killing an embryo or by serving a low-caste man" (GDh 21.9). This we shall explain in the eleventh book. And it has been stated in the fifth book (MDh 5.89):

Untruthful in conduct and of improper behavior, she speaks harsh and false words to her servants; she eats even before the performance of the *balikarma* offerings; and she lacks faith in the feeding of Brahmins during rites for the gods (*daiva*) and ancestors (*pitrya*). Wasteful and habitually extravagant, she does not protect the household utensils and furniture, but purchases them at high prices. Cruel, she has a tendency to beat her servants and others excessively out of mere suspicion. She embezzles the daily expenses. *Adhivedana* refers to marrying another woman on top of her. (9.80)
He states that supersession may apply to other wives as well:

"A barren wife may be superseded in the eighth year; one whose children have died, in the tenth; one who gives birth only to daughters, in the eleventh; but one who speaks unpleasantly may be superseded immediately. (9.81)

In that regard, a barren wife should be superseded in the eighth year, but one whose children have died in the tenth. For there would be no justification for superseding a barren wife, as she lacks the capacity to produce offspring, which would result in the failure of the performance of the injunctions regarding the procreation of offspring and the injunction for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*). Indeed, the establishment of the fires is not prescribed for one who has no son; the same applies to a woman who bears only daughters and whose children have died. However, in the case of a wife who speaks unpleasantly, there is no supersession because there is no fault [on her part]; this rule applies only when there is no forbearance. (9.81)
But she who is sickly, yet beneficial and endowed with virtuous conduct—she may be superseded after having been informed, but she must never be treated with contempt. (9.82)

Devoted to her husband and intent on his service, she is here subject to the rules regarding both seeking permission and being disregarded, because these conditions apply to the aforementioned [wives]. The mention of the "sick woman" implies the barren wife and the wife who has given birth to daughters as well. Since there is no difference in their status as wives and since there is no cause for actual contempt, "disregard" (avamānana) refers only to occasional instances—such as verbal reprimands and the like—for the purpose of instruction. (9.82)
But a woman who, having been given in marriage, should depart from the house in anger, she must be restrained immediately or abandoned in the presence of the family. (9.83)

For a woman who has departed due to anger as the cause for her dissatisfaction, abandonment (*tyāga*) and confinement (*saṃnirodha*) are prescribed according to the circumstances. However, this is not by means of food, clothing, and so forth, which arise from whatever is available; rather, it is the removal of anger through affection on that occasion, or being rebuked by the mother-in-law, father-in-law, and others. Confinement is the supervision by guards. Abandonment has been explained: it is non-intimacy and the avoidance of sharing a bed. "Family" refers to kinsmen, namely those on her father's side and those on her own side. (9.83)
But she who, despite a prohibition, drinks liquor even on festive occasions, or goes to a theatrical performance or a social assembly, shall be fined six *kṛṣṇalas*. (9.84)

Regarding the prohibition [of drinking] by those related to the teacher: this punishment applies to women of the Kṣatriya and other castes; it is not scripturally prescribed for Brāhmaṇa women. For in their case, there is no release through mere punishment, but rather through a great one. Furthermore, in their case, there is no suspicion of drinking during festive occasions (*abhyudaya*). Indeed, among those for whom wine is not prohibited, a zealous engagement in drinking is observed whenever they have gathered for festivals as a matter of rule. It is precisely this that the text prohibits even during festive occasions. And this punishment is to be inflicted by the husband; for even though the king has the duty of governing, it is understood that "the husband is the master of his wives. Other masters as well possess independence regarding a certain degree of punishment over their dependents, such as servants. Festive occasions (*abhyudaya*) refer to celebrations such as the birth of a son or a marriage. *Prekṣā* refers to witnessing performances by actors and the like. *Samāja* refers to a gathering of people, even a very large crowd. This punishment applies to a woman who is curious about such events. (9.84)
If twice-born men should marry women both of their own class and of other classes, seniority, honor, and the right to the household shall belong to them according to the order of their castes. (9.85)

If women who have married out of desire—whether they be of the same caste or of different castes—should obtain husbands and marry them, their seniority shall be determined by the order of their castes and in accordance with their birth, not by age nor by the order of marriage. Regarding honor on the occasion of offering fruits and other gifts, the sequence of castes is as follows: first for the Brāhmaṇī, then for the Kṣatriyā and the Vaiśyā. As for the principal house, that belongs to the Brāhmaṇī; thus, among women of the same caste, the order of marriage is declared to be the determining factor. (MDh 9.85)
The wife alone, and no one of a different caste under any circumstances, shall perform the service to her husband’s body and the daily religious duties for all [the deceased]. (9.86)

The wife herself shall perform the service of the husband’s body, characterized by cooking and other such necessary tasks, as well as giving gifts, feeding him, and attending to him while he sleeps. However, there is no fixed rule regarding the massaging of his back and feet, washing them, and so forth. When they are both present at the same time, the sequence of these bodily services follows the order of their castes. The daily religious duties (*naiṣṭhika-dharmakārya*) consist of the evening meal offering (*sāyam-anna*), as prescribed in MDh 3.111 and elsewhere, as well as smearing the fire-sanctuary, sipping water (*ācamana*), and the offering of water-libations (*tarpaṇa*). || 9.86 ||
This is a declamatory statement (arthavāda) of censure:

"But he who, out of delusion, causes [the rite] to be performed by another woman of his own caste who is already established [in the household], is just like a 'Brāhmaṇa-Cāṇḍāla' as seen before. (9.87)

But he who causes this rite to be performed by another woman of a different caste while a woman of the same caste is available—he, though a Brāhmaṇa, is considered a Caṇḍāla on account of his former [conduct]. (9.87)
To one who is distinguished, handsome, excellent, and worthy, he should give his daughter according to the prescribed rite, even if she has not yet reached marriageable age. (9.88)

In the phrase *utkṛṣṭāyābhirūpāya*, there is a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). The meaning is: "to one who is excellent and more handsome. Alternatively, *utkṛṣṭāya* and *abhirūpāya* are separate qualifiers: "to one who is excellent by virtue of birth and so forth, and handsome. One who has attained beauty (*rūpa*) or form (*ākṛti*) directly is *abhirūpa*. Or, it may denote natural disposition; even a learned man of good character is called *abhirūpa*. "Equal" means equal in birth and so forth. A *vara* is a husband or son-in-law. Even though she has not yet reached [marriageable age], or is unfit, because she is under the power of desire, she is a girl who has not yet reached the age of youth; in another Smṛti, she is called a *nagnikā* (VaDh 17.70). She is one in whom desire—that is, longing—has not arisen, being eight or six years old, but not an absolute infant. For such is the indicative mark (*liṅga*): "an eight-year-old" (MDh 9.94).

This very same indicative mark [of passion] applies even to a marriage entered into for the sake of religious duty (*dharma*). Otherwise, if passion alone were the motivating factor, they ask: "How could there be a marriage with one who has not yet reached puberty? That is incorrect; for even those seeking wealth marry a young girl. Not every motivation is strictly ritualistic, as was established in the third chapter [of this work]. (9.88)
A maiden, even if she has reached puberty, may remain in her father's house at his pleasure until death;
yet he must never give her in marriage to one who is devoid of good qualities. (9.89)

The giving away of a maiden should take place before her first menses. Even if her menses have appeared, one should not give her away until a qualified groom has been obtained. "Qualification" consists of excellence in learning and valor, a handsome appearance, being endowed with a mature age, avoidance of what is forbidden by worldly custom and scripture, affection for the maiden, and so forth. (9.89)
A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years;
but after this period, she may seek a suitable husband. (9.90)

"Seminal fluid" refers to the period of fertility; even when she possesses it, he should remain in her house for three years. Beyond that, in the absence of a superior [suitor], he should himself choose a suitable match of the same caste. (9.90)
If she should obtain a husband of her own accord when one is not being given to her, she incurs no guilt whatsoever, nor does he whom she obtains. (9.91)

After three years have passed, there is no fault on the part of the husband whom she chooses if he does not give her away; since the absence of fault for the maiden was already stated by the preceding rule, this [verse] is intended to address the fault of the one being chosen. And it is recorded in the Smṛti that the appearance of the menses occurs at twelve years of age. (9.91)

A maiden choosing her own husband shall not take for herself any ornament belonging to her father, nor that which belongs to her mother, nor that given by her brother; if she should take it, she would be a thief. (9.92)

If the ornaments were given at the outset by her brothers and others with the intention that she would choose him herself, but they did so without her knowledge, he should return those ornaments to them alone. However, if they give them to her while she is already of such a disposition (i.e., already betrothed), then there is no forfeiture. Therefore, it is not right for the ornament to undergo a change of ownership when the situation has become otherwise—namely, when their intention was, "We will not give her to him. There is an alternative reading in the masculine gender, *stenaḥ syāt* ("he would be a thief"), by which they say the groom becomes a thief; therefore, he must have the ornament taken away from him. 9.92.
One who takes away a girl who has reached puberty should not pay a bride-price to her father;
for by obstructing her menses, he would be overstepping his authority as master. (9.93)

This is the prohibition of the bride-price (*śulka*) for a girl who has reached puberty and for whom a price was to be paid. And that [prohibition] would override ownership (*svāmya*). It has been stated: "In childhood, she shall remain under the control of her father" (MDh 5.146). Upon reaching another stage of life, the father’s ownership ceases because he does not take [the bride-price]. Since the reason applies equally even to a girl for whom no price is to be paid, the father’s ownership is terminated. Departure is the cessation [of authority]; obstruction is the hindering of the purpose of procreating offspring. Some say this verse is non-human (divine). 9.93.
A thirty-year-old man should marry a charming twelve-year-old girl; or one of twenty-four years may marry an eight-year-old, for he who is quick to act perishes in his duty. (9.94)

The meaning of the instruction is that a girl should be married after such a period of time has elapsed as to make her younger [than the groom], and not that marriage must take place at exactly this specific age. Furthermore, the number of years is not to be taken literally as heard in the text. What then? She should be married after a long period of time so that she is younger. For this is not heard in the context of the marriage ritual itself, which would—by being a qualification of the person to be consecrated—exclude that time [of ten years or twenty-five years] as a subordinate element of the rite. But surely, even that which resides in another sentence can indeed be an injunction regarding a subordinate element.

True; here, due to the excellence of the context and its placement in the text, another intention of the Teacher is inferred. Likewise, there is the practice of the learned. Furthermore, since this time is not possible for a son who is to undergo marriage again, the statement "he may perform the marriage rite again" (MDh 5.166) would otherwise be untenable. || 9.94 ||
A husband obtains his wife as a gift from the gods, not by his own will;
doing what is pleasing to the gods, he should always support that virtuous woman. 9.95.

The meaning of the verse is that a virtuous wife (*sādhvī*) should not be abandoned by her husband, even if she is possessed of faults such as hostility or speaking unpleasant words; this is the remaining praise. As for the rule, "He shall confine her in a single room" (MDh 11.175), which is prescribed even for an unvirtuous woman, that applies to a single instance of infidelity. In the case of repetition, however, there is indeed abandonment; otherwise, nothing would be accomplished by the injunction, "He shall support her if she is virtuous. Furthermore, regarding the passage: "One who has been deprived of her authority, who is soiled, and who subsists on mere morsels of food... [the following applies].

"One should cause the unfaithful wife to dwell on a contemptible bed. (YDh 1.70) And that [dwellings] depends upon the husband's will when he has the capacity; however, in the absence of his will, there is simply abandonment.

As for what he will state later, beginning with "Even to those who have fallen [from their caste], clothing, food, and drink should be given" (MDh 11.187), we shall explain that this is a prohibitory statement intended to prevent the acceptance of lodging at the commencement of subsisting on alms during penances such as those for killing a Brahmin. In any case, however, there is no maintenance of an unfaithful wife. Nor is any abandonment prescribed here by which one might infer that the rule refers specifically to sexual intercourse. From the mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas) such as "Soma gave her" (RV 10.85.41), it is understood that the gods are the givers.

Alternatively, because she becomes the wife of the deity at the time of marriage, it is said: "one should obtain a woman given by the gods. One should not take her according to one's own desire. Just as other things such as cattle or gold may be obtained in a marketplace, so too is this wife not to be acquired; therefore, it is said, "not by one's own will. She is "dear to the gods" (devānāṃ priyam), meaning beneficial for the gods. When a wife has been abandoned, there is no benefit to the gods on account of rites such as the Vaiśvadeva; therefore, one should support her even if she is hostile. In the event of her degradation (pātitya), the husband may take another wife who possesses the requisite qualifications. (9.95)
Women were created for the purpose of procreation, and men for the purpose of continuing the lineage;
therefore, the sacred scripture declares that religious duty is common to both, performed together with the wife.

Procreation is the taking of a conception; lineage is the implantation of the embryo. For that reason, because the birth of offspring depends upon both, the Veda declares the duty of man to be common to both sexes when performed together with his wife. Therefore, since a woman cannot have independent entitlement [to ritual acts], she must not be abandoned even if she is hated. (9.96)
If the giver of the bride-price dies after the bride-price has been paid for a maiden,
she should be given to the husband's brother, provided the maiden consents.

In a case where the bride-price (*śulka*) has been received by her father or others, but she has not yet been given away, and she is established as being to be given solely by word of mouth—if, in the meantime, he (the intended groom) should die, then—like other property—she would fall to the brothers-in-law (*devara*), either to all of them like Yudhiṣṭhira and the others, or in their absence to the *sapiṇḍa* relatives. To specify the particular rule for this situation, it is stated: "She is to be given to the brother-in-law. This means she is not to be given to all the husband's brothers nor to the *sapiṇḍas*, but rather to one brother-in-law alone; and even then, only with the consent of the maiden.
Now, if the girl is no longer available, what is the disposition regarding the bride-price (*śulka*)?

If the girl prefers a life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), then the bride-price belongs solely to the girl’s paternal kin. If, however, she seeks another husband, then having relinquished the previously received bride-price, it is given to another after being taken from him. (9.97)
Even a Śūdra, when giving away his daughter, must not take a bride-price;
for by accepting a bride-price, one performs a concealed sale of his daughter. (9.98)

Regarding the taking of a bride-price (*śulka*) by mutual consent, the rule has already been stated previously. Someone might have this doubt: "The taking of a bride-price is not a fault, since a specific distinction is mentioned in the scripture for one whose bride-price has been received. To dispel this doubt, he says: "Even a Śūdra should not take a bride-price. When there is engagement through mutual desire, the scriptural injunction applies; it is not that the scripture prescribes the act itself as something that ought to be done. Just as the drinking of liquor is not authorized by the scripture merely because a penance is prescribed for one who has drunk it. That which was spoken of under the name "bride-price"—namely, "for he who takes a bride-price out of greed" (MDh 3.51)—the specific distinction for which that subsequent recitation was shown has already been demonstrated. (9.98)
But this is what neither others nor any virtuous men have ever done:
that having made a promise to one, it is then given to another. (9.99)

This [verse] prohibits what was stated [in verse 9.98]: "When the bride-price has been received, if the giver of the price dies and the maiden so desires, she may be given to another. It means that if, after promising her to one who has paid the bride-price, she is given again to another after receiving the bride-price once more, the maiden herself should exercise the right of choice (*svayaṃvara*). This is the very meaning [of the verse]. (9.99)
Indeed, even in former births, we have never heard of such a thing:
the sale of a daughter concealed under the name of a "bride-price" (śulka). 9.100.
The meaning is: "We have not heard this from anyone before, in previous births or in other kalpas. (9.100)
Let there be mutual fidelity until death;
this should be known as the supreme duty of husband and wife in brief. (9.101)

Non-deviation [from fidelity] applies to all activities through the principle of verbal expression without distinction. Thus Āpastamba says: "She must not be unfaithful in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma. And these alone constitute the highest good: dharma, artha, and kāma. As it has been said: "The established rule is that there are three aims of life" (MDh 2.224). Furthermore, they say that non-deviation here means non-abandonment; otherwise, just as with women, a man would not be permitted to marry more than one wife.

That is incorrect. There is a scriptural statement regarding the man: "But for those who act out of desire" (MDh 3.12), as well as "A barren wife may be superseded in the eighth year" (MDh 9.81); however, there is no such [rule] for the woman. Furthermore, there is another indicative mark: "One man has many wives, but one woman does not have many husbands simultaneously" (AitB 12.11). That which exists until the end of life is *āmaraṇāntika*; the meaning is that its end occurs upon the death of either one. This should be understood briefly as the preeminent duty of women and men. || 9.101 ||
Likewise, once they have performed their rites, the woman and man should always strive so that,
even when separated from one another, they do not transgress against each other.

They should strive with such effort that they do not transgress one another; "transgression" means overstepping, or the failure to remain together in the pursuit of dharma, artha, and kāma. Having performed their rites—that is, having completed the sacraments of marriage and so forth—they should remain inseparable thereafter. This concluding verse does not teach any meaning not already stated. 9.102.

This is the transitional verse connecting the preceding and following sections: "This duty of women and men, together with the rules for sexual pleasure, has been declared to you; as well as the acquisition of offspring in times of distress. Now, learn the law concerning inheritance. (9.103)
When the duties of husband and wife have been declared, as well as the production of offspring, this is the occasion for the partition of the law of inheritance. (9.103)
After the father and the mother have passed away, the brothers, having assembled, shall divide the paternal inheritance equally; for they have no power over it while the two are alive.

The optative suffix (*liṅ*) in "they should divide" (*bhajeran*) expresses that the time has arrived; this has been explained in detail in the fifth [chapter]. Alternatively, it refers to the moment at which [the inheritance] was transferred. 9.104.
The eldest alone shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the rest shall depend upon him, just as they did upon their father. (9.105)
By the mere birth of an eldest son, a man becomes a father of a son and is released from his debt to the ancestors; therefore, he deserves everything. 9.106
He upon whom one pays off a debt, and through whom one attains infinity—he alone is known as the son born of dharma; others they know as sons born of desire. (9.107)

The phrase "the others" is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). For if one were to grasp the intended meaning exactly as it is heard [literally], the younger brothers would be rendered unworthy of a share; and from that, there would follow a contradiction with what is to be stated later. (9.107)

The eldest brother should protect his younger brothers like a father protects his sons; and they, in accordance with dharma, should behave toward their eldest brother as sons do toward their father. 9.108

They are to be protected like sons, but they are not to be despised for their immaturity by means of wealth and the like; rather, they too should cultivate the thought, "This man is our father. Thus it is said: "And they should behave toward him as toward a son" (9.108).
Another praise:
"The eldest son either causes the family to prosper or brings it to ruin;
the eldest is most worthy of honor in the world, and the eldest is not censured by the virtuous. (9.109)

He alone who is preeminent in virtue causes the family to prosper; he alone who is devoid of virtue brings that family to ruin. When the eldest brother possesses virtuous conduct, even the younger brothers behave likewise; yet they too may come to dispute with one who is lacking in virtue. (9.109)
He who is the eldest and behaves as an elder should be honored like a mother or a father; but he who does not behave as an elder should be respected merely as a kinsman. (9.110)

The conduct toward the eldest [brother] is like that toward a son: affection, protection, non-neglect regarding his body and wealth as if they were one's own, and turning him away from improper acts. However, he who behaves otherwise should be treated like a kinsman with rising to greet him and salutations, and honored like a maternal uncle or a paternal uncle. If he acts otherwise, his subordination ceases. (9.110)
Thus they may dwell together or separately out of a desire for dharma; dharma increases through separation, therefore separation is consistent with dharma. (9.111)

Because one lacks the independence to act according to one's own will regarding rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma—which are accomplished through one’s own property and are independent [of others]—separation is impossible; therefore, this division, which is established by logic for the sake of accomplishing those rites, is stated: "Or separately, out of a desire for merit. It is not, however, that non-merit arises from non-separation; rather, separation itself is merit, just like the Agnihotra and other rites. But surely, since non-separation is a cause for obstructing the performance of merit, it must indeed be non-merit?

This is not a fault. Transgression occurs upon the non-performance of what one is obligated to perform. Furthermore, one whose wealth has not been partitioned lacks the qualification [to perform rites], because he lacks the possession of the sacred fires (*agnimatva*), since the formal adoption of the fires is ordained only at the time of partition. However, for one who has already married while his father is still living and has likewise adopted the fires at that very time, there is no lack of qualification; thus, for him, there is no such thing as "non-partition. Even he, if he has fallen away from the adoption or otherwise possesses sufficient wealth to perform the prescribed duties, would incur no transgression even while living together [with his father]. For it has been stated that partition or non-partition is not inherently virtuous or non-virtuous in its own nature.

But surely, on account of the statement, "For brothers who are undivided, a single religious duty prevails" (NSm 13.37), there is indeed the manifestation of religious duty prior to partition, just as in the case of husband and wife, because of the joint performance [of rites]; since wealth is common property, it must be used by all acting together.

This does not apply to the *agnihotra* and similar rites. For the *agnihotra* and other such sacrifices are performed in the *āhavanīya* and other sacred fires; and since the *āhavanīya* and others are defined by their consecration (*saṃskāra*), as seen from the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), they do not admit of being related to either [the sacrificer or another]. Furthermore, there is a prohibition against one who offers oblations in a fire belonging to another: "One should not sacrifice in the fires of another. Nor is there an injunction for these rites in the domestic (*gṛhya*) fire, even though it is mentioned in the Smṛtis; for the word "house" (*gṛha*) is used here in its specific sense of the sacred fire, and thus the same principle applies. This is because the feeding of guests and so forth is recited in the midst of the "Great Sacrifices" (*mahāyajña*).

"One should perform the domestic rites according to the rule in the nuptial fire, as well as the performance of the five sacrifices" (MDh 3.57). Thus, the authority [for these acts] resides solely in the *Gṛhya* texts. Therefore, this statement, "There is one duty" (NSm 13.37), should be understood as referring merely to the *śrāddha*, works of public utility (*pūrta*), the distribution of food, and so forth. 9.111.

The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as his preferential share, and whatever is the best among all the goods; half of that shall be the share of the middle son, and a fourth for the youngest. (9.112)

Some maintain that this Smṛti rule regarding the appointment for redemption (*uddhāraniyoga*) pertains to a past time and is not to be practiced today, because Smṛtis are restricted to specific times. They argue that the designation of it as something to be practiced is intended so that spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*) may arise from knowledge alone, just as in the case of the *Dīrghasattra* sacrifice; for no one is seen performing the *Dīrghasattra* nowadays, yet Brahmins still study its injunctions. Thus it has been said: "The duties in the Kṛta age were different" (MDh 1.85). Therefore, just as there is a restriction of place, a restriction of time must also be understood to apply to religious duties (*dharma*). For a duty enjoined is not necessarily performed in every location; indeed, local duties (*deśadharma*) are described as being established within specific regions. Otherwise, if they were performed everywhere, these duties would not be designated by reference to particular places. Accordingly, the text reads: "This [is the law] which is followed by learned twice-born men," etc. (MDh 9.66). Consequently, the Smṛti rules concerning the appointment for redemption and the slaughter of cows, though enjoined, are not to be practiced.

This is not well-founded. For such a restriction of time is nowhere heard of, except in the case of specific rules regarding evening, morning, festival days (*parvan*), and so forth. As for the statement, "The duties (*dharma*) in other ages are different" (MDh 1.85), that has already been explained in the very first [chapter]. Indeed, this is not a cause for the systematic arrangement of *dharma* according to the distinction of the ages (*yuga*). It has also been stated that there is no restriction of place based on the Middle Country (*madhyadeśa*) or the Eastern Country (*pūrvadeśa*), apart from [the rule concerning] land sloping toward the east and so forth, as seen in the passages: "The local customs (*jātijānapada-dharma*)... (MDh 8.41) and "...that which is practiced by the virtuous" (MDh 8.46). Furthermore, the performance of long sacrificial sessions (*dīrghasattra*) is possible even today. As for the word "year" (*saṃvatsara*), its application to days was shown in the very first [chapter]. As for the claim that no one is seen performing them nowadays, that is due to the inability to provide the means for performance in many ways, or due to a lack of desire for the fruit, or due to atheism (*nāstikya*), even though the enjoined matter is prescribed as if it were obligatory (*nitya*). As for the passage, "While Vena was ruling the kingdom" (MDh 9.66), this is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) showing that the practice began from that great antiquity; it is not an instruction regarding time.

The twentieth part belongs to the eldest. From all the property, the twentieth part must indeed be set aside and given to the eldest. For the middle son, it is half of that, the fortieth part. Likewise, for the youngest, it is a quarter; relative to the eldest, this is the eightieth part. Once this has been set aside, the remainder is to be divided into three parts. Among all the goods, whatever is the best or most excellent belongs to the eldest alone. Alternatively, there is the reading: "Even among the goods, the supreme best. This means that from whatever goods—whether superior, inferior, or middling—there exist, that single item which is the most excellent belongs to him alone; this is what is being stated. Where there are cows or horses, the one best [animal] must be given to the eldest; it is not to be taken in exchange for another object or for its price. This is the rule for the preferential share (*uddhāra*) for all three when they possess merit, since the preferential share is seen to apply to those who have qualities. (9.112)
The eldest and the youngest shall take [their shares] as prescribed;
those who are other than the eldest and the youngest shall have the middlemost wealth. (9.113)

For one who has more than three sons, having set aside for the eldest and the youngest—as prescribed—the shares of those endowed with merit, that which was stated in the immediately preceding verse as "the fortieth part" of even many middling sons who possess merit must be shared among them. However, for all middling sons who are equal in merit, the previously mentioned fortieth part is to be set aside for each one individually. Thus, the statement "that shall be their middling wealth" is expressed in two ways: either the "middling wealth" specified in the preceding verse is to be given to all of them collectively, or it is to be given to each one individually with respect to their status as eldest or youngest. Of these, the first alternative is appropriate for those lacking in merit, as they are not entitled to much wealth; the second applies only to those possessed of merit. (9.113)
The first-born son shall take the best of all kinds of wealth, as well as whatever else is particularly excellent; furthermore, he shall receive one choice item from every ten.

With the first half-verse, he restates what was said [in MDh 9.112]: "and whatever is the best among all substances. The word *jāta* is a synonym for *jāti* (kind) or denotes a variety. *Agraja* means the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*). *Agrya* means the most excellent (*śreṣṭha*). And even if it is a single garment or ornament that is of superior quality, he may take one that is better than ten, or better than a group of ten members. If there are ten cows or horses, then he should take the one that is most excellent. Or, he does not obtain anything less than a group of ten; the word "ten" (*daśa*) refers to a group.

Others, however, explain that the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the reflexive pronoun (*svārthe*). They read the plural form "ten *daśatas*" as "ten excellent ones" (*daśaiva daśato varān*). One should accept ten excellent [cows]. Another tradition records them as being distinguished by that [number]: "Of animals with solid hooves or two feet, [one should take] ten each" (GDh 28.12–13). || 9.114 ||
There is no deduction for those who have performed their own duties well;
however, something whatsoever should be given to the elder as a means of increasing his honor. (9.115)

The preferential share (*uddhāra*) mentioned previously regarding ten cattle does not apply here. As for brothers who are distinguished and accomplished in their own duties, such as Vedic study and the like—the phrase "in ten" is explained as being merely illustrative. That preferential share which was stated in the verse concerning ten is entirely absent here due to the connection with [specific] duties; however, even by them, something slightly more than the standard—consisting of a method for increasing prosperity and bringing honor—should be given to the eldest. (9.115)
Thus, when a preferential share has been set aside, one should assign equal shares [to the rest];
but if no preferential share is set aside, this following shall be the distribution of shares for them: || 9.116 ||

When the preferential share has been set aside and separated, one should allot equal shares from the remaining wealth; when it has not been set aside, the allotment of shares shall be as will be described hereafter. (9.116)
The eldest son shall take one share in excess; the next younger brother, one and a half shares; and the youngest brothers, one share each—thus is the law established. (9.117)

"With one part more" means he should take his own share increased by one part; that is to say, he should receive two parts. "Then the younger brother" means immediately after him, he receives one and a half (half of two). "The youngest," those born after him—all these [younger brothers] shall receive an equal share, meaning neither more nor less. || 9.117 ||
The brothers shall each give to their own respective sisters a fourth part from their own individual shares; those who refuse to give shall become outcasts. (9.118)

The word *kanyā* is generally used for unmarried girls; furthermore, in another Smṛti, the term *kānīna-putra* is recorded with the phrase "of those not yet given in marriage" (*aprattānām*). Therefore, this share is declared to belong to one who is unmarried.

From their own shares, with respect to their own caste, brothers should give a fourth part of their share to their sisters from their own portion. Where there are many daughters, the allotment of a fourth part must be made with respect to a brother of the same caste. And thus is the meaning: the son shall take three parts, and the daughter one-fourth.

As for what some have said: "The father’s act of giving away daughters who are not yet given away is a great benefit, because while the father lives, they are consecrated [in marriage] according to his will even with wealth as a price; but when he is dead, they become heirs. That is equally applicable to the son as well; and regarding a matter based on scriptural statement (*vācanika*), what is this objection? Now, if the intention is that "the practice of giving has marriage alone as its purpose," then custom is weaker than *smṛti*. Nor is it absolute. And since it is not absolute, this restriction is properly established by *smṛti*.
As for what has been said by someone else: "Only that which serves the purpose of marriage should be given, and not a fourth part as it is stated in the scriptures."

He should be told this: there is no fixed amount of wealth to be given at a marriage. Just as it is said that "one hundred and twelve [cows] are the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)," it is heard in scripture: "One should marry her after having clothed and adorned her," or "One should give her a dowry (*saudāyika*). Furthermore, ornaments consist of gold, gems, pearls, coral, and so forth, and are divided into many kinds. In that regard, it is not known how much wealth should be given or what kind of ornament should be provided; therefore, for the sake of defining the limit, it is appropriate that it should be "a fourth part of one's own share. And in this matter, there is neither contradiction with the scriptures nor contradiction with reason.
Other Smṛti texts likewise support this position:
"But those who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their brothers who have already been consecrated;
and the sisters, having been given a fourth part from their own share," (YDh 2.128).

Likewise: "She may take a share until her marriage; thereafter, the husband shall maintain her. (NSm 13.26) This is its meaning: where there is only a small amount of wealth belonging to the brother and the sister such that the maintenance of the girl cannot be provided by a one-fourth share, in that case the girl may take an equal share until her marriage. But thereafter, according to another Smṛti, she should take even a small one-fourth share. How then is mere maintenance to be ensured? To this it is said: "thereafter, the husband shall maintain her."

They explain that the mention of "brother" (bhrātṛ) is intended to mean a uterine brother (sodarya). What is the intention? The word "brother," when used without a qualifying prefix, functions in its primary sense only for a uterine brother. Furthermore, the separate statement [in the text] serves as an indicative mark (liṅga).

For she who has no uterine brother (*sodarya*), her inheritance [301] or her *saudāyika* property [302] does not accrue to her. If it is argued that a half-brother (*vaimātreyo*) will give it, he does not give it in the absence of another scriptural statement. The term "brother" (*bhrātṛ*) includes those who have the same father but different mothers [303]. It is logical, however, that it applies to paternal cousins and others only by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). In this way, the polysemy of the word "one" (*eka*) is not accepted. Furthermore, the practice of other legal codes (*smṛti*) is superior [304], for it is recited therein: "That which remains after the paternal debts have been paid, and whatever was inherited from the father—that should be divided among the brothers" (NSm 13.32). The meaning is that they should divide the remainder after setting aside what must necessarily be given by the father, such as the repayment of debts; and just as the discharge of debts is mentioned, so too is the giving of a daughter, because it is a necessary duty: "And [the gift] to daughters is the *prādānika* [inheritance]" (KAŚ 3.5.21). In this [latter passage], neither the word "sister" nor the word "brother" is heard, which might otherwise give rise to this doubt.

As for the statement that [the property] is "separate," this refers to the share of each individual within the collective; thus, the phrase "from all [of them]" is also appropriate. This is stated [in the following]: they are not forced to give by compulsion because of the sin incurred by those who do not give, since it is said, "those who refuse to give would become outcasts. For when someone is the owner of a certain portion in a given matter, he is said to "take" it, and not that "he must give this to him. Just as it is not said that "a brother should give to a brother," so too, what is stated [regarding the king taking the property] applies to those who are not owners. (9.118)
One should never take an unequal share of goats, sheep, or one-hoofed animals;
for it is ordained that an unequal share of goats and sheep belongs to the eldest alone. (9.119)

The "single-hoofed" refers to horses, mules, donkeys, and so forth. At the time of partition, if goats and sheep cannot be divided equally in number, they shall belong to the eldest alone; he need not bring them to equality by adding other portions of property, nor should he sell them and then have their price paid out [to the others]. The term *ajāvikam* is a dual compound formed with optional singularization (Pāṇini 2.4.12). || 9.119 ||
If a younger brother should beget a son upon the wife of the elder, the division of the estate there shall be equal; such is the established law. (9.120)

Since the rule of the eldest son’s authority would otherwise extend by analogy to the uterine brother just as it does to the father, the following is stated to preclude that: "In that case, the division shall be equal. There is no preferential share (*uddhāra*), nor is there the rule that "the eldest shall take one more [share]" (MDh 9.117), nor even the rule that "something at all may be given" (MDh 9.115). It shall be equal. With whom? With the younger uterine uncle who begot him. However, it will be stated later that the son of a woman not authorized to bear a child is indeed unworthy of a share. And this is an indicative mark [of the principle]: although the word "brothers" is used in the verse "The brothers, having come together" (MDh 9.104), the division must still be made with the nephew (*bhrātṛputra*) when no [actual] brother exists. (9.120)

It is not consistent with dharma that the subordinate should take precedence over the principal; since the father is the principal in procreation, one should therefore honor him according to dharma. (9.121)

The *kṣetraja* son is subordinate (*upasarjana*), meaning secondary; having supplied the words "equal to the primary (*pradhāna*) legitimate (*aurasa*) son," [the author states that] this is not consistent with *dharma*, that is, with the scriptures. For the legitimate son indeed receives the entire senior share (*jyeṣṭhāṃśa*) like his father. But this *kṣetraja* son is subordinate; therefore, one should treat him according to *dharma*. *Dharma* here refers to the previously mentioned arrangement of shares.
Now, since this son is also a first-born son, why does he not receive a share like the legitimate son?

Therefore, he says: "The father is primary in procreation. Here, the "father" intended is the progenitor; he is primary in the production of offspring. This [son], however, is secondary, being begotten by one of lesser status. By supplying the words "the subordinate is equal to the primary," the verse is understood. This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), and since it serves as an explanatory statement for the preceding prohibition of the eldest’s special share, an interpretation must be made by relying on some basis for the terms "primary" and "subordinate. Others read: "Therefore, one should abandon him according to the law (*dharma*)."

That is incorrect, because an equal portion is prescribed for all cases; furthermore, since this is an explanatory statement (arthavāda), one should not entertain any suspicion regarding an alternative option. 9.121.
If a doubt should arise as to how the division [of the estate] should be made in the case where there is a younger son born of an elder wife and an elder son born of a younger wife: || 9.122 ||

The elder (*jyeṣṭhā*) is she who was married first; the younger (*kaniṣṭhā*) is she who was married later. Regarding the children born of these two, a doubt is raised as to whether seniority should be determined by the order of their mothers' marriages or by the order of their own births; this will be resolved later for the sake of reaching a consensus. (9.122)
The eldest son shall take one bull as his preferential share;
the others shall have bulls inferior to that, according to their respective mothers. (9.123)

The one born first is the "eldest" (*pūrvaja*); he is declared to be the recipient of the bull. Therefore, those other bulls besides that [first] one who are not the eldest should be given by making them into single shares for many [sons]. And thus, for the son of the eldest wife (*jyaiṣṭhineya*), this much has been stated as the additional share: namely, the best bull; its superiority is merely by virtue of quality (*guṇa*) and not by number. [This applies] to those inferior to that eldest-born. To how many? He says: "from their own mothers," because seniority is primarily determined by the mother. Therefore, in this case, seniority based on the mother is relied upon, not seniority from birth. (8.123)
But the son born of the eldest wife, though he may not be the eldest by birth, shall take a bull and sixteen cows;
the remaining sons shall then divide the rest according to their mothers—this is the settled rule. (9.124)

An alternative supplementary portion for these [sons] is now stated: "If a son born to a non-elder wife is the eldest, he shall take fifteen cows and a bull. Because of the mention of the bull, cows are obtained; as in the expression, "the second of this cow," the bull is not intended as a separate object. The others, the remaining sons, shall take the cows according to their mothers; that is, whichever mother is senior, he shall take the senior cow, and whichever is junior, he shall take the junior one.

Alternatively, this additional share (*uddhāra*) mentioned for the eldest son is stated in addition to what was already established previously; there is no elision (*praśleṣa*) of the word *anaḍut* here. The remaining younger brothers shall take their shares according to their mothers. The phrase "according to their mothers" is explained [as follows]:
since these two verses are merely explanatory (*arthavāda*), no effort is made at a strict logical distinction; this is simply an introductory statement. (9.124)
But this is the established conclusion: among sons born of wives of equal status, there is no seniority according to the mother; seniority is said to be according to birth. (9.125)
"Similar" means belonging to the same class [of being]. 9.125 ||
Even in the Subrahmaṇyā invocations, it is recorded that the summons is made by the one eldest by birth;
and among twins conceived together, seniority is recorded as being determined by birth.

This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) intended to establish seniority by birth. The mantra called *Subrahmaṇyā* is employed by the Chāndogas in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice for the purpose of summoning Indra, beginning with: "O Subrahmaṇyā, O Indra, come! (*subrahmaṇyo indra āgaccha*). Because of the multiplicity of its applications, the plural form is used. Regarding this, it is said: [In the formula] "Devadatta’s father sacrifices," the father is designated by means of the first-born son. Primacy is primary (*mukhya*) based on birth; any other [primacy], however, is secondary (*gauṇa*) due to its connection with the mother's marriage. Even in the case of twins whose embryos were infused at the same time, primacy is determined by birth. (9.126)
A sonless man may, by this rite, make a daughter his "appointed daughter" (putrikā), [stipulating]: "Whatever offspring may be born of her shall be the one who performs my funeral rites. (9.127)

"Whatever offspring may be born of her, that shall be for me a *svadhā*-maker. The word *svadhā* here signifies the purpose of the son’s duties, such as the *śrāddha* and other rites for the benefit of the deceased. However, this specific term need not necessarily be uttered. Thus says Gautama: "A childless father, having sacrificed to Agni and Prajāpati, may set aside a daughter [as his heir], after declaring, 'This offspring is for my sake. According to some, she becomes a *putrikā* by mere intention alone" (GDh 28.18–19). Thus, a daughter becomes a *putrikā* even without the employment of mantras and the like, but not in the absence of the formal declaration (*saṃvāda*). Even if the intention is formed within the heart, it is said that until it has been made known by speech, the son-in-law might act contrary to the agreement; therefore, one should formally designate her as a *putrikā*. (9.127)
In accordance with this very ordinance, Dakṣa, the Lord of Creatures, formerly fashioned those daughters himself for the sake of the increase of his own lineage. (9.128)

Dakṣa, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), who was skilled in the method of procreating offspring, is cited as the example here. This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) known as a "deed of another" (parakṛti). 9.128.
With a joyful heart, he gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven to King Soma, having honored them all.
"Having honored [them]"—this is what is prescribed here. Because of the indicative mark [liṅga] "ten," etc., they also maintain that one may make many figurines. 9.129.
As one's self, so is one's son; a daughter is equal to a son.
While she remains as one's very self, how could another take away the wealth? (9.130)

It has been stated [in MDh 9.127]: "Whatever offspring she may have, that shall be mine. And offspring is an heir to the estate. Therefore, since it would otherwise not follow that the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) who has not yet produced a son should inherit the wealth when her father dies, this is prescribed by way of an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). While she remains as his very self for the sake of producing a son, the wealth belongs to him; the production of a son belonging to her is not applicable here. Alternatively, it means "while she exists as his own self in the form of a father. The word *duhitṛ* (daughter), though a general term, should be understood from the context as referring specifically to the appointed daughter, according to the rule: "The daughter is equal to a son. (9.130)
Whatever may be the mother’s separate property (yautaka), that indeed is the share of the unmarried daughter;
and the daughter’s son alone shall take the entire estate of one who dies without a son.
The term *yautaka* refers to the woman’s property by virtue of its distinctness; for in that case, she alone possesses exclusive ownership.

Others, however, maintain that it refers only to what is received as a dowry (*saudāyika*) and not to the property of a related woman; for in that instance, she has independence, as it is said: “Upon obtaining dowry property, independence is prescribed for women” (KSm 905).
But others [hold that it refers to] only the remainder of what was used from the daily allowance given by the husband, which is intended for food, ornaments, and so forth.

They say that what is accepted by a young woman is her *yautaka* (separate property); it is indeed the portion of an unmarried girl (*kumārī*). Because of the mention of the "unmarried girl," this does not apply to one who is not an unmarried girl. Furthermore, because the particle *eva* (indeed) functions as a restatement of what is already established, it sets aside the general context [of inheritance]. Consequently, *yautaka* also pertains to the case of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) who is an unmarried girl. And thus Gautama, having stated, "The woman’s property belongs to her offspring" (GDh 28.24), says, "To the daughters who are unmarried and unsettled" (GDh 28.24). In that context, "unsettled" refers to those who, though married, are childless and destitute, and have not obtained a firm standing in their husband's house.

And the daughter’s son alone shall take the entire property of one who has no son other than a legitimate (aurasa) son; however, when a legitimate son exists, he will state what share [the daughter’s son] receives. Here too, it is specifically the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*) who is meant by "daughter’s son," not every such son, because—as in the previous case—the abandonment of the general context is justified only on the grounds that this refers to separate property (*yautaka*). (9.131)
For the daughter's son shall take the entire inheritance of his father who has no [other] son;
he alone shall offer two funeral cakes, one to his own father and one to his maternal grandfather. (9.132)

"To the maternal grandfather and the great-grandfather who are without sons. Some have explained that since the entire inheritance of the *pautrika* (son of an appointed daughter) and the *dauhitra* (daughter's son) has already been stated by the preceding [text], this verse is intended to prescribe the offering of the *piṇḍas* by way of restating that fact; they read the text as "hared yadi" ("if he should take"). According to their view, one should offer the *piṇḍas* only in the case where he takes the entire inheritance. However, when the alternative position—that "the division there shall be equal" (MDh 9.134)—is adopted, then one should not offer them; otherwise, since the offering of the *piṇḍas* would already be established by the rule "whoever takes from whom, he should give to him," this repeated statement would be redundant. Furthermore, the restatement of the taking of the entire inheritance would likewise be purposeless.

That is incorrect. The long-established reading is precisely this: “He shall take [the estate] of a father who has no son. Furthermore, the word *pitṛ* is more commonly known to denote a biological father than a maternal grandfather. Therefore, if the husband of the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) is childless by his other wives, while the appointed daughter herself has a son, then by the birth of that very son, both the father and the maternal grandfather are to be understood as having sons. But when the progenitor (*bījī*) has sons born of other wives, then the son of the appointed daughter—even if born of a wedded wife of the same caste—shall neither inherit the property of the progenitor nor offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to him. For the relationship of begetter and begotten is one thing, while the relationship between offspring and the owner of the offspring is another. There are those who possess offspring despite not being the progenitors, such as those born of a wife’s womb (*kṣetraja*) and others; and there are progenitors who possess sons despite not being the fathers of their bodies, such as Viśvāmitra, Ajīgarta, and others. Thus, in the definition of the legitimate son (*aurasa*), the term “his own” (*sva*) is used in the phrase “in his own field” (*svakṣetre*). And the “field” belongs to the father alone; for the husband is merely the one whose choice she must follow, and thus he is the master only over the mother’s family. Therefore, it should be stated thus: in the case where the husband of the appointed daughter has no other sons, and the son of the appointed daughter takes the entire estate, in that case he shall perform the necessary offering of the funeral cake. But when the progenitor becomes possessed of sons, then that son of the appointed daughter shall certainly not offer the funeral cake to the progenitor. Now, it is said that he is a “daughter’s son” (*dauhitra*). The meaning is “son of the appointed daughter” (*pautrikeya*). Just as in the case of the maternal grandfather’s side, it is heard that he shall also offer [the cake] to the father, so too in other cases he shall offer to other sides. Nor does the injunction that he shall offer in the case of taking the whole estate imply a prohibition for other cases, because [the obligation] to offer to both the father and the grandfather is not otherwise established. The indication is a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*); since it is restated, the indication is that he should offer to the other [alone], whereas by this [text] it is restated that he offers to both simultaneously. Just as to the father and the maternal grandfather, so too to the grandfather and the great-grandfather, and likewise to the two beyond them. (MDh 9.132)
In this world, according to the law of dharma, there is no distinction between a son’s son and a daughter’s son;
for both of them were produced from the very body of their parents.
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) supplementary to what precedes. How so? Because there is no distinction between those two, namely, the mother and the father. (9.133)
But if, after a daughter has been appointed, a son is subsequently born, the division of the estate shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman. (9.134)

In that case, the division is equal; there is no senior share for the son born [to her]. For a woman has no seniority; it is only the share of the inheritance that is prohibited from being treated as a senior portion, but not her respectful conduct toward elders. (9.134)
But if the appointed daughter (putrikā) should somehow die without having borne a son,
her husband shall take that wealth without hesitation.
[The commentary on this verse is corrupt, and editors are often guessing at the meaning.]

However, because the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) has no owner, it is said that her husband does not acquire a right to her property. Now, is the appointed daughter consecrated by marriage, or is she not at all? If she is consecrated, she becomes a wife; for marriage is the act that makes one a wife. And consequently, [if she were so consecrated], her property would be [lost to her lineage]. If she is not consecrated, one incurs the offense of approaching a maiden (*kanyāgamana*), and there is also a transgression of the rule: "He should always be devoted to his own wife" (MDh 3.45). Let it be as you wish. [Objection: But in this case, is this verse not rendered meaningless?

This is not a fault. Since this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended for completeness, the commencement of the verse is indeed appropriate for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that "just as this offspring does not belong to the husband, so too does the wealth not [belong to him]. Furthermore, there are many verses in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra] that function as explanatory passages.

Alternatively, let it be granted that she is not "refined" (*saṃskriyate*). However, under this view, the act of approaching a maiden (*kanyāgamana*) would follow as a consequence. Why? Because once it is established that one born of such a woman is the son of the maternal grandfather, the context [of the prohibition] pertains to the one who approaches her by way of defining the transgression of the injunction. Furthermore, these [acts] are not non-falling [from caste] (*apataniya*). ++ ++++ [End of fragment]

Furthermore, on what basis do you raise this objection—thinking that the term "maiden" (kanyā) implies the inclusion of [all those who have not yet had intercourse]—that the mention of "maiden" would apply [too broadly]? For there are three kinds of maidens: first, one who has not yet engaged in sexual union with a man; second, one who is protected by her family and devoted to the gods; and third, one who is in the prime of youth. In that regard, if it were simply "one who has not been united with a man," then even for a woman who has already been married, the designation would still apply because she has not yet departed from her initial state of non-union. For generally, in this treatise, the word "maiden" denotes the absence of sexual union with a man.

Now, as for the phrase "devoid of sacramental rites" (*saṃskārahīnā*), that too is not [correct]. For, from the very first word, with the intention of recollection, it is understood there—by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) on the strength of other possible means of knowledge—that they are "beneficial" (*hitāḥ*). As it has been said:
"The mantras associated with the taking of the hand are established only for maidens;
never among non-maidens among men, for they have lost their capacity for religious rites. (MDh 8.226)

In this context, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the statement regarding the omission of ritual duties (*dharma*), she who has been enjoyed by a man is called a "non-virgin" (*akanyā*). By contrast, in its opposite case, she who has not been enjoyed is called a "virgin" (*kanyā*). In all instances, the ritual duties (*dharmas*) are understood as being performed in accordance with the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*). And these are not all [of them]; rather, they are only those for which there is authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*). For instance, in the term *kānīna*, both the father’s ownership (*svatā*) and the absence of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) are understood. For if only the absence of sacramental rites were intended, then the sons of a married woman or a wanton woman (*svairiṇī*) would be *kānīnas*. And if only the characteristic of the father’s ownership were intended, then even the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) would be designated as a *kānīna*.

As for what was said [at 366]: “But then, a transgression of the rule would result regarding one’s own wife,” this is not its meaning: that one should go to others than one’s own wife. For he does not desire another’s wife, nor does he desire other wives. If that were the case, since this [rule] would already have covered it, the prohibition against another’s wife would be redundant. What, then, is the point? It is that delight should be maintained toward one’s own wife, so that through the practice of cultivating delight, an excellence of joy arises. The statement, “He does not desire another woman, nor other wives; being thus, he does not fall away from his duties,” is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). Alternatively, even for one devoted to his own wife, they might approach her on forbidden days (*parva*); in such a state of deep sleep, there is no offspring at all. Furthermore, there is no prohibition against another’s wife, because, since she has not been married by him, there is no designation of her as a “wife” (*dāra*) by anyone.

What, then, is the correct interpretation here regarding the phrase "not to be married"? For there are eight forms of marriage (*vivāha*), and these receive their distinct designations—such as *brāhma* and so forth—based on the different modes of acceptance. However, in this case, the husband has no act of formal acquisition (*svakaraṇa*) over her, because the father’s ownership has not been relinquished. Furthermore, when the prohibition against marrying a girl who has no brother is mentioned, it indicates that an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) is not to be married, according to the rule: "One should not marry a girl who has no brother, for [the son born to her] becomes his [the father's] offspring. This prohibition is contextual (*prākaraṇika*), and if it were transgressed, the very status of the marriage as a sacrament (*saṃskāra*) would not exist, just as a Śūdra woman lacks the qualification for the *āhavanīya* fire in the establishment of the sacred fires. Since the prohibitions against marrying one's mother's sister and others possess a scriptural basis (*upalabhyamānamūlatva*), even though they are contextually dependent, they preclude the sacramental nature [of the marriage]. Consequently, when a girl of desirable appearance is unavailable, the learned (*śiṣṭas*) marry one who is tawny (*kapilā*) or otherwise deficient; likewise, they perform the joint practice of religious duties (*sahadharmānuṣṭhāna*). In cases where a girl has lost her virginity (*kṣatayoni*) or has had another prior husband, even if she belongs to the same *pravara* lineage and so forth, they do not perform the functions of a wife under any circumstances. It is precisely for this reason that some provide an explanation of visible defects (*dṛṣṭadoṣa*) regarding the rule "one should not marry a tawny girl" (MDh 3.8), lest it be understood as being of the same uniform character as the prohibition against marrying a *sapinda* relative, even though both are contextual.
But how can there be no suspicion of marriage in the case of one who marries his brother’s wife, given that there is an explicit prohibition?

It is said in reply: A supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) is heard regarding this prohibition: "For that [woman] becomes his offspring. By this, it follows that she is not a wife for the sake of *dharma* only so long as offspring is produced; however, let her indeed have joint authority in the pursuit of wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*). Even granting this, the lack of marriage remains unrefuted because of the absence of the formal act of making her one's own (*svakaraṇābhāvāt*).

But would not, on that view, the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) be simply a maiden-born son (*kānīna*)? For he would not belong to his father, since he is the offspring of two [parents] who have not undergone the sacramental rites (*asaṃskṛta*). However, according to the view that sacramental rites are essential, the son of an appointed daughter possesses both characteristics—belonging to the father and the state of having undergone the sacramental rites—and thus it is logical that he differs from the maiden-born son, provided one of these two attributes is directly perceived. To this it is replied: We do not say that the definition of a maiden-born son does not apply to the son of an appointed daughter. Indeed, this is his definition: "A maiden, however, who gives birth to a son in secret within her father's house... [Manu 3.173].
"One should call that son born of an unmarried maiden by the name of the 'Kānīna,' [belonging] to the one who marries her. (MDh 9.172)

And its meaning is as follows: that which possesses such characteristics must be understood here in this treatise as being included among the types of *kānīna* sons. And when there arises the expectation, "Whose offspring is he?", the second sentence—"born of a maiden from her husband"—is provided.
