Alternatively, it is not the referent (*padārtha*) itself that is being defined here; rather, the relationship is being regulated. The single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) is simply this: one should declare that such a *kānīna* son belongs to the husband as his relative. Furthermore, even though the referent remains the same, the relationship is indeed differentiated by the distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhi*), according to the distinction between privacy and publicity. [379] Others say: if the referent is indeed that very same thing, then the relationship between the word and its meaning for the term *kānīna* must be understood as uncontradicted. If they remember *kānīna* as referring merely to offspring in general, let the usage of *kānīna* apply to the paternal *kānīna*. [380–381]

Others, however, say that it is memory (*smṛti*) itself that is established as the specific [criterion]. For the term *kānīna* is not applied everywhere to the mere offspring of an unmarried girl; rather, it is applied to one characterized by the *Mānava-smṛti*. We also accept this. Even though there is no usage [of the term] when the [status] is certain, the understanding of its specific qualities—such as the attainment of merit—is indeed logical based on usage, even when there is a remaining memory [of the rule]. (9.135)

Whether she has been formally appointed or not, if a mother obtains a son from a man of equal status, she becomes the mother of a grandson through him; he shall offer the funeral cake and inherit the wealth. (9.136)

Upon examining the preceding and following statements, this [text] is understood through hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) to concern specifically the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*). It has been stated that even the son of an unappointed daughter is an heir to the grandfather's wealth; how much more so, then, the son of an appointed daughter? Thus, because it serves as a supplement to another [rule], and because there would otherwise result in the futility of the injunctions regarding the appointed daughter, this is not intended for the purpose of the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) obtaining the inheritance.

But surely, in another Smṛti, the entitlement of the daughter’s son alone to offer the rice-balls (piṇḍa) is heard: “The same applies to the maternal grandfathers” (YDh 1.226). Here too, setting aside the context, it is logical to understand that the scope refers to the daughter’s son alone by the force of the direct scriptural statement: “He should give the piṇḍa and take the wealth. Likewise, another [text] has stated: “For the daughter’s son [inherits] the entire inheritance,” and so forth.

To this it is replied: Regarding what was stated, "of the maternal grandfathers" (YDh 1.226), does that plural number refer to individual persons (*vyakti*), or is it used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*) with the intention of including the maternal great-grandfather and others? If the view of individual persons is adopted, it would follow that the offering of the *piṇḍa* is to be made to only one maternal grandfather, just as in the case of the *śrāddha* and other rites. And that is contradictory once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed. For thus they say: "From this point forward, one should give [the offerings] to three. Now, if it is argued that for anyone other than the father, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* itself will not be performed, that too is not correct, because there is no prohibition against it. Furthermore, regarding the figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*), since there is no distinction in proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*), there would be a lack of understanding if the specific figurative meaning were not known; and by the force of the Smṛtis and other authorities, there is the abandonment of the immediate context (*prakaraṇa*). Thus, a contradiction arises, for a specific term is extracted from its context, just as in the case of the rule "there are twelve *upasads* for the *ahīna*" (cf. PMS 3.3.15–16). Moreover, it has already been stated that the phrase "or those who have not performed [it]" refers to something else. Therefore, this [rule] concerns the *pautrikeya* son. (9.136)
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains infinity;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun.

By the birth of a son and by the service rendered through him, one conquers—that is, attains—the ten sorrowless worlds, beginning with heaven; that is to say, one is born there. Likewise, through a grandson, one obtains infinity, meaning a long-lasting residence in those very same worlds. Through the son of a grandson (a great-grandson), one reaches the realm of Bradhna, the world of the Sun; one enjoys radiance and is no longer obscured by any darkness. 9.137
Because a son delivers his father from the hell named Put, he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-Existent One himself. (9.138)

This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) supplementary to the rules for procreating offspring. The hell named *puṃs-nāman* and the fourfold birth of living beings are designated as occurring on earth. A son who is born rescues one from that; the meaning is that he is born into the divine realm (*devayoni*). For that reason, he is designated as "son" (*putra*). (9.138)
In this world, no distinction is found between a son’s son and a daughter’s son;
for even a daughter’s son delivers him in the hereafter, just like a son’s son. (9.139)

In this context as well, the daughter's son (dauhitra) should be understood as specifically the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra). For even a daughter's son rescues him in the next world, just like a grandson; this too is merely an explanatory praise (arthavāda), since the matter has already been ordained. There is no difference between these two; for one [the grandson], the mother belongs to another family, while for the other [the daughter's son], the father does. Therefore, even a daughter's son constantly rescues him—the deceased—after death from the aforementioned hell in the next world. (9.139)
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should first offer the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) to his mother;
the second to her father, and the third to that [father’s] father. (9.140)

"In that very case, he should offer two funeral cakes (piṇḍas)—one to his father and one to his maternal grandfather" (MDh 9.132). Here, the offering of the funeral cake by the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) is stated within the context of the maternal grandfather. Therefore, this is another sequence for the offering of the funeral cake by the son of an appointed daughter: he should first offer the cake to his mother, and so forth; but the second [cake] is again for his father. It should be understood that "of his very father" refers to the father of the appointed daughter herself. However, those who read "of his father" (*pitus tasya*) offer the first cake to the appointed daughter and then offer it to her biological father. And "of his father's father" refers to the third cake for the father of the biological father himself. But in this alternative view, the offering of the cake to the maternal grandfather would not have been mentioned. (9.140)
But he whose adopted son is endowed with all good qualities shall indeed inherit that estate, even though he has come from another lineage. (9.141)

"Neither brothers nor fathers, but sons are the heirs of the father's estate" (MDh 9.185); thus, the right of all sons to inherit the estate has been stated. However, when a legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*) exists, the other sons, such as those born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), are entitled only to subsistence. "The legitimate son of the body alone is the master of the paternal wealth; however, for the sake of kindness toward the others, he should provide them with a livelihood" (MDh 9.163).

Therefore, it is already established that the adopted son (dattrima) is an inheritor of the estate. However, this statement is for the purpose of securing his share even when a legitimate son (aurasa) exists; otherwise, nothing would be effected by it.
As for how large his share shall be, some say it is equal to that of the legitimate son, since there is no specific instruction to the contrary.

That is incorrect. For if equality were intended to be expressed, then just as it was recited in the section concerning the *putrikā* (appointed daughter), it would have been recited here as well: "In that case, the division shall be equal" (MDh 9.120). Therefore, it is said that, like the *kṣetraja*, the allotment of a sixth, eighth, or other share must be applied. To this, too, there is something to be said: just as a specific share was stated for the *kṣetraja*—namely, "but the sixth part for the *kṣetraja*" (MDh 9.164)—so too will he state one for the *dattima*. Consequently, the purpose of this repetition must be considered.

But the Teacher (Upādhyāya) says: because of the repetition [of the term] and the absence of a specific qualification, it is logical that the share of the *kṣetraja* son be less than [that of the legitimate son], but not an absence of a share, nor an equal share, nor equality with the *kṣetraja*. (9.141)
An adopted son shall never take the family name or the inheritance of his biological father;
for the funeral cake follows the family name and inheritance, and the *svadhā* offering ceases for one who gives it to the wrong lineage. (9.142)

Furthermore, the fact that the adopted son (*datrima*) does not take the lineage or the wealth from his biological father has already been stated; for, having departed from that lineage, he does not inherit the family name or the estate. And since there is no taking of the lineage or the estate, he does not offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to the biological father either. For the funeral cake follows the lineage and the estate; it is only for him whose lineage and estate are inherited that the post-mortem rites, such as the offering of the funeral cake and water, are performed. [The phrase] "it departs from him" means it ceases. By this, the funeral cake, the *śrāddha* rite, and so forth—which are the means for the utterance of *svadhā*—are indicated. Thus, this principle applies to one who gives his own son to another: [the rites] cease with respect to him; they need not be performed for him. This same logic applies to the son born of a remarried woman (*sahoḍha*), the abandoned son (*apaviddha*), and the son of two fathers (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*), regarding their status as benefactors to both [fathers].

Others, however, explain *na haret na hārayet* as having the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied; they say that, like a son of two fathers (*dvaimātura*), one must provide for both. But the latter [explanation] is merely an introduction to the subsequent benefit. They interpret it thus: if the son does not take the family name and the estate, then it should be explained in this way. Yet this is not correct; for no evidence has been stated for the existence of a different meaning. (9.142)

The son of a woman not authorized [to bear a child] and the son obtained from a brother-in-law by a woman who already has a son—neither of these two deserves a share, for they are born of an adulterer and born of lust. (9.143)
It has been stated that when a husband dies without a son, a woman must seek the authorization of her elders for the procreation of a son; this [verse] is a restatement of that very point.

If a woman, though not authorized by her elders, should procreate a son out of a desire for offspring—under the delusion that "I am indeed the field of my husband, and the son born of the field (kṣetraja) is the heir to his property"—the son born of her is not an heir to the inheritance. This is because, according to the scripture, the designation "son of the field" applies only to one produced through the specific ritual procedure prescribed for sons of the field and the like; and it is precisely by that [scriptural authority] that the right of this son of the field to inherit is here precluded. However, the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) is not forbidden, even if he is born of a fallen man (*patita*). But Nārada records a specific distinction.
Those who are born of a woman not authorized by her husband—whether by one man or by many—are all non-partakers of the inheritance;
they are the sons of the seed-givers alone.

“They shall offer the funeral cake to the biological father if the mother was taken for a price; but if she was obtained without a price, the offering of the cake belongs to the husband alone. (NSm 13.18–19)

Because of the scriptural statement, because there is no injunction for their production as there is for the *kṛtrima* and other types of sons, and because they are not enumerated among the sons, those born from the seed (*bījaja*) of the three *varṇas* are entitled only to subsistence and are not heirs to the estate. For it is recorded that, without distinction, all sons [are entitled to maintenance] when the father has died; furthermore, since the remaining wealth of the father must be distributed for the benefit of the sons, they certainly receive subsistence. In this same way, those born from the seed of a *sapiṇḍa* relative of a son such as the *aurasa* are to be provided with only a share for subsistence. However, there is no status as an heir to the estate, because the status of being an heir is heard of only in reference to the specific enumerated types of sons [in the verse]: "If two [sons] should be co-heirs... (MDh 9.162). This has already been stated.

According to this view, those born of women not formally wedded and so forth would receive the inheritance of the progenitor elsewhere, because they lack a share [in the primary estate]. This "inheritance" (*riktha*) should be understood as sufficient for their maintenance. Since she has been mentioned [in the context of] the purpose of a share, she is spoken of as being like a slave-girl; she is one among those defined as "these seven sources of slavery" (MDh 8.415), whose employment is to be understood as being carried out for that purpose. One born of her is not a slave, as there is an absence of the designation "son"; even for a Śūdra, one born of such a woman shares in the means of subsistence, just like those born of Brāhmaṇas and others.

But another says: even those who perform fixed tasks are slaves, such as the bath-attendant, the barber, the cook, and the fire-tender. Likewise, women who are restrained by desire and maintained with food and clothing become slave-girls. Similarly, when there is no son for a woman who has sons, she may be authorized by her husband’s brother (*devara*). But how can there be authorization (*niyoga*) for one who already has a son? The intention is that it is the husband’s brother himself who is authorized for the sake of desire under the pretext of procreating a son.

Both [the husband and the woman] are born from an adulterer; however, the state of being born of lust applies specifically to one born of a woman who already has sons. In the case of a woman whose first marriage was for the sake of wealth, her subsequent activity is solely for the sake of a son, not out of lustful desire or greed. (9.143)
Even if a man has procreated on an appointed woman, if it is done contrary to the prescribed rule,
he is not entitled to his father's inheritance, for he was begotten by one who has fallen from his status.

"Non-observance" refers to the abandonment of the rules regarding white garments and so forth; the meaning is that such a person does not deserve the inheritance, nor is he a *kṣetraja* son. Since the husband and the brother's wife have been enjoined by the scripture, it is proper that they incur the status of outcasts (*patita*) if they proceed to procreate a son by abandoning those rules, as their intercourse was permitted only under those specific conditions. (9.144)
A son born to a woman appointed for that purpose is considered as one's own legitimate son; according to the law, that seed belongs to the owner of the field, and so does the offspring. (9.145)

The phrase "just like a legitimate son" (*aurasa*) is prescribed here for the purpose of securing the eldest share; otherwise, it would not have been stated. By this rule, the *uddhāra* (extra portion) of the eldest share is obtained by the *kṣetraja* son born of the eldest wife. Consequently, this is an exception to the rule that he "shares an equal portion with the sons" (*upasarjanaṃ pradhānasya*, MDh 9.121). Since both [texts] are authoritative, the application of the optional alternative depends upon the specific qualities [of the son]. Indeed, there is no other purpose for this verse, as everything has already been stated previously. It is said thus by way of praise because the seed belongs to the owner of the field (*kṣetrika*), the owner of the soil, since it performs its function therein. For this very reason, he says "according to *dharma*," meaning according to the scriptural ordinance. In this regard, the other means of proof is that offspring is seen in the form of physical birth. This verse is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*). (MDh 9.145)
He who takes charge of the wealth and the widow of his deceased brother shall procreate offspring for that brother and hand over that very wealth to him. (9.146)

This rule is stated for the case where there is no brother whose property has been partitioned; however, the previous rule applies to one who lives together [with his brothers]. This much is the distinction between the preceding and the following rules. He should be understood as having procreated offspring for his brother according to the law of *niyoga*. He should give it to him alone, and not to his mother as well. By this very indication, women are entitled only to maintenance, and not to sovereignty over their husband’s wealth, since it will be stated otherwise later on. "His" means that he should give the wealth of that brother whose property was partitioned. (9.146)

If a woman, being authorized, obtains a son from another man or from her husband's brother, they declare that son to be born of lust, not entitled to the inheritance, and produced by an illicit union. (9.147)

The reading *aniyuktā* (unauthorized) should be understood as a *praśleṣa* (elision of a vowel). If it is argued that this contradicts what was stated previously—since, if that were the case, [the verse] would be redundant—it has been stated here and there that the avoidance of redundancy is achieved in that manner. However, the predecessors do not accept that. Therefore, the following is the explanation: even if born of an authorized (*niyuktā*) woman, he does not deserve the paternal inheritance. Regarding the phrase "born of desire" (*kāmajam*): although he proceeds from the authorization (*niyoga*) and not from mere lust, nevertheless, desire is necessarily present therein; hence it is said, "born of that desire. He is called thus because, being "wrongly born," he is unfit for the purpose for which he was produced. And thus, this is a prohibition of the previously mentioned entitlement to a share, and therefore it is an optional alternative (*vikalpita*). As for the reading *aniyuktā*, the teacher says that it would not at all be consistent with the subsequent reading. 9.147.
This rule for the division [of inheritance] among those born of a single womb should be understood; now learn that which pertains to those born of many wives of various kinds. (9.148)

For those born of women of the same caste from a single source, there is indeed the taking of the entire inheritance. Now, they explain [the rule] regarding women of various castes from multiple wives: the term "in many" (*bahuṣu*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Others, however, consider it to be intended as a restriction. For those born of many women of various castes, there is the distribution of shares to be described later, beginning with "he shall take four shares" (MDh 9.153). But for those born of a single woman of a different caste, there is indeed the taking of the entire inheritance. 9.148.
If a Brāhmaṇa has four wives in the direct order [of castes], this is the rule recorded for the division [of property] among the sons born of them. (9.149)
The mention of "successive" (*anupūrva*) is a restatement of the sequence shown in the third [chapter]; this also serves the purpose of promising the summary that is about to be stated. || 9.149 ||
A plowman, a bull, a vehicle, an ornament, and a house—these shall be given as the additional share of the Brahmin, along with the best portion from the principal estate. (9.150)

*Kīnāśa* means a plowman; it is also applied to a miser. Because such a person is impossible [to encounter] in this context, he is not included. Thus says a *mantra*: "Indra was the lord of the plow, the Maruts were the plowmen; may the plowmen come to the pressed [Soma] with their draft-animals" (cf. AV 6.30.1). *Yāna* refers to a carriage and so forth. *Alaṃkāra* refers to rings and other ornaments worn by the father. *Veśma* means the principal [residence]. And as for "one share": from however many shares there may be, one which is the principal one must be given to him. Having set aside this much from the estate (*madhyaka*), the remainder is to be divided for the eldest according to the method to be described. (9.150)

From the inheritance, the son of a Brāhmaṇa shall take three shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, two shares; the son born of a Vaiśya woman, one and a half shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share. (9.151)

Even though it is taught that there is oneness [of the inheritance], this same method of calculation is shown to apply when there are two or many heirs who are equal sharers. However, when the number is uneven, the calculation is as follows: [9.151]
Or, having divided the entire collection of inherited property into ten parts, one who knows the Dharma should make a righteous partition according to this rule. (9.152)

"Inherited" means that which consists of wealth. "Righteous" (*dharmya*) means derived from the proclamation of Dharma. He does not approve of what was stated previously, because of the verse containing the formal proposition (*pratijñā*) that is about to be spoken. (9.152)
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, three shares;
the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share. (9.153)

Although here [in this text] no distinction is made regarding the hearing of shares for the sons of Kṣatriyas and others, in another Smṛti, a different specific share is heard for two particular [sons] based on their respective lineages (*āgama*):
"Land acquired through acceptance as a gift (*pratigraha-bhū*) must not be given to a son of a Kṣatriya woman;
even if the father should give it, when he is dead, the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take it. Thus it is said.

Land acquired by acceptance as a gift is "land obtained through acceptance. There is no prohibition regarding land acquired through purchase and other such means. Thus it is stated elsewhere: "But one born of a Śūdra woman from a twice-born man does not deserve a share of land"; this prohibits land in general for the son of a Śūdra woman. And this should be understood to apply to cases where other wealth exists; otherwise, the rule regarding the tenth part would remain applicable. Furthermore, in the absence of other wealth, there would be no livelihood at all.

I, however, say this: while the granting of a share (*bhāga*) is prohibited, the provision [of land] for the sake of livelihood (*prajīvanārthatva*) is certainly not forbidden. If it is asked what the distinction is, [the answer is: under the view of a share, since ownership of the property arises for everyone everywhere, it would apply even to giving, selling, and so forth; whereas in the other case, the livelihood belongs only to that which is produced from it. Furthermore, rice-food as a livelihood is obtained by a Śūdra from the son of a Brāhmaṇī alone—what is the use of allotting a portion of land? Thus it has been said: "He obtains the root of that livelihood according to the rule for a resident pupil" (GDh 28.39).

True; however, his subsistence must be provided on account of the paternal estate. And if it were not provided at the time of partition, then the twice-born brothers—perhaps being of bad conduct or due to some other cause—might take it away through gifting, sale, or other means. In that case, his livelihood would be cut off. But once it has been assigned, he does not obtain anything else without his permission, except for what is specifically appointed [for him]. (9.153)
Whether there be a legitimate son or even no son at all, one should not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman. (9.154)

A "virtuous son" (*satputra*) is one who exists, specifically a son of a Brāhmaṇa woman or even a son of a Brāhmaṇa man; he is intended to be one who is actually present, not merely any son of a twice-born man. Consequently, if there is no son of a Brāhmaṇa, even though sons of Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas exist, [the heir] receives an eighth share; and if there is only a son of a Vaiśya, he receives a third. Others, however, say that the term "sonless" (*aputra*) refers to the absence of any son of a twice-born man without distinction. According to this view, the remaining wealth—after the tenth share has been set aside—goes to the *sapiṇḍas*.

But this is a faultless arrangement: when the plural number refers to the security of property (*yogakṣema*), then the Śūdra takes a tenth part; however, if it is sufficient for the livelihood of only a few people, then it belongs to the son of the Śūdra alone.

The rule regarding sons born to Kṣatriyas and others from women of the same or different castes is shown in another Smṛti: "Sons born to a Kṣatriya [from wives of the three higher castes] shall receive three, two, and one shares; those born to a Vaiśya shall receive two and one shares" (YDh 2.129). Sons born to a Kṣatriya from women of his own caste down to the Śūdra caste, according to the order of the castes, are entitled to three and so forth shares. Thus, in that case, the Śūdra sons of a Kṣatriya receive a sixth part of his property, and the Vaiśya sons receive a third.

Others, however, state the implication of this verse: when one gives to the son of a Śūdra wife, then having calculated the total wealth, a tenth part should be given by him, and not more than that, even though he possesses independence; as he will say: "Whatever his father may give" (MDh 9.155).

In this view, the two words "saputraḥ" and "dadyāt" are more appropriately construed as being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Otherwise, the connection—"he whose father has a son, whether living or dead, shall give"—would be awkwardly constructed. By the term *saputra*, there is the designation of his son and others; by the phrase "shall give," there is the designation of the living son, the *sapinda* relatives, and so forth.

And therefore, if the sons of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya do not exist and there are only the Brāhmaṇa and the Śūdra, then the Śūdra does not receive only the tenth part; rather, he receives a very small amount of wealth, not more than that. Where there are ten cows, four belong to the Brāhmaṇa, one to the Śūdra, and five to the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya. When those two are absent, then five cows are to be divided between the Brāhmaṇa and the Śūdra according to that same proportion. If the Brāhmaṇa were to take all of them, he would neither be a sharer of a part nor a sharer of four parts. Therefore, the rule "he shall take four parts" (MDh 9.153) is a calculation applicable when there are four brothers. Even for the Śūdra, the status of receiving a tenth part applies only when there are four [brothers]. In the case of two, three, or four [brothers], both receive an increased share. (9.154)
The son of a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya does not share in the inheritance;
whatever his father may give to him, that alone shall be his wealth. (9.155)

The son of a Śūdra woman does not inherit the property of the twice-born. Is this always the case? No, he says: whatever his father may give, that alone is his. Whatever share of a tenth part was assigned for him by his father, that alone belongs to him; he receives nothing more than that paternal portion. Regarding this, Śaṅkha has also stated: "The son of a Śūdra woman does not share in the wealth. Whatever his father gives him, that alone is his share; however, they should give him another pair of cattle. The phrase "at the time of partition, the brothers... is the completion of the sentence.

Others, however, maintain that this rule applies to the son of an unmarried Śūdra woman, arguing that there is no indication here of a marriage. The word *śūdrā* denotes a specific caste; therefore, whatever his father might give—namely, whatever means of subsistence was given to him by the father—that alone should be given. If, however, he has already made some arrangement for his livelihood through that [inheritance] for as long as he lives, then that itself is his wealth, and nothing further need be given to him by his brothers. As Gautama says in the very section concerning the son of a Śūdra woman: "Even in the case of women not formally married, if he serves them, he may receive a share of the means of subsistence according to the rule for a pupil" (GDh 28.39).

In their opinion, those born of an unmarried Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman obtain the inheritance. However, it is not known what share they receive therein. If it is argued that "the share is the same as that of married women," even there, there is neither an indicative mark nor a scriptural statement regarding unmarried women. How is there none? Because [Manu] states, "The legitimate son of the body is indeed one alone" (MDh 9.163), the status of being an *aurasa* son applies to those born of a lawful wife (*dharmapatnī*), and the definition of an *aurasa* does not apply to those born of unmarried women. Furthermore, it has been stated: "And likewise the son of an unauthorized woman" (MDh 9.143), and so forth.

Now, this [verse] concerns the wife of one who has no brother. In that case, even though the practice of *niyoga* has been abolished and there is a prohibition stating "the son of an unauthorized woman" (MDh 9.143), the notion that it applies to her [the brotherless wife] arises. If so, does it not also apply here to those born [of such unions]? Therefore, regarding women other than one's own [wife], all sons born without *niyoga* are "sons of unauthorized women," and the means of subsistence for all of them has been declared. (9.155)
All sons born of wives of equal caste to twice-born men, having given a preferential share to the eldest, shall divide the remainder equally. (9.156)

The word "or" (*vā*), being unintelligible without a second alternative, becomes complete in its sense by referring to the subject at hand. Since the prohibition against a Śūdra inheriting the entire estate applies only to those of equal or unequal caste, it is understood to concern only the twice-born (*dvijāti*). Consequently, it is stated that if a Brāhmaṇa has no son by a Brāhmaṇī wife, sons born of Kṣatriyā or other wives shall inherit the entire estate. Likewise for a Kṣatriya, his son by a Vaiśyā [inherits].

But this is not the meaning: that after giving the preferential share (*uddhāra*) to the elder, all those born of women of a different caste (*asavarṇā*) should share equally with the sons of the same caste (*savarṇā*), because that would contradict the previously stated reduction of one share.

Even if it were argued that equality is indeed appropriate when the sons of the same caste lack qualities while the others possess them—as it has been said: [459] "It is stated: 'According to some, a son of the same caste who behaves unjustly does not receive [the inheritance]' (GDh 28.40)."

This is incorrect, because caste (jāti) is absolutely distinct [from birth]. As the teachers say: "Or rather, ownership arises from being born [to the estate]. Therefore, this is the explanation here: those who are born to women whether they be of the same caste or of a different caste—even when such women are not [legally] present—shall divide the share of the wife with the deducted portion (*uddhāra*), just like those of the same caste. (9.156)
For a Śūdra, however, only a wife of his own caste is prescribed, and no other;
those born of her shall have equal shares, even if there be a hundred sons. (9.157)

A marriage in the inverse order [of castes] is not permitted for a Śūdra; this is a restatement of what has already been said. The statement that "those born of her shall have equal shares" is made because there is no fifth distinct caste; thus, his wife is only one of his own caste (savarṇā), and no other. (9.157)
Of the twelve sons whom Svāyambhuva Manu has named for men,
six are kinsmen and heirs, while six are kinsmen who are not heirs.

This is the section on the Sūtra-sthāna that is about to be explained. The word *bandhu* is a synonym for *bāndhava*. There are six who take the lineage and inherit the estate, while the others are the opposite. The true nature of this matter will be demonstrated further below. (9.158)
The legitimate son of the body, the son begotten on the wife, the adopted son, the made son, the son secretly born, and the cast-off son—these six are both heirs and kinsmen. 9.159.
The son of an unmarried girl, the son received with a pregnant bride, the purchased son, the son of a remarried woman, the self-given son, and the Śūdra son— these six are kinsmen who do not inherit.
The indication of the number by means of two verses is for the purpose of demonstrating the two groups. 9.159–160.
Just as one obtains such a result when crossing water with a bad boat, so does one obtain such a result when crossing over darkness with bad sons. (9.161)

Because the *kṣetraja* and other sons are mentioned alongside the *aurasa* (legitimate son), there arises a suspicion that they are equal [to him]. This [verse] is for the purpose of refuting that. Bad sons, such as the *kṣetraja* and others, are not capable of providing the same benefit as an *aurasa* son. Even though no specific distinction is heard [in the text], they explain it thus because of the context.
Others, however, consider "bad sons" to be those born of women who were not authorized (*aniyuktāsutān*).
The meaning is this: while these [other sons] exist, one should not consider oneself successful by thinking, "I have a son. Rather, one must again exert effort toward procreating an *aurasa* son.

The darkness is the suffering pertaining to the next world, born of evil deeds; it is the suffering caused by the non-discharge of debts, as expressed in the text: "By offspring [one pays] to the ancestors" (TS 6.3.10.5). || 9.161 ||

If there should be two sons, one legitimate (aurasa) and one born of the wife (kṣetraja), who are co-heirs, each shall take that paternal inheritance which belongs to his own father, and not the other. (9.162)

In the case of a eunuch (*klība*), when a *kṣetraja* son has already been previously obtained—according to the rule, "He who is born on the bed of one who is deceased or diseased" (MDh 9.167)—if his eunuchhood should somehow later cease through medicine, the simultaneous existence of both a *kṣetraja* and an *aurasa* son becomes possible. However, the rule "Of those two, whatever belongs to the father of each" (MDh 9.191) would not be applicable, because the biological father alone is his progenitor; thus, he would receive only that man's inheritance. Even if the biological father were designated as a "father" by virtue of the act of procreation, the son would still be called *kṣetraja* figuratively, as he is the offspring of the owner of the field. In that situation, if the mother has taken possession of the wealth while the *aurasa* son is still a child, and a male offspring is somehow produced by one who acted improperly, and if the wealth was acquired by him through affection and other means such that the boy has no *sapiṇḍa* relatives, then in this state of affairs, the fact that the inheritance belongs to him serves as the indicative mark (*liṅga*). This shows that sons born of women not authorized for levirate (*aniyuktā-suta*) and others become heirs to the estate of the biological father when *sapiṇḍa* relatives are absent.

Others, however, explain it thus: when there is an heir already born [to the biological father], the *kṣetraja* son receives the inheritance from the biological father (*janayitṛ*), and not from the owner of the field (*kṣetrika*), provided that a legitimate son (*aurasa*) exists for the latter. And his share when a legitimate son exists has been stated: "The legitimate son and the *kṣetraja* son are both sharers in the inheritance of the father" (MDh 1.165). Likewise: "But the *kṣetraja* shall receive a sixth part" (MDh 9.164). He demonstrates how those two become co-heirs—that is, how their wealth comes into the hands of one person—just as they are described. (9.162)
The son of the body alone is the master of the paternal wealth;
however, for the sake of compassion toward the others, he should provide them with a means of subsistence.

When there is a legitimate son of the body (aurasa), all others, such as the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) and the rest, are non-heirs; they shall receive only a means of subsistence from the legitimate son of the body. This is out of compassion and is blameless. He who does not give incurs sin. (9.163)
But when dividing the paternal inheritance, the legitimate son (aurasa) should give a sixth share of the father's wealth to the son begotten on the wife (kṣetraja), or even a fifth share. (9.164)

When only the mere subsistence [of the son] has been established—as in the case of a purchased son (krīta) and others—this alternative regarding the share of the *kṣetraja* son is stated; and that [share] depends upon his qualities. 9.164.
The two sons, the aurasa (legitimate) and the kṣetraja (soil-born), are entitled to shares of the father’s inheritance;
ten others, however, in due order, are entitled to shares of the family name and the inheritance. (9.165)

The first half-verse [475] is merely a restatement of the rule previously mentioned; it does not, however, constitute a different rule. The equality of the *kṣetraja* son with the *aurasa* son is not intended.

Those belonging to the *gotra* are entitled to a share of the inheritance (*riktha*). It has been stated that a share of the inheritance is equivalent to what is necessary for subsistence. Regarding the adopted son (*dattaka*), they cite another Smṛti text which says he is like the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*). In due order: the legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*) and the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) are co-heirs simultaneously; for the others, however, the latter is the heir only in the absence of the former. As for these, regarding the statement "six are heirs, six are non-heirs" (MDh 9.158), the mention of "inheritance" (*riktha*) for both heirs and non-heirs by way of dividing them into two groups is not inconsistent, provided there is a legitimate son, in which case they are "non-heirs. The first six provide great assistance, while the other six are inferior. The first six—those other than the legitimate son—are equal in their results; likewise, the subsequent six are inferior to them. Yet, with respect to their own respective sub-groups, they are indeed equal. There is no distinction between those listed earlier and those listed later. (9.165)
But that son whom one should personally procreate in one's own field, when it has been consecrated, one should know him as the legitimate (*aurasa*) son, the first in rank. (9.166)

The word *sva* (one’s own) expresses ownership; it does not denote belonging to the same caste (*samānajātīyatā*). By this, [it is implied that] an *aurasa* son is one born from a woman who has been consecrated (*saṃskṛtā*) by oneself; otherwise, the word *saṃskṛtā* would be intended as a negation [of the consecration]. Consequently, even if she were consecrated by another, he would still be an *aurasa*. Furthermore, when the word *sva* has the aforementioned meaning, the sons of Kṣatriyas and others are also *aurasa*, for they possess no other characteristic of a son.

Others, however, considering the term "of the first kalpa" (*prāthamakalpika*) to be a qualification of the *aurasa* [son], believe that sons born of Kṣatriya women are *aurasa* even if they do not possess the complete characteristics [of a Brāhmaṇa]. But if this were the explanation, then just as an *aurasa* son born of one's own consecrated field (*svakṣetra-saṃskṛtā*) might lack complete characteristics, so too would one born of an unconsecrated woman of one's own [caste] attain that status; what then need be said of the *aurasa* status of Kṣatriyas and others? At any rate, they remain sons and partakers of a limited share. Now, it may be argued: "In the absence of the defining characteristics of the *aurasa*, the *kṣetraja*, and so forth, how can there be the status of a son, given the restriction to twelve types?"

To this it is replied: What is the use of a definition? [The relationship] is well-established through worldly convention (*vyavahāra*). For instance, people in the world say that whoever is born from someone is the son of that person. Likewise, when someone applies the term "father" to one who is not the progenitor, he is corrected by another, saying: "This is not your father; for you were not born from him. Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that the progenitor is the father and the one born is the son.

The purpose of undertaking this definition, however, is for the sake of specific designation (*viśeṣavyapadeśa*). As for the claim that "sonship" (*putratva*) belongs to one who produces a *kṣetraja* son and others, that is based on functional necessity (*kāryanibandhana*), because sonship is established even for one who has no biological son through the performance of the required rites, whereas birth is not, since birth is what is excluded [in the case of such substitutes]. Thus, these are called "substitutes" (*pratinidhi*) by them. For if sonship were based solely on birth, there would be no distinction between the *aurasa* (legitimate), *punarbhava* (born of a remarried woman), and *niyuktāsuta* (son of an appointed widow) sons, as their birth is equal. Furthermore, if it were based on performing the functions of a son, then no one at all would be "sonless. As for common worldly usage, it is inconsistent (*vyabhicārī*), since we observe the term "father" being applied even to one who is not the biological progenitor.

Therefore, even though there is an application [of the term], the usage of "son" (putra) should be understood—like the usage of "wife" (bhāryā) and so forth—from worldly convention due to the excellence of the object, like the words "Indra" and others, and from the scriptural injunctions regarding its origin, just as in the case of the term "wife."

In this regard, the statement that the *aurasa* (legitimate son) is "primary" (*prāthamakalpika*) should be understood as referring to legal procedure (*vyavahāra*). It is not [primary] in terms of legal procedure; rather, it refers to service (*upakāra*). By means of his service to the father, it is observed that the *aurasa* is able to provide greater service; thus, he is designated as "primary. Furthermore, the designation of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) is intended with respect to the diminution of service. For these other sons cannot function as substitutes for the primary son, because a substitute is possible only for a subsidiary component (*aṅga-upacāra*) of an action already commenced. A son, however, is not a subsidiary component of the ritual action, because the act of procreating offspring is a secondary action (*guṇakarman*). Therefore, while the status of being a son exists for the *kṣetraja* and others, the mention of them as "substitutes" is for the purpose of praising the status of the *aurasa*. This is just as when it is said, "Other animals are indeed non-animals (*apaśavaḥ*), but cows and horses are animals," where the statement that other animals are "non-animals" is made in order to praise cows and horses.

And when it is held that whoever is born from someone's seed is his son, this has been demonstrated in the *Mahābhārata*: although Pāṇḍu, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Vidura, and others were born from Dvaipāyana, they are not designated as "the sons of Vyāsa. Furthermore, it has been established how the status of being a legitimate (*aurasa*) son for those such as Kṣatriyas serves a specific purpose; otherwise, regarding the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*), there would result an excess over the number twelve [of sons].

Let it be so; what is the harm? Let this son be the thirteenth. Because he yields fruit equal to a legitimate son (*aurasa*), he is included among them, owing to that equality. And thus says another Smṛti: "The son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāsuta*) is equal to him" (YDh 2.132). || 9.166 ||
A son born on the bed of a man who has died, is impotent, or is diseased, from a woman appointed according to the sacred law, is known as a *kṣetraja* (son of the soil). 9.167.
"Of one who is diseased" means of one afflicted by diseases such as consumption (rājayakṣman) for which there is no remedy. The remainder is clear. 9.167.
If, in times of distress, the mother or the father should give a son with water to one who is similar [in status] and with affection, he is to be known as a son given in adoption (dattrima). 9.168.

The word *ca* (and) is appropriate to be recited as "the mother and the father"; for it is not proper to give the offspring of both [parents] if one of them does not consent. Alternatively, the word *vā* (or) may be recited; and thus it has been said: "Either the mother or the father may give [the child]," and "Of those two, the father is superior" (NSm 1.33). This refers to the context of assigning [the child] to another purpose. Now, one might object: since the mother’s ownership [of the child] ceases [upon marriage], she has no status as a giver of the son to the father.

True. Regarding the statement "from the father," it was stated that [the son must be] "similar" because the rule "in the absence of the progenitor, the mother [is the source]" (NSm 1.33) pertains to a specific application. And Vasiṣṭha says: "A woman shall neither give nor receive a son" (VaDh 15.3). This "similarity" is not by birth; rather, it is by qualities corresponding to the family. Thus, even a Kṣatriya or others may be suitable as a *dattaka* for a Brāhmaṇa. The mention of "affection" (*prīti*) is for the purpose of prohibiting [adoption] out of greed or other such motives. 9.168.
But he whom one may make similar to oneself, who is discerning of virtues and faults, and who is endowed with the qualities of a son—he is to be known as the "artificial" (kṛtrima) son. (9.169)

In this case as well, "similar" (sadṛśa) is to be understood solely in terms of quality (*guṇa*). As for those who explain it as "of the same class" (*savarṇa*), for them the reading *sajātīya* would be appropriate if that were the intended meaning; however, similarity is not [intended] by way of genus (*jāti*), but rather as has already been stated.

[He is] one who discerns virtues and faults. Some say: "One does not perform [the duties] so long as he has not attained legal capacity (*vyavahāra*), for he does not yet know virtues and faults. But then he knows thus: 'He by whom I was born, and by whom my maintenance is now performed as a son—he too, I am his son. Because there is no status of a son other than that which is accepted, he must be regarded in that very way; however, there is no difference between the two cases. (9.169)
He who is born in a house but whose father is not known is one born secretly in the house; he belongs to him from whose wife he was begotten. (9.170)

Nor would it be known who the mother is if she has gone out many times due to confusion; in that case, his caste would not be known, for it was said by the ancients: "One whose seed-giver is unknown [is defined] by the mother. And this applies where there is no suspicion of a man of lower caste; for if such suspicion exists, there is the possibility of a *pratiloma* (inverse-caste) birth. Due to being *pratiloma*, he has no entitlement to the duties of a son anywhere. (9.170)
A son whom one may adopt after he has been abandoned by both his parents or by either of them is called an *apaviddha* (abandoned son). 9.171.

By one who has given birth to many children, who is unable to support them, who is in extreme distress, or due to some defect such as a lack of devotion to mother and father—but not on account of having fallen from caste (pātitya), for it is shown that such a person has no entitlement whatsoever to the duties toward a son—this too is a form of abandonment by one or the other. Acceptance [of the child] is done with the thought that he is a son, and not merely out of a desire for his life. (9.171)
If a maiden, however, should secretly give birth to a son in her father's house, one should call him by the name "Kānīna" (maiden-born); he is produced from the maiden, not from the husband. (9.172)

This verse has been explained previously [513]. The allotment of shares for those sons who are self-given (*svayaṃdatta*), artificial (*kṛtrima*), or abandoned (*apaviddha*) has also been determined earlier. Furthermore, the prohibition against accepting land as a gift applies only when other wealth exists [514, 515]. (9.172)
If a woman who is pregnant is married, whether her condition be known or unknown, the child belongs to the one who marries her; such a son is called *sahoḍha*. (9.173)
If one should purchase from his mother and father a son for the sake of offspring, he is that man's "bought" son (krītaka), whether he be similar or dissimilar [to him]. (9.174)
She who, having been abandoned by her husband or being a widow, produces offspring by her own will after marrying again, is called *paunarbhava*. (9.175)
If she is one whose virginity is intact, or even if she has returned from another, she deserves to undergo the marriage rite again with her new husband. (9.176)
He who is deprived of his parents, or abandoned by them without cause, and offers himself to someone—that is known as "self-given" (svayaṃdatta). || 9.177 ||
The son whom a Brāhmaṇa may father out of lust upon a Śūdra woman is a mere corpse even while still alive;
therefore, he is known as a Pāraśava.

The phrase "out of desire" (*kāmāt*) is a restatement of [the rule] "but for those who act out of desire" (MDh 3.12). Even one who assists by offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth is equal to a corpse; he is non-beneficial because his assistance is incomplete. || 9.178 ||
If a son is born to a Śūdra by a female slave or the female slave of a slave, he may, with permission, take a share; such is the established law. (9.179)

A son born even to a *śūdra* from an unmarried woman who has not been authorized [for such intercourse] is indeed a legitimate son (*suta*). Thus, although the term "slave-girl" (*dāsī*) refers to the slave himself, nevertheless, according to the scriptural statement, a son born of her belongs not to the slave, but to the master of the slave. If permitted by his father, he shall take an equal share with the legitimate son (*aurasa*) when the inheritance is being divided during the father's lifetime; otherwise, if the father should say, "This one is to have an equal share with you. But when the father does not grant permission, it is stated in another *Smṛti*: "Even one born of a slave-girl by a *śūdra* shall, if desired, be a sharer of the inheritance" (YDh 2.137). "If desired" means whatever share the father permits. "When the father has died, the brothers shall make him a half-sharer" (YDh 2.138). "They shall make him [a half-sharer]" means that, in relation to their own shares, they shall each take two parts for themselves and give one part to him. "If he has no brothers, he shall take everything, except for the son of a daughter" (YDh 2.138). In the absence of legitimate sons (*aurasa*), he alone shall take the entire estate, provided there is no daughter’s son (*dauhitra*). If such a daughter’s son exists, the same rule applies to him as to the legitimate son, because no other [heir] is mentioned and because he is present in the mind due to being the subject under discussion.
But for Brahmins and the other castes, the sons of female slaves are entitled only to subsistence and do not share in the inheritance; such is the settled rule. (9.179)
The wise declare that these eleven sons, beginning with the son of the wife (kṣetraja) as previously described, are substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the failure of religious rites. (9.180)

In the absence of the primary [son], there is a substitute; therefore, it is implied that these [other sons] are to be adopted when the legitimate son (*aurasa*) is absent. A different order for these is stated in another *smṛti*: for instance, by some the son born of a secret marriage (*gūḍhotpanna*) is the fifth, while by others he is the sixth. In this regard, the order of recitation is not a formal constituent part here, precisely because the sequence is presented without fixed restriction. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate later that the purpose [of the sequence] does not constitute a constituent part.

On account of the omission of ritual duties, the injunction "one must procreate offspring" is established so that its neglect may not occur; for this injunction is obligatory. It must be fulfilled by the householder in some manner or another. Among these, the primary method is through one's own legitimate son (*aurasa*); in the absence of that, these secondary methods (*anukalpa*) should be resorted to. (9.180)
These sons who have been mentioned incidentally as being born from the seed of others: they belong to him from whose seed they were born, and not to anyone else. (9.181)

They explain that in the absence of what was previously mentioned, this is a prohibition of the rule: those substitutes which were stated as being to be performed in the absence of a legitimate son (aurasa) are not to be performed; because they are born from the seed of another, they are the sons of that [man] alone and not of the other. The meaning is that they do not belong to the one by whom they are adopted.

Therefore, since the former [text] prescribes and this one prohibits, there is an option (*vikalpa*). And that option is settled with respect to the inheritance: the *kānīna*, *sahoḍha*, *punarbhava*, and *gūḍhotpanna* sons do not share in the inheritance; however, the *dattaka* and others do share in the inheritance when there is no legitimate son (*aurasa*). Furthermore, the *kānīna* and others do not take the father’s wealth even when there is no legitimate son; they receive only food and clothing, whether a legitimate son exists or not. For it has been said: "It is right for the wise man to give to all of them as much as he is able."
For one who does not provide food and clothing to an extreme degree would indeed be fallen. (MDh 9.202) || 9.181 ||
If among brothers born of the same father one should have a son, Manu has declared that they all become possessed of sons through that son. (9.182)
If among all the wives of one husband even one should have a son, Manu has declared that they are all possessed of sons by virtue of that son. (9.183)
In the absence of a more worthy person, one who is less worthy is entitled to the inheritance;
however, if there are many of equal status, all are sharers of the estate. (9.184)
Neither brothers nor fathers, nor sons are the heirs to the father's estate;
rather, the father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, as shall the brothers. (9.185)
Water should be offered to three; the funeral cake proceeds to three; the fourth is the giver of these; a fifth is not assigned. (9.186)
The wealth of each person shall belong to his nearest sapinda;
after him, it shall go to a sakulya, or else to the teacher or the pupil. (9.187)
But in the absence of all these, Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas, pure, and self-controlled shall be the heirs; thus the Dharma is not violated. 9.188.
The property of a Brāhmaṇa is always inviolable by the king; this is the established rule. However, in the absence of all [heirs], the king may take the property of the other castes. (9.189)
For one who has died childless, one should obtain a son from a member of the same lineage; whatever wealth there may be, that one should bestow upon him. 9.190.
But if two [sons] born of two [different men] should dispute over the wealth of their mother, each shall take what belonged to his own father, and not the other. (9.191)
When the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the maternal inheritance equally. (9.192)
Whatever daughters they may have, to them also something should be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth, according to their merit and with affection. (9.193)

That which is given before the nuptial fire, that which is received from the father's house, that which is given as a token of affection, and that which is obtained from a brother, a mother, or a father— this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman.

Whatever was given as a post-nuptial gift (anvādheya) and whatever was given by a husband who was pleased—this shall be the property of the offspring of a woman who has died while her husband is still living. (9.195)
Whatever property exists in marriages contracted according to the Brahma, Daiva, Arsha, Gandharva, or Prajapatya rites,
it is ordained that it belongs to the husband alone when the wife dies childless.
Whatever wealth may have been given to her in marriages such as the Āsura and others, it is ordained that upon her death without offspring, it shall belong to her mother and father.
Whatever property may belong to a woman, however given by her father, that a Brāhmaṇī wife shall take; or it shall belong to her daughter, or to her offspring. (9.198)
Women should not carry out any acquisition from the midst of the large family, nor even from their own wealth, without the permission of their husband. (9.199)
Whatever ornaments may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do so fall from their status. (9.200)

Those who have no share [of the inheritance] are the impotent, the outcaste, those blind from birth, the deaf, as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of sense organs. (9.201)
However, it is right for a wise person to give to all of them according to his ability;
food and clothing should be provided indefinitely, for one who does not give becomes fallen. (9.202)

It has been shown that this applies to all, including the impotent and others, as they are the subject under discussion. "Entirely" means for as long as one lives. Since food and clothing are for the purpose of maintaining the body, it should be understood that wages must also be given to servants and other attendants who are useful for that purpose; for it is not possible for the blind and others to live without an attendant. For those who hold the view that marriage is permissible, maintenance must be provided for them along with their wives. According to one's capacity—that is, in proportion to one's wealth—food, clothing, and so forth should be given. The term "outcast" (*patita*) is a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). (9.202)
If, however, there should somehow be a desire for wives on the part of eunuchs and others, their offspring, having produced [their own] progeny, shall be entitled to the inheritance. (9.203)

Desire is the longing for union, which is the cause of pleasure. When that exists, one should marry. In that case, offspring—whether a son or a daughter—born into the lineage is entitled to the inheritance, the division of the estate. As for the daughter’s share, it has been stated previously. However, as for the impotent man who lacks seed, although he may indeed have a desire for sexual intercourse, how could there be the production of progeny for him?

And it has been said: "He who is born of the bed [of another], or of one who is deceased, impotent, or diseased" (MDh 9.167). By this verse, the fact that marriage is motivated by passion (*rāga*) is demonstrated; for if it were motivated by duty (*dharma*), how could there be marriage for those who are ineligible for ritual acts? Furthermore, the eligibility for initiation (*upanayana*) is shown for those who are blind from birth, the lame, and the impotent whose seed is wind; however, the insane and others are not eligible for initiation—how, then, could they have marriage?

And the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*) has its purpose fulfilled within the context already mentioned; for if, by the force of the inclusion of "etc.," everyone were to be included, then even one who has fallen from his caste (*patita*) would be included, which is not desired because it contradicts the *Smṛti* texts.
Alternatively, this rule should be understood as applying when those who have completed their studies and contracted marriage become insane or otherwise afflicted.
But surely, for those who have contracted marriage, the phrase "if there is a desire for wives" (*yady arthitā tu dāraiḥ*) would be inappropriate?

This is not so, because for those who have already married, there can be no desire for a wife. However, the ancients saw a purpose even for this righteous marriage; therefore, since a eunuch has the right to perform the Smārta rites, a marriage for that purpose is indeed appropriate even in the absence of such a desire. But regarding the Śrauta rites, since the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) occurs only after one has fathered a son, a eunuch has no right to them. Furthermore, that which is logically the motivating cause [of the marriage] must be demonstrated. (9.203)
Whatever property the eldest son acquires after his father has died, the younger brothers have a share in it, provided they are devoted to learning. (9.204)

If one should produce an increase in yield from a field—whether through some clever stratagem or by means of friends inherited from one’s paternal line, such as the king, ministers, or domestic priests—that belongs to all [the co-owners] in common. One must not think: "This was not previously acquired by my father; I have obtained this; it is mine alone. This rule applies to those who live by their learning (*vidyājīvinaḥ*), such as artisans, craftsmen, and the like, as well as to physicians, actors, singers, and so forth, because of the expression "those who preserve their learning" (*vidyānupālinaḥ*). (9.204)
But if all those who were ignorant should acquire wealth through their own efforts, it is the settled rule that there should be an equal division of it, as it is not ancestral property. (9.205)

Non-earned property consists of [wealth acquired through] agriculture, trade, service to the king, and so forth. In that regard, one should not take account of slight inequalities [in the amount]. Even there, if something has been acquired by anyone to a great extent, there is indeed no division [of it among the heirs]. However, the statement is intended to prohibit the eldest’s special share (*jyeṣṭhāṃśa*) in such cases. But when there is only a slight excess, an equal distribution of shares for all is prescribed. Because of the causal phrase "not inherited from the father" (*apitrya*), this same rule applies even to the property of one who dies without offspring. (9.205)

But whatever constitutes his wealth from learning shall belong to him alone; the same applies to what was received through friendship, at a wedding, or as the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka). (9.206)

That which is acquired through learning—such as teaching and the like—or through skill in a craft; likewise, that obtained from a friend; and that which is received on account of marriage (*audvāhika*); and also that obtained for the sake of progeny (*sāntānika*). That which is received for officiating at a sacrifice (*mādhuparkika*) is [also included]. Although this too constitutes wealth acquired through learning, nevertheless, because it is acquired specifically by means of the occasion of officiating at a sacrifice, it is designated separately. Others hold that *audvāhika* is what is obtained from the house of the father-in-law, since it is received on account of the marriage ceremony. (9.206)
But he among brothers who, though capable by his own labor, does not desire wealth, shall be excluded from his share after being given something for his subsistence. (9.207)

When brothers live together and manage their father’s existing wealth through agriculture and other means, if one among them does not participate in such management, this exclusion is prescribed for him: "He is to be excluded from his own share. This means he is to be removed from the distribution. Whatever profit was generated by his own labor from the wealth he managed should not be given to him; however, there is no prohibition regarding the paternal principal itself. Even in that case, he is not to be entirely excluded; rather, having taken for himself a portion of the fruit of his own hardship sufficient for his subsistence, the remainder should be given to him.

Alternatively, he should be excluded and separated; he must not be allowed to live together [with the others]. Since the wealth was acquired through a common exertion of power at a later time, there may be an equal division of shares. In this regard, Nārada has shown the method for determining the shares: according to that rule, one who has emerged from or departed from [the community] receives a larger share, while one who has remained unmentioned receives a smaller share. (9.207)
That which has been acquired by one's own effort through labor, without depleting the paternal estate, being obtained by one's own exertion—that he need not give against his will. (9.208)

The non-giving of knowledge that one has acquired by oneself has already been stated. By this [verse], it is declared that what is obtained through other means, such as agriculture and the like, need not be given.

But surely, this verse need not have been spoken; for it would follow simply from the principle that "what is obtained by one's own effort—that is, by one's own exertion—one need not give if one is unwilling. What, then, is the purpose of the verse concerning wealth acquired through learning and so forth? It is said: because in the case of mantras, marriages, and similar matters, one’s own effort does not necessarily suffice for everything, they are designated separately. (9.208)
But whatever paternal property a father may acquire that was previously unobtained, he need not share that with his sons if he so desires, as it was acquired by himself. (9.209)
If the father seeks something other than what was acquired by himself, that which he has personally earned shall not be divided against his will even by sons who have attained their legal rights.
Furthermore, while the father is still living, what is the time for the partition of the sons?

It is said: When the father himself divides the property among his sons, it has been stated: "When the mother’s menses have ceased" (NSm 13.3), and "or while he [the father] is living and desires [to divide]" (GDh 28.2). Likewise: "When the father is free from desire, or when his passion has ceased" (NSm 13.3). Otherwise, however, as soon as the sons are born, they immediately become masters of their grandfather’s wealth. And so it has been said: "Land acquired by the grandfather, or a fixed endowment, or even movable property..."
In that case, there would be equal ownership for both the father and the son. (YDh 2.124)

Even though the son possesses ownership, as long as [the other sons] have not yet attained it, all [sons] are entitled to share in the grandfather’s wealth because there is no distinction whatsoever; for partition is preceded by [the establishment of] ownership. The father’s wealth must not be employed in transactions such as pledges or sales once a son has been born; however, its application for purposes such as yoga or the maintenance of the family has already been shown. Even though the sons possess ownership in this state according to established practice (*ācāra*), it is inferred from the observation of a censure—namely, "those who are divided against their father's will" (GDh 15.19)—that those who divide [the estate] by force are sinful. Just as ownership arises through the acceptance of a gift from an unworthy person (*asatpratigraha*), yet the fault lies with the individual, so too that which is inherited through lineage is indeed impure in this way. Therefore, when another means is possible, the father should not be petitioned [for his consent], for in that case it would be unrighteous (*adharma*).

Even wealth acquired by oneself must certainly be divided once one recognizes that the sons have attained their rights and possess merit. And it has been said: "When established in age, the father shall divide his sons; he shall give the eldest an excellent share and the others equal shares" (cf. NSm 13.4). Nor does this refer to the grandfather’s wealth; for in that case, the father has no power to grant an additional share to the eldest, since the ownership of both [father and son] is equal. As for the statement: "A division made by the father—whether unequal or excessive—is declared to be lawful" (YDh 2.120), they maintain that this applies to the grandfather’s property as well, but only to a very small extent; for where two full shares have not been taken, it would indeed be an exception in the case of self-acquired property. (9.209)
If those who were divided while living together should divide again, the division in that case shall be equal; there is no right of primogeniture therein. (9.210)

The meaning of this verse is clear. Regarding the rule of partition, the statement is intended to remove any suspicion that a preferential share (*uddhāra*) might still be expected; for there is the declaration: "It is the settled rule that [the property] does not belong to the father" (MDh 9.205). This implies that a preferential share of the paternal estate would normally be taken. However, in this case, the statement is made because of the concern that, by virtue of past circumstances, the paternal property may no longer exist. (9.210)
If the eldest or the youngest among them should be deprived of his share, or if either of them should die, his portion is not lost. (9.211)

If, among brothers, the eldest or the youngest brother is excluded from the distribution of shares—at the time of distribution being the "time of partition"—due to a cause such as falling from his caste (pātitya) or other reasons for non-partition, or if he dies, his share is not lost. This is the procedure regarding it: Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.119.
The uterine brothers, having come together and assembled, shall divide it equally; as shall the brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters. (9.212)

Those whose wealth is commingled (*saṃsṛṣṭa*)—namely, the uterine brothers (*sodarya*)—should take [the inheritance], as well as the uterine sisters (*sanābhayaḥ*). Uterine sisters who are unmarried (*aprattā*) are indeed designated as "uterine" (*sanābhi*); however, those who are married (*prattā*) undergo the status of their husband's lineage (*gotra*), and thus they are no longer "uterine" (*sanābhayaḥ*) in relation to their brothers. Regarding the phrase "and those who are commingled," the word "and" (*ca*) includes the sisters. However, one should not entertain the doubt that "the uterine brothers and those brothers who are commingled" [are the ones entitled]. If that were the case, it would follow that even non-uterine brothers who are commingled would receive a share. Indeed, there are both uterine brothers who are not commingled and uterine brothers who are commingled; where both exist, they should take their respective shares through partition. And this would not be contradictory.

But a uterine brother who is a reunited coparcener shall take the wealth; one who is not a uterine brother shall not take it. Even if he is not a reunited coparcener, a uterine brother shall take it, but not one born of a different mother. (YDh 2.143)

This is the meaning: a stepbrother does not take [the inheritance], even if he is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* (one who has reunited), when a uterine brother exists, even if that uterine brother is not a *saṃsṛṣṭin*. Among the uterine brothers, only he with whom [the deceased] was reunited takes it, and no other, despite their being uterine. Thus it is said: "But a *saṃsṛṣṭin* takes the share of a *saṃsṛṣṭin*, and a uterine brother that of a uterine brother" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.142). However, when there are no uterine brothers at all, then only those stepbrothers with whom he was reunited shall take it, and not others. They say that for uterine brothers who have been divided but live together in close proximity, even though they are divided, a special duty arising from their common origin is recognized as existing through their physical presence.
Therefore, even among those who have been partitioned, if one of them dies, the uterine brother alone shall take [the share]; his portion is not lost.
Nor should it be objected that "at that time, no portion had arisen for him, so how can a loss be considered?
For it has been stated: "When [the right] has arisen, he is to be called the owner," and "For they have no power while [the parents] are living" (MDh 9.104). || 9.212 ||
In this regard, it demonstrates that immediately after the father’s death, ownership belongs to the sons:
"If an eldest brother, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers, he shall lose his status as the eldest, he shall receive no share, and he must be restrained by the kings. (9.213)

"Insult" (*vinikāra*) refers to contempt shown during royal ceremonies and the like; "deceiving others with wealth" means [the elder] is to be honored like a kinsman even if he is not the eldest—this has been stated. This is not a prohibition of all conduct appropriate for an elder in every respect. Furthermore, "not receiving a share" means being ineligible for the portion due to the eldest. He is to be restrained because no specific instruction is given; that is, by means of verbal punishment and the punishment of reproach, and by monetary punishment when the offense corresponds to the value of the property involved. (9.213)

All brothers who are engaged in improper occupations do not deserve a share of the wealth; nor should an elder brother make a separate acquisition for himself without giving a portion to the younger brothers. (9.214)

Those engaged in improper occupations, those who practice forbidden acts, those who act without authorization, those who have not taken a wife, and those whose wives are slave-girls—since there is a separate prohibition against one who has fallen from his caste (*patita*), this prohibition applies to those who persist in such [improper] conduct. If, having accepted their wealth for use, one should carry it as interest or as a separate gift (*yautaka*), then for those who are managing it for the sake of the family, one should set aside what belongs to the other brothers, thinking: "When they ask, 'Where is that wealth? I shall show them the principal. Such [wealth], even with its interest, he should cause to be given to all of them. However, if at that very time he should show it to the brothers, saying, "This extra amount is seen; take it according to your shares, and I too will carry the interest on that separately from my own," then they have no share; that [gift] belongs to him alone. (9.214)
If brothers who have not divided their inheritance should rise up together [in business], the father must by no means allot unequal shares to their sons. (9.215)

Regarding what was stated: "The partition made by the father is declared lawful for those who have been divided unequally or unequally [in status]" (YDh 2.120), there is a prohibition of that in this specific case. "Rising together" means that all of them acquire wealth; some through agriculture and the like, some through receiving gifts, some through service, and some by protecting what has been acquired and employing it as needed when they are not present. All of that, having been pooled together, must be divided equally. Nothing more than the father's share should be given to anyone out of affection or similar motives. (9.215)
But one who is born after the partition shall take only the paternal wealth;
or, those who may have reunited with him, he shall divide that property with them. || 216 ||

After the partition, if the father has taken two shares during the division—as stated in the rule, "he shall receive two shares" (NSm 13.12)—that very amount must be accepted by him if the father so desires, whether before or after the father's death. In that case, the brothers may not object, saying, "Why does he take two shares? However, if the father has no such desire, then an equal share, equivalent to their own, must be set aside for him.

The paternal share belongs only to those who have reunited after their father’s death. As it has been said: "One should give or take the share for one who is born and for one who has died" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.142). For one who is born, the reunited kinsmen alone should give [the share]; and after the father's death, they should give his share equally, with the understanding expressed in the verse: "Those who were divided, [if they reunite] together... (Manu Smṛti 9.210). Vasiṣṭha has shown that "for a sister, there is no division at all until her delivery. (9.216)
The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring;
and when the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth. (9.217)
This verse has been explained. || 9.217 ||
When all debts and assets have been distributed according to the rule, whatever may subsequently be discovered, all that should be divided equally. (9.218)

If, through ignorance, a portion was divided as too small or too large, it should be known by others and made equal. Furthermore, after the division has taken place, there is no "extra share" (uddhāra) for the eldest regarding what is subsequently acquired. 9.218.
Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women, security of possession, and pasture land are declared to be indivisible. (9.219)

The unity [of ownership] is intended for clothes, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, and water. A *patra* is a vehicle, such as a carriage or a cart. An ornament is a ring or the like. Clothing is of equal value, not of high price. Water refers to wells, ponds, and so forth. Women refers to female slaves. *Yogakṣema* is that from which security (*kṣema*) arises during acquisition (*yoga*); it includes ministers, domestic priests, counselors, elders, and the dwelling place (*vāstu*).
