From that [dwelling], protection against thieves and others is obtained. And it is recited in another Smṛti: "There is no partition regarding the dwelling place. Regarding *pracāra*, it is where cows graze. He says, "In a *pravetra* [or pasture]. By this, he demonstrates that what was stated by the father—"for there is no transgression of Dharma here"—is untenable; for those prohibitions apply to things not seen [in common], and thus there would be no unrighteousness (*adharma*) from their transgression. (9.219)
This division of property among you sons and the procedure for their rites has been declared; now learn in due order the law concerning gambling and betting. 9.220.
The king should prohibit gambling and betting within his kingdom;
these two vices bring about the end of kings who rule the earth. (9.221)
Gambling and betting are open forms of theft;
therefore, the king should always exert effort to suppress them. (9.222)
That which is performed with inanimate objects is called "gambling" (dyūta) in the world;
but that which is performed with animate beings is to be known as "betting" (samāhvaya). 9.223.
The king shall cause to be executed all those who engage in gambling or betting, or cause others to do so, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born. (9.224)
He should quickly banish from the city gamblers, actors, cruel men, those belonging to heretical sects, men engaged in forbidden occupations, and liquor-sellers. (9.225)
These, existing in the kingdom as the king’s hidden thieves, constantly afflict the virtuous subjects through their improper actions. || 9.226 ||
In ancient times, this gambling was seen to cause great enmity;
therefore, a wise man should not indulge in gambling, even for the sake of amusement. (9.227)
Whosoever man should practice such an act, whether secretly or openly,
there shall be a choice of punishment for him according to the king's will.

The various conceptual constructions (*kalpa*) are mental constructs (*vikalpa*). It is said by the King himself: "Learn the law of gambling" (MDh 9.220); from that point onward, two or three verses are prescriptive (*vidhāyaka*), while all the rest are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*). [585] 9.220–228.
But a member of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra caste who is unable to pay a fine shall attain freedom from debt through labor; a Brāhmaṇa, however, shall pay it back very gradually. (9.229)

Kṣatriyas and others who are destitute of wealth must not be brought to ruin by means of imprisonment. Rather, they should be made to pay the fine through their labor—specifically, that work which is appropriate for them and useful to the king. A Brāhmaṇa, however, should be made to pay gradually, without detriment to his family; for him, the acts of confinement and corporal punishment are forbidden. The verse previously cited concerned the subject of creditors; this one concerns the subject of fines. Thus, there is no tautology. (9.229)
The king should inflict punishment upon women, children, the insane, the elderly, the poor, and the sick by means of whips, split bamboo, ropes, and the like. (9.230)

Regarding *dama* [587]: even when performing labor, only those who are poor and incapable are taken; they are to be beaten with whips (*śiphā*) and the like, because they are equal to those who have committed great sins (*mahāpātakin*). *Śiphā* means a creeper; *vidala* means tree bark. 9.230.
But those who, having been appointed to official duties, ruin the affairs of the litigants while being consumed by the heat of wealth—those the king shall render destitute. (9.231)

Those officials, such as the royal representatives (*rājasthānīya*) and others, who are appointed and authorized to oversee the legal proceedings and other affairs of litigants—both plaintiffs and defendants—if, while being scorched by the heat of wealth, they should ruin those cases by taking money from one side or the other, the king must render them destitute; confiscating all their property is the punishment to be inflicted upon them.

For courtiers who act through habitual practice, even though there exists the prescription of other punishments to be mentioned later, this very punishment is the appropriate one. Furthermore, those others such as army commanders and the like who, having been appointed to assist someone, seize wealth and then cause its destruction—they too are to be punished in this very same manner.

Others, however, read the text with the elision of the vowel *a* (i.e., *aniyuktāḥ*), meaning: "those who are not appointed. This punishment applies to those who, due to royal favor or superior force, provide assistance to one person for the purpose of ruining the business of another.
The phrase "by the heat of wealth" is not intended to be emphasized; rather, the term "unauthorized" (*aniyuktā*) alone is the primary factor. || 9.231 ||
He shall put to death those who forge royal edicts, those who corrupt the subjects, those who kill women, children, or Brahmins, and likewise those who serve his enemies. (9.232)

Those who forge forged edicts (*kūṭaśāsana*) are those who declare that what was not even commanded by the king was indeed enacted by the king. An edict (*śāsana*) is a royal decree. A document written by a scribe authorized by the king—such as "one must not eat in this person's house," "this favor has been granted to him by command," or "this rule has been established by the king"—is an edict; it is called an edict because it is constrained by the king's command. They produce and maintain such forgeries. They are corrupters and sowers of dissension among the subjects who are angry or greedy. They are killers of women, children, and even Brahmins. They serve enemies—that is, they serve the king's foes—and move back and forth in secret. (9.232)
Whatever may have been decided and adjudicated anywhere, one should know that it is done according to dharma; one who has come into existence [as a successor] shall not overturn it. (9.233)

In whatever royal court a legal matter has been adjudicated—that is, settled and finalized upon the completion of the judicial proceedings—the king should recognize that as indeed done, provided it was not merely spoken with truthful words but was also formally decreed and a punishment was imposed. He must not reverse that decision except by imposing a double fine. As it is said: "Having imposed a double fine, he may reopen that case" (NSm Mā 1.56). || 9.233 ||
In the previous case, the revocation was due to the receipt of wealth; this case, however, is due to another cause, such as ignorance and so forth.
Whatever legal matter the ministers or the judge may have decided otherwise, the king himself shall decide that matter and fine them one thousand [paṇas]. (9.234)

The minister includes those such as the *rājasthānīya* and others; he, along with [the perpetrator], shall be fined one thousand [paṇas]. Just as in the case of the fine of one hundred paṇas for Garga, the completion of the sentence occurs through the collective sense [of the group]. (9.234)

The slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—all these men are to be known individually as perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin). 9.235.

A Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor is a perpetrator of a mortal sin (mahāpātakin). A thief is one who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa—not just anyone at all. This restatement of what has already been said is for the sake of what follows. 9.235.
And for these four who do not perform expiation, he shall prescribe a lawful punishment involving both corporal and monetary fines. (9.236)

But surely, only a Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor is a sinner; and for him, there is no corporal punishment, according to the rule: "There is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa" (GDh 12.46). In that case, how can it be said that [the punishment applies] to all four? Some say: the term "outcast" (*patita*) is understood here as including one who has associated with such persons, even though he was not previously mentioned, by virtue of the force of the number "four.
Others, however, say that "branding" (*aṅkana*) is what is connected to the body, and that this also applies to the Brāhmaṇa.
Others, however, say that because of the word *api* ("also"), this punishment applies to all five;

or even to four, and by the word *api*, also to the fifth who is associated with them. Regarding the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, corporal punishment has already been stated previously: "One should put to death those who kill women, children, or Brāhmaṇas" (MDh 9.232). By this [verse], branding—which involves the internal body—is specifically intended. The term *dharmyam* means that the severity or lightness of the penalty must be made proportionate to the offense. (9.236)
For violating the teacher’s bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern banner;
for theft, the foot of a dog should be made; and for killing a Brahmin, the figure of a headless man.
The branding on the forehead is for the purpose of non-prohibition, because of the scriptural injunction: "They shall not be branded on the foreheads by the king" (MDh 9.240). || 9.237 ||
Indeed, being unfit to eat with, unfit to sacrifice for, unfit to study with, and unfit to marry, they shall wander the earth in misery, excluded from all religious duties. (9.238)

Since the prohibition of [partaking in] communal feasts (*saṃbhojana*) and so forth is already established by the very mention of "all things" (*sarvadharma*), these specific items are included here in order to demonstrate the gravity of the offense. *Saṃbhoga* means eating together in one place and listening to songs and the like. *Saṃyājana* means officiating at sacrifices for those very people, or officiating at sacrifices together with them; the same should be understood for *saṃpāṭha* (reciting together). Regarding *asaṃpāṭhyāvivāhinaḥ*: this is a *dvandva* compound meaning both those with whom one should not recite and those with whom one should not marry. Regarding *dīnāḥ*: even though one possesses wealth, to abandon pieces of cloth and such by eating alms-food and the like associated with them, and due to the extreme contempt shown by others. (9.238)
But these, having been branded with the mark, must be abandoned by their kinsmen and relatives; they shall be without compassion and without salutation—such is the command of Manu. 9.239.

"Those whose characteristics have been established" means that when the relationship of cause and effect has been determined. Even if they are afflicted by disease and other such conditions, one should not show them compassion; and even if they possess qualities such as seniority, they are not to be saluted with rising from one's seat and other such gestures. This alone is to be understood as the dharma, by virtue of the force of the statement. (9.239)

But those of the higher castes who perform the prescribed penance as declared shall not have a mark branded on their foreheads by the king; rather, they should be made to pay the highest fine. (9.240)

For those of the [three] higher castes other than the Śūdra who perform penance, there is no branding; however, as punishment, they shall be made to pay the highest fine of one thousand paṇas. (9.240)
For offenses against a Brāhmaṇa, the middle amercement shall be imposed; or he may be banished from the kingdom, along with his wealth and his belongings. (9.241)

The phrase "but those performing penance" (*prāyaścittaṃ tu kurvāṇāḥ*) from MDh 9.240 is not required here. For these offenses, such as the killing of a Brahmin, a Brāhmaṇa is to be fined the middle amercement. The word "unintentionally" (*akāmataḥ*) is drawn forward from the subsequent verse. After being fined, he should be made to perform penance, along with his belongings; this applies to a virtuous Brāhmaṇa who is worthy of favor. Or, if it was unintentional, he should not be exiled. "But others who have committed these sins unintentionally deserve the forfeiture of all their property; but if intentionally, they deserve banishment. (9.242)

Other castes, such as the Kṣatriyas and others, who have committed these sins—the great crimes (mahāpātakas)—unintentionally and without desire, shall be deprived of all their property. Some authorities maintain that this punishment is an alternative to the preceding one even for those performing penance; however, for intentional acts, death is prescribed for them. For a Śūdra, if he acts unintentionally, there is branding and confiscation of all property; if intentional, there is death. (9.242)
A righteous king must not take the wealth of one who has committed a mortal sin;
for by taking it out of greed, he becomes tainted by that very guilt. (9.243)
But has it not been established that the king’s livelihood consists of punishment by means of wealth? Why, then, is such wealth not included here?
It was stated in the intervening passage [at 9.243]: "Those whose punishment has been removed by the king... etc.
Having cast that staff into the waters, he should offer it to Varuṇa;
or he should present it to a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct.

Meditating with the mind on the words "This is for Varuṇa," one should give it into the waters—that is, cast it into the waters—or else give it to a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct. 9.244.
Varuṇa is the lord of punishment, for he is the wielder of the rod over kings;
a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas is the lord of the entire world. (9.245)

This is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the preceding injunction regarding the performance [of the penance]. Varuṇa rules over the punishment for those who have committed mortal sins (*mahāpātakin*); since he is the wielder of the rod, the leader, and the ruler of kings, it follows by this that the Brāhmaṇa also is the master of that wealth and should be understood as such. (9.245)
In that place where the king avoids the acquisition of wealth from evildoers, there men are born in due time as long-lived. (9.246)
And the crops of the people ripen individually according to how they were sown;
children do not die prematurely, nor is anything deformed born. (9.247)

These two verses are also well-known explanatory statements (*arthavāda*). In the phrase "they are born by time," the present birth is not intended; rather, it refers to those already born and those yet to be born. "Deformed" means deprived of hands, feet, and eyes. (9.246–247)
But a king should slay with various terrifying means of execution that low-born person who, out of lust, oppresses Brāhmaṇas. (9.248)

One born of the lowest caste is a *śūdra*. "Harassment" (*bādhana*) consists of the seizure of wealth and other property, as well as physical torment. "Various means" (*citrā*) refers to diverse methods such as impalement on a stake, bloodletting, mutilation of limbs, being struck with swords, and so forth—those which cause agitation and inflict suffering for a long duration. (9.248)
As much demerit is seen for a king in killing one who should not be killed, so much is seen in releasing one who deserves to be killed; but merit belongs to him who restrains the wicked. 9.249.

The fault incurred in executing one who should not be executed is equal to that incurred in releasing one who deserves execution. For a king as described—who takes a sixth part [of the produce]—there must necessarily be sin (*pratyavāya*) if he fails to perform his own duty; however, for one who does perform it, there is never the attainment of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). As for this discourse on dharma, such as "dharma indeed belongs to him who punishes," all of it is merely an *arthavāda* intended to praise the performance of one's own duties.

This instruction regarding killing, however, has the purpose of bringing about subjugation. Therefore, it should be carried out by means of various methods of killing as they have been heard [in the scriptures]. In the case of instructions concerning visible worldly ends (*dṛṣṭārtha*) for the sake of achieving the administration of a kingdom, there is a specific teaching stating that one should kill warriors according to what is observed. Since the purpose of the instruction in that context is a visible one, killing is not mandatory. This being the case, there is no fault for one who restrains [an enemy] by other means, such as imprisonment and so forth. (9.249)
Thus has been declared in detail the determination of legal procedure for two parties disputing with one another in the eighteen titles of law. 9.250
This verse is for the purpose of concluding all conventional discourse. 9.250.
Thus, performing his duties according to the Dharma, the lord of the earth should seek to acquire territories not yet obtained and protect those already acquired. (9.251)
The meaning is that one who is intent on contentment should not think, "I shall desire what has not yet been obtained. (9.251)
But having settled in a suitable location and constructed a fortress according to the treatises, he should constantly exert the greatest effort in the removal of thorns. (9.252)

Having carried out what was stated in the seventh chapter—namely, the settlement of the country and the construction of fortresses—he should perform the removal of thorns (*kaṇṭakoddharaṇa*). By that means as well, the protection of the realm is accomplished. The word "thorn" (*kaṇṭaka*) is applied to thieves and others because they share the common quality of being causes of affliction. (9.252)
He demonstrates this very point:
"By protecting those of noble conduct and by clearing away thorns, kings who are devoted to the protection of their subjects go to the third heaven. (9.253)

That which is enjoined by the noble scripture (*ārya-śāstra*) must be performed; this is a prohibition against the practice of other [duties]. The term *tadvṛtta* is a compound with the elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopī samāsa*), meaning those whose livelihood (*vṛtta*) consists of that [protection]. By this, the poor, the helpless, and the *śrotriya*s who pay neither taxes nor tolls are included. For it is logical that by protecting them, one goes to heaven. As for others, however, because they have been purchased by means of their livelihood, there is sin (*pratyavāya*) in failing to perform [the protection], as will be stated later: "And he falls away from heaven" (MDh 9.254). Through the payment for the protection of their livelihood, there is merely the absence of sin, but not heaven. Alternatively, the statement regarding the attainment of heaven refers to the observance of the rules of livelihood, as stated previously. As for others, it is seen that they are purchased by means of their livelihood. The king’s mention of heaven is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Even the non-protection of those without a livelihood is prompted by the [king's] own livelihood, since that king stands in the place of a share of his own kingdom. Just as artisans who live by their craft—"Artisans shall perform one work every month" (GDh 10.31)—are made to perform work by the king for the sake of collecting taxes while practicing their craft for the purpose of their livelihood, so too the king, being provided with a livelihood and engaged in the protection of his subjects, is made to perform the protection of the noble ones by the scripture as if it were a compulsory duty (*nityakarman*). For just as one who has consecrated the sacred fires (*agnyāhita*) performs the obligatory rites according to the Vedic injunctions concerning desire (*kāmaśruti*), and not for the sake of attaining heaven and so forth—since those rites are not enjoined for the sake of a specific fruit, yet they are nonetheless performed—so too should this be understood. Therefore, Kātyāyana-Viṣṇusvāmin says: "Whatever mention of a fruit exists, all of it is explanatory praise. The truth in this matter has been demonstrated below. (9.253)
But that king who collects taxes without punishing thieves, his kingdom becomes agitated and he is excluded from heaven. (9.254)

The governance of the kingdom according to the scriptures cannot be accomplished without the restraint and punishment of thieves through execution and other means. Therefore, for one who accepts his livelihood yet feels loathing toward the execution of thieves, there is fault in both respects: in this world, it is a transgression against the state; in the next, it is the loss of heaven. And it is logical that one who has accepted taxes but fails to provide the corresponding protection is guilty of wrongdoing. (9.254)
But that kingdom which is fearless and relies upon the strength of its arms increases constantly, like a tree being watered. (9.255)
This, which is already well-known in common worldly usage, is restated here as a supplementary rule to the procedure for the execution of a thief (9.255).
The king, whose eyes are his spies, should recognize two kinds of thieves who steal the property of others: those who are open and those who are hidden. (9.256)

Spies who are hidden within the kingdom and who possess knowledge of the king's affairs—those by whom he sees, as if they were his eyes, are one whose "eyes are spies. Just as there is no legal procedure for thieves in the world regarding those who are openly known as such, whereas there is one for others, such as forest-dwellers or night-prowlers, [the king] employs them as common [thieves] for the purpose of suppressing [crime]. (9.256)
Those who live by various wares are deceivers by open means;
but those such as thieves and forest-dwellers are deceivers by concealed means. (9.257)

In this regard, those who steal by means of specific weights and measures for the sake of trade, and who manipulate the arrival, storage, and departure of goods, are merchants who are open cheats (*prakāśavañcaka*). But those who steal in secret at night are thieves (*stena*); forest-dwellers (*āṭavika*) live in desolate regions. Furthermore, there are others who carry off by force; it is not only these, but also others whom we shall describe below. (9.257)
Bribe-takers, those who practice fraud, deceivers, gamblers, those who live by predicting auspicious events, and fortune-tellers, together with diviners; 9.258.

*Utkocakas* are those who, for the sake of someone’s business, engage in the accomplishment of that task by receiving a bribe from a king, a minister, or another official. *Aupadhikas* are those who act with deceit; they say one thing but do another. Having displayed affection in person, they proceed to provide assistance through forceful means. Or, even without taking a bribe, having ascertained through some other cause that another person’s business will certainly be accomplished, they seize wealth from the other, saying, “I shall do this for you. Alternatively, *upadhi* (deceit) refers to the display of intimidation. *Vañcakas* are gamblers, meaning those who always play for the sake of acquiring wealth. Or, the word may stand separately: *vañcakas* are deceivers. Having said, “We ourselves shall perform this task for you; we are not elsewhere,” they do not do so. Approaching [villagers], they rob them by various and diverse means. *Śivamādhavas* and others subsist upon Śiva, that is, the Sun. Those whose livelihood consists of giving auspicious instructions are astrologers and the like who teach rites for pacification (*śānti*). Alternatively, they subsist on the wealth of the wealthy, saying, “For your sake, I propitiate this deity—Durgā and Mārtaṇḍa. Or, those whose livelihood is the pronouncement of auspiciousness are those who say, “May there be auspiciousness for you. They are inauspicious yet appear auspicious. *Prekṣaṇikas* praise the characteristics of men by showing their palms to everyone. (9.258)
High ministers who act improperly, physicians, those skilled in the practice of arts and crafts, and clever courtesans— || 9.259 ||

The high ministers (*mahāmātra*), counselors, chaplains, and others who are close to the king; if they act improperly; physicians and doctors; those engaged in the practice of arts, such as painters, leaf-cutters, and sculptors—these take wealth by performing services, that is, by displaying their own artistic skill even when it is not required for the task at hand. Likewise, courtesans and clever women do so through their service and by feigning affection. The term "acting improperly" (*asamyakkārin*) applies to all these cases. (9.259)
One should recognize such people as the manifest thorns of the world, as well as others who move in secret—ignoble men wearing the marks of the noble. (9.260)

The phrase “and so forth” (*evam-ādyān*) is used because it is impossible to enumerate all the various methods of rogues who steal the property of others. For instance, they tell a woman who is indifferent that she is being neglected by her lover, or that he is deeply in love with her; or a servant, pretending to be one, may lead away the gold of a person of honest nature, though he is not actually their employee; or fools are led away by being told, “You are Brahmā, you are Bṛhaspati! When the purpose has been accomplished, those who move in secret become very humble, changing from speakers of pleasant words into speakers of unpleasant ones. (9.260)
Having identified them through secret agents who perform their duties with good conduct and by means of spies in various disguises, he should uproot them and bring them under his control. || 9.261 ||

Those who perform that task—those who perform similar tasks and have previously performed that task through the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), or else those who are currently being made to perform that task—will come having gained access for the sake of accomplishing their inclusion and will speak. Likewise, there will be others as well, spies of various disguises. (9.261)
Having publicly proclaimed their faults according to the reality of each person's own action, the king should duly administer punishment in proportion to the gravity of the offense. (9.262)
For indeed, without punishment, it is impossible to restrain the wickedness of thieves who harbor evil intentions and move about secretly upon the earth. (9.263)
Assembly halls, water-stations, bakeries, taverns, and shops selling intoxicating foods; crossroads, sacred trees, public gatherings, and theaters—these [are places to be avoided]. (9.264)
Dilapidated gardens, forests, and the workshops of artisans; empty houses, as well as groves and pleasure parks. (9.265)
The king should cause such regions to be patrolled by both stationary and mobile military outposts, as well as by spies, for the purpose of suppressing thieves. (9.266)
He should cause him to be discovered by his accomplices who followed him and were aware of his various deeds,
and he should encourage him through clever former thieves.
By means of instructions regarding food and drink, by visiting with brahmins, and by discussions of heroic deeds, they should bring about their assembly. (9.268)
Those who do not submit there, and those who are instigators from the root, the king should forcibly slay, along with their friends, kinsmen, and relatives. (9.269)
A righteous king shall not execute a thief without the stolen property; however, he may execute one caught with the booty along with the implements, without further deliberation. (9.270)
Moreover, whoever in the villages provide food to thieves or give them space for their goods—all of them as well he should cause to be executed. (9.271)
He should swiftly punish those appointed to protect the realms and the vassal kings who have been incited, if they remain neutral during attacks, just as one punishes thieves. 9.272.
And even one who lives by the Dharma, yet has fallen away from the commitment to the Dharma—
he too should be burned with punishment, for he has strayed from his own duty.

Those who do not run to the aid of others to the best of their ability when a village is being plundered, when a sacred site is being destroyed, or when a robbery is observed on the road, shall be banished along with their belongings. (9.274)

If they have the capacity [to resist], yet act out of laziness or similar motives, they are to be banished. However, for those who have made a secret pact with thieves, their execution has been prescribed previously by the rule, "he shall cause them to be slain" (MDh 9.270). Their belongings—such as cattle, horses, and so forth—are also to be banished; they must not be confiscated, for one should not be rendered destitute of possessions, though their wealth may be seized. (9.274)
He should have executed with various punishments those who steal from the king's treasury, those who act in opposition to him, and those who instigate his enemies. (9.275)

The treasury (*kośa*) is the place where kings store their accumulated wealth; those who steal from it are to be executed regardless of the type or quantity of the goods. This also applies to those who act with hostility. Furthermore, regarding those who obstruct the importation of what the king intends to bring from other lands—such as noble horses and the like that are rare in the eastern regions, or elephants originating from the Kalinga country for those in the north—and likewise those who turn allies into enemies or, having done so, align them with the enemy; and those who incite or encourage the foes: these he should have put to death. It has been stated, however, that because they act out of independent motives, execution is not necessarily required in every case. (9.275)
But those thieves who commit robbery at night by breaking into a house,
the king should have their hands cut off and impale them upon a sharp stake.
In the first instance of breaking a seal, one should have the fingers of the offender cut off;
in the second, his hands and feet; in the third, he deserves the death penalty. (9.277)

One who "unravels the knot" is a *granthibheda*. Unraveling (*bhedana*) refers to the loosening of a knot; a "knot" (*granthi*) refers to a knot in the end of a garment or the like. Alternatively, those who, having seized some property, wish to carry it off by untying the knot through some pretext are *granthibhedas*. For them, upon the first offense, there is the amputation of fingers; upon the second offense, the hands and feet; and upon the third offense, death. (9.277)
The king should punish those who provide fire, food, weapons, or shelter to thieves, as well as those who facilitate their plunder, just as he would the thief himself. (9.278)

Those who provide fire—meaning those who give fire for the purpose of removing cold and so forth—and those who provide weapons such as knives and the like, as well as those who store or manufacture stolen goods, all should be known as thieves. Although the provision of space and concealment was mentioned previously, it is stated here again for the sake of summary. (9.278)
One who destroys a tank should be killed by drowning in water or by some other form of pure execution;
or, if he repairs it, he should be made to pay the highest fine.
The mention of a "tank" (taḍāga) is intended as an illustration.
Some maintain that this same fault applies even to the taking of water from a river;

however, that is incorrect. For the offense in breaching a large tank is great, whereas it is small in the case of breaching a river. Indeed, this very same rule applies even when water is drawn by breaching the embankment of a tank. (9.279)
One should put to death without hesitation those who break into storehouses, armories, or temples, as well as those who carry off elephants, horses, or chariots. 9.280.
But he who diverts the water of a tank already established, or cuts off the flow of water, shall be made to pay the first amercement. (9.281)
He who, except in an emergency, should discharge impurity upon the royal highway, shall pay two kārṣāpaṇas and must immediately clean away that impurity. (9.282)

If one should discharge impure urine or feces on the royal highway, in a village, a city, or on a street; or if a Caṇḍāla or similar person should bring it from elsewhere and deposit it there—this refers to when there is no emergency, for it is stated that such acts are excessive even when driven by the force of an emergency. One should have a Caṇḍāla or similar person remove it by paying him a fee, or do it oneself if another is unavailable. (9.282)

Furthermore, one who has fallen into calamity, or an elderly person, a pregnant woman, or even a child, deserve only a reprimand; and that [matter] must be cleared up—this is the established rule. (9.283)

"One in distress" refers to those previously mentioned. "The elderly and others" refers to those who are unable to go outside the village; they are suspected of even shedding blood, and are suspected of designating even what is impure [as pure]. One must not act in this manner again. If one acts so again, there is great transgression before the king. Such speech, pregnant with anger, is a form of censure, and that must be purified—this is the instruction for the king. If the perpetrators are not known, then the street should likewise be cleared by the *caṇḍālas* and others. (9.283)
For all physicians who practice falsely, there shall be punishment:
the first amercement for non-human beings, but the middle amercement for human beings. (9.284)

Physicians are those who practice medicine. For them, the administration of medicine in a wrongful manner occurs in two ways: either through ignorance of the application of the medical treatises, or even when the treatises are familiar, through lack of diligence or a desire for gain. Regarding non-human beings such as cattle, horses, elephants, and so forth, the first degree of *sāhasa* (violence) is to be applied; likewise, in the case of human beings, the middle degree applies. If, by such improper practice, the patient should perish quickly, then a heavy punishment must be ordained. (9.284)
One who breaks the crossing-bridges, flagstaffs, or images shall repair all of that damage and pay five hundred [paṇas]. || 9.285 ||

*Saṃkrama* [704] refers to the path by which they pass over, descending by means of such signs as touching water and so forth. A bright garment, a banner, or a mark [705] belongs to kings, ministers, and others; likewise, a staff is used in temples of the gods and for images—so it has been explained. One should repair, restore, and bring back to its original state [706]. (9.285)
For the adulteration of unadulterated goods, as well as for their breaking and the false boring of gems, the punishment is the first amercement. (9.286)

When one who seeks profit defiles substances that are themselves unadulterated—such as when a grain-seller mixes excellent, faultless grain in the field with straw and chaff; or when saffron and the like are mixed with other substances such as non-saffron; or when gems and pearls are broken, meaning they are split in two; or when they are "pierced through" (apavedha), meaning they are pierced at a place where they should not be pierced—in these cases, punishment must be imposed. Gems are of inferior, middling, or superior quality; therein, the penalty should be determined: for middling gems, a middling fine; for superior gems, a superior fine. (9.286)
But he who deals unfairly with those who are equal, whether by measure or by price, shall incur the first or indeed the middle amercement. (9.287)

Regarding those goods for which an exchange on the basis of equality is prescribed—such as, "Sesame seeds may be exchanged for grain of equal value" (MDh 10.94)—if one acts unfairly therein, he might, for the sake of trade, give sesame and take back a large quantity of grain such as rice (*vrīhi*) and so forth; or, in the absence of a direct barter, he purchases from the grain merchants at a price higher than its value through a commercial transaction. Alternatively, suppose one person has an upper garment (*uttarīya*) or a pillow (*upabarhaṇa*) to sell, while another has certain cloths (*śāṭaka*); in that case, the cloths are useful to the one who possesses the pillow, and they are of equal value to the pillow. There, having recognized the utility of the latter, he gives [the cloth] as if it were of equal value and takes a higher price. He is said to "act unfairly with equals by means of price. Both of these—the buyer and the seller—are subject to punishment. The phrase "acts by means of price" (*mūlyataś carati*) has the same meaning [as the previous clause]; likewise, in this alternative view, the word *vā* serves merely to complete the meter. In the first and middle cases mentioned, buying and selling are presented as options depending upon the relative worth of the goods. (9.287)
And he should place all the prisoners along the royal highway, so that those miserable, deformed evildoers may be seen there. (9.288)

One should establish or construct prisons in well-known locations, such as the royal highway, so that those who are suffering may be seen there; this indicates that they may be situated elsewhere as well, and that they should be made to wander through those areas. By this, he implies that other forms of torment for those held in confinement should also be inflicted. They are "distorted" by falling into other states such as extreme emaciation of the body, through fasting or eating only a little; the rest is clear. (9.288)
One who breaks down a wall, fills up a moat, or destroys a gate should be banished immediately. (9.289)
The punishment for the destruction of fortifications such as walls and the like is exile. Moats are excavated portions of the ground. (9.289)
In all cases of malevolent sorcery, a fine of two hundred [paṇas] shall be imposed; likewise for root-magic performed by those who are not authorized, and for various types of magical rites. (9.290)

*Abhicāra* (malevolent magic) is the killing of others by means of unseen methods through the power of mantras and the like. For those engaged in this, this punishment applies when the person targeted for *abhicāra* is not one who should be targeted. One is not exempt from liability merely because the *abhicāra* was directed against those who should not be targeted; in such cases, the punishment for killing a human being must be understood to apply. The inclusion of the term "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of ensuring the punishment applies without distinction to both worldly and Vedic rites. Vedic examples include the *Śyena* sacrifice and others; worldly examples include seizing a tree, using dust, piercing with needles, and so forth. *Mūlakarma* refers to acts of subjugation and the like. "Trustworthy persons" (*āpta*) refers to sons, wives, and others; those other than these are "untrustworthy" (*anāpta*). *Kṛtyā* refers specifically to types of *abhicāra* performed through the power of mantras and the like, well-known among spirits and other entities as causes for expulsion, enmity toward friends and kinsmen, hatred, and causing mental derangement. (9.290)
One who sells seed that is unfit for sowing, one who steals such seed, and likewise one who destroys a boundary marker, shall suffer the punishment of mutilation or death. (9.291)

Having declared non-seed to be seed, one sells it by concealing its true nature. Seeds of grain, vegetables, and the like, which have been soaked for a long time, sprout in the field, yet they cannot be called sterile (*vandhya*). One extracts the seed from the field—that excellent seed which sprouts quickly—and having removed it, one sells it after substituting something that merely resembles it, such as another type of grain. Alternatively, they extract the sown seed from the very field and carry it away. *Maryādā* is the established order rooted in scripture and local custom. *Vikṛta* refers to disfigurement, such as the cutting off of ears or noses. (9.291)
A king should have a goldsmith who is the most wicked of all thorns,
if he persists in unjust conduct, cut into pieces with razors.

Among all those thorns previously mentioned, the goldsmith is the most sinful. If the genitive case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), how is it that there is no absence of compounding due to the rule *na nirdhāraṇe* (Pāṇini 2.2.10)? His status as the most sinful arises because even by stealing a very small amount, he incurs great guilt; furthermore, the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold constitutes a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*). Therefore, one should have him cut into pieces if he persists in such injustice. They steal by means of counterfeiting, using false scales, heating, cutting, and so forth; they take [the gold]. And in this case, there is no requirement regarding the quantity of the object being stolen, nor any regard for the caste of the owner. However, repetition (*abhyāsa*) is taken into account because of the severity of the punishment. But in the first instance of such activity, the shaving of flesh with a razor should be determined as a monetary fine. It has been established that the sin of those being punished departs through corporal restraint. (9.292)
In cases of the theft of Sītā-grain, weapons, or medicine,
the king, having considered the time and the specific circumstances of the act, shall determine the punishment.

*Sītā* is the land being ploughed; *taddravyāṇi* refers to the implements such as the plough and the spade. A punishment should be prescribed for the theft of these. Is it [determined] by mere whim? No, he says: "having considered the time and the purpose. When the time for ploughing has arrived, the punishment is great. And when that [land] has not been ploughed, if there is a loss of a great harvest, then it is even greater. *Āsādya* means having known it to be imminent. But at other times, it is according to the nature of the object and so forth. Likewise for weapons such as swords and the like, at the time of battle; for medicine, at the time of its use for medicinal purposes. If, because that medicine was stolen and not used, great suffering arises for the patient, and another [medicine] is not available at that time—or if what is available would take a long time to use due to the need for processing by decoction and so forth—such considerations may prevail in determining the king's punishment. Regarding weapons, which are the king's instruments; otherwise, for one who fears enemies or thieves from the countryside, then the punishment is great. If it is small, the punishment is small. (9.293)
The sovereign, the minister, the capital, the realm, the treasury, the army, and likewise the ally—these are the seven constituent elements; thus the kingdom is said to have seven limbs. (9.294)

Once the removal of thorns (*kaṇṭakaśuddhi*) is completed, the duties of a king (*rājadharma*) that are solely useful for the administration of the kingdom are now discussed. Just as when these [duties] are performed the kingdom does not perish, so too when the administration of justice (*vyavahāradarśana*) or the removal of thorns is carried out, the preservation of the kingdom is equally ensured. Furthermore, those who rely upon the queen, the princes, the king’s favorites, and the military commanders are generally the "thorns. One should not, at times, remove them with the following thought: "In the event of a fear of internal unrest, the highest purpose is served by the commander-in-chief and the feudal lord; what is the use of suppressing this offender against the realm? For that reason it is said: "The realm is equal [to the king], starting from the sovereign," because it constitutes a constituent element (*prakṛti*) of the kingdom. And the relative weight or lightness of these constituents is stated for this very purpose. If there is great unrest caused by a minister, it must be averted. Even if the realm is weaker than that [minister], one should not act impulsively, thinking, "I will effect the removal of thorns after first informing [the others] through some means. Therefore, having been extracted even from the instruction of the seventh chapter, this is understood here as a specific rule.

The sovereign is the king himself. The minister consists of the counselor and the priest; the commander is the general. The city is the capital where he dwells; the realm (*rāṣṭra*) consists of the provinces. The treasury (*kośa*) is the accumulation of wealth such as silver, gold, and coins. The army (*daṇḍa*) consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—or alternatively, it refers to the power of punishment, such as legal sanctions and the like. The ally (*suhṛt*) is one who shares the same purpose, as it has been said: "Therefore, the friend is next [to the treasury]" (MDh 7.158). These are the constituents (*prakṛti*) of the kingdom—the causes or components—just as the potsherds are to a jar. Alternatively, the word *prakṛti* may denote their inherent nature. Thus, the entire kingdom, consisting of these very elements, has been enumerated. Its detailed classification is seventy-two-fold, and any other further subdivisions therein have already been mentioned. (9.294)

Among these seven constituent elements of sovereignty, one should know that, in their respective order, each preceding one is more significant and its misfortune more grave than the following. (9.295)

A calamity to one's own forces is more serious than a calamity to an ally; for one who possesses his own forces is able to favor an ally. The same applies to the army and the treasury: when the treasury is destroyed, the army is likewise destroyed. Similarly, regarding the treasury and the kingdom: when the kingdom is destroyed, from where can the treasury arise? Furthermore, when there is fear of the destruction of the kingdom, the capital city must be protected with great effort, for it is there that all constituent means and resources are found. Among these, the minister is the most important; for when the chief minister is lost, the entire force is shattered. It is well known that when the self is destroyed, everything is destroyed. Thus it has been said: "The self, however, must be protected above all. (9.295)
And so there is this illustration:
"In this world, of the seven-limbed kingdom which is propped up like a triple-staff, nothing excels anything else because of the specific quality of each in relation to the others. (9.296)

"Of one who is supported, like a triple staff": this refers to those who are supported by one another through the state of being mutual bases. He says this very thing: because of the excellence of their respective qualities, they stand in a relationship of mutual assistance to one another, and because each arises from the destruction of the other—just as the totality of earth, seed, and water results in the production of a sprout. Therefore, the worshipfulness of all of them is stated here. Indeed, there is a distinction of weight and lightness in this matter; however, the claim that "nothing is superior" is intended only to mean that one must act with great care toward the protection of friends and others. For when a friend is destroyed, the kingdom is destroyed after some time, provided there is an obstruction by a powerful force; it does not happen immediately. This is the basis for the relative lightness [of the offense]. (9.296)
In various specific tasks, however, one particular factor is distinguished;
that by which a particular effect is accomplished is said to be the most excellent in that context. (9.297)

There is no object that is not of use to a king; for there may be a task that is accomplished by an inferior person and not by one of high status. Therefore, all subjects must be protected with effort; the kingdom must not be oppressed by unjust punishments and the like, and it must be diligently guarded against disturbances such as thieves. This is the essential meaning. Thus, this [verse] is a supplement to the section on the removal of thorns (kaṇṭakaśuddhi). 9.297.
Through one's conduct, through the application of energy, and indeed through the performance of actions, one should constantly know the strength of oneself and of others. (9.298)

One should constantly know the power of both the enemy and oneself. One must always understand this: "What does he intend to undertake? What can be done by me against him? And what am I capable of doing against him? How is this to be known? By means of spies, as described in the seventh chapter. Through the application of energy—those who have been gratified by gifts and other means are joined with energy—and through the successful results of agriculture and other undertakings. Furthermore, it is through action itself that one knows the capacity for various tasks; for by observing the commencement of works such as fortifications, one understands that the enemy is powerful, since those very works bring about the attainment of wealth and from that, the emergence of capability. (9.298)
Having reflected upon the gravity or lightness of all oppressions as well as calamities, one should then undertake the task. (9.299)

Afflictions (*pīḍanāni*) include the torments of hell, famine, and falling [into calamity], as well as drought, excessive rain, cycles of rats, locusts, thunderbolts, and so forth. Misfortunes (*vyasanāni*) arise from desire and anger, or are presented through the intervention of fate resulting in the loss of one's own son. Nevertheless, one should not always be characterized by over-exertion (*utsāha*), nor should one be characterized by complacency (*saṃtoṣin*). Furthermore, once the consideration of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) has been conducted, and the daily income and expenditure have been determined, and the conduct of the kingdom—which accords with the desires of the subjects—has been ascertained to some extent through the reports of spies; or else, through other activities such as the enjoyment of the pleasures of dance and song, the various duties (*karmāṇi*) must be understood. (9.299)
One should indeed undertake actions again and again, even when exhausted;
for prosperity attends the man who perseveres in his undertakings. 9.300

"A man who is intent upon his duties is joined with prosperity"—this is a restatement of an established fact. Even if, due to some reason, the fruit of a performed action has not been obtained in some way, one must nevertheless neither become discouraged nor remain complacent. Alternatively, once the consideration of the six measures of policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) has been carried out, and the daily income and expenditure have been understood to some extent, and the condition of the kingdom as desired by the subjects has been ascertained from the mouths of spies, then further actions should be undertaken through other activities for the enjoyment of pleasures such as dance and song. The mention of "man" implies: let alone the king, even an ordinary person from the countryside prospers through the glory of diligence. Thus it is said: "Until death, one should seek prosperity" (MDh 4.137). 9.300.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages—all these are the conduct of the king; for the king is said to be the age itself.

For this reason as well, the king must be intent upon the undertaking of action; one who does not undertake action would be a Kali age, and that is a great fault. Nor should the king think, "The so-called Kali is a specific period of time well-known from the Itihāsas; how could I be such? because all these ages are the very conduct of the king. This is explained in the following verse (9.301).
When he is asleep, it is the Kali age; when he is awake, it is the Dvāpara age; when he is intent upon actions, it is the Tretā age; but when he moves about freely, it is the Kṛta age. (9.302)

One who is habitually inactive and asleep becomes Kali; one who understands the means for advancement and puts them into practice becomes Dvāpara while awake; one who applies himself to determined actions becomes Tretā; and one who, with the attainment of the fruits of action, assumes all forms according to the scriptures, becomes Kṛta. || 9.302 ||
A king should conduct himself with the splendor and conduct of Indra, Arka, Vāyu, Yama, Varuṇa, Candra, Agni, and the Earth. (9.303)
Tejas means semen, the product; that is to say, virility. || 9.303 ||
Just as Indra pours down rain during the four months of the rainy season, so should one practicing the vow of Indra shower his own kingdom with the fulfillment of desires. (9.304)

In this context, a restriction to a specific month is not intended; rather, it means that during four months the rain-cloud pours down continuously. Therefore, what is meant is that he should fill his own kingdom with all desired objects at all times. He should act in such a way that the inhabitants of his own kingdom remain devoted to him. (9.304)
Just as the sun draws up water with its rays for eight months, so should he draw taxes from the kingdom; for that is the constant vow of the sun. 9.305
Just as the sun takes up even a small amount of water with its slight heat, so too should one take taxes; this is the meaning of the simile. (9.305)
Just as the wind enters all beings and moves through them, so too should one enter by means of spies; for this indeed is the "Wind-like Vow."
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when the time has come, so too must subjects be restrained by the king; for that is the vow of Yama.
In the event of an offense, one should behave with impartiality toward both the beloved and the hated. 9.307.
Just as one who is bound by Varuṇa with his nooses is clearly seen, so should he restrain the wicked; for this is indeed the vow of Varuṇa. 9.308
Those who do not perform their duties should be restrained without exception, so that they do not flee. 9.308.
Just as men rejoice upon seeing the full moon, so do the subjects rejoice in that king who observes the lunar vow.

At the time of appearing before the subjects, one should be free from anger, adorned with ornaments, and have a joyful countenance; the meaning is that [the people] shall be freed from distress and suffering. 9.309.
One who is endowed with majesty, radiant, and always intent on punishing evil-doers, and who is a destroyer of wicked vassals— that is remembered as the Agneya vow.
"One who is extremely provocative and wicked" refers to the Agneya vow; [such persons are] the neighboring kings and ministers who are equipped with many means of action. (9.310)
Just as the earth supports all beings equally, so too is the vow of a king who sustains all beings. 9.311
The earth is the ground; likewise, the poor, the helpless, and the lineage members are to be supported. 9.311
Employing these and other means, always vigilant, the king should suppress thieves both within his own kingdom and in those of others. (9.312)
The concluding verse: By these observances of the gods, and by others understood from worldly custom. 9.312.
Even when fallen into the greatest calamity, one should not provoke the Brahmins;
for if they are angered, they may instantly destroy him along with his army and his mounts. (9.313)

Even if one whose treasury is exhausted is punished by a more powerful king, nevertheless, even in times of distress, the property of a Brāhmaṇa must not be seized; nor should they be provoked by contempt or similar treatment. (9.313)
By whom was fire made to consume all things and the great ocean rendered undrinkable? By whom was the waning moon made to wax full? Who would not be destroyed by provoking them? (9.314)

In order to establish the meaning previously stated, he reiterates a world-renowned historical narrative concerning the greatness of the Brāhmaṇa. Regarding these matters, the relevant accounts should be understood from the Mahābhārata. (9.314)
Who could prosper by harming those who, when provoked to anger, might create other worlds and world-protectors, or turn gods into non-gods? (9.315)

It destroys and obscures; because there is no distinction among memories, even the destruction of the highest ones constitutes a contraction, as was demonstrated by the sage Vyāsa when Yudhiṣṭhira cast aside the Gāṇḍīva bow. 9.315.
"Those upon whom the worlds and the gods always depend, and for whom Brahman itself is their wealth—who, desiring to live, would harm them? (9.316)

The three worlds are the earth and the others. The gods depend upon the Brāhmaṇa by means of oblations. Due to his preeminence in teaching and the abundance of his ritual acts, the Brāhmaṇa is the refuge of the gods, whereas the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya are not so. 9.316.
Whether ignorant or learned, a Brāhmaṇa is a great deity;
whether consecrated or unconsecrated, he is like the fire, which is a great deity. (9.317)

One should not show contempt toward those who rely on their birth alone, without regard for their learning, as in the case of acts such as giving; just as [it is said], "one should not do this with one's foot," in reference to the sacred fire (MDh 4.54). 9.317.
Even in cremation grounds, the radiant fire is not defiled;
when offered oblations in sacrifices, it increases all the more. (9.318)
The meaning of this is clear: even one of bad conduct is not to be despised; such is the sense. || 9.318 ||
Thus, even if they engage in all kinds of unworthy actions,
Brahmins are to be honored in every way, for they are the supreme deity.
Those who persist in what is undesirable or forbidden should be punished according to the scriptures with mild measures, and not by attacking them suddenly as one would treat other castes. 9.319.
When the Kṣatriya power has increased excessively toward the Brāhmaṇas in every respect, the Brāhmaṇa alone should be the restrainer; for the Kṣatriya is born from the Brāhmaṇa. (9.320)

When a Kṣatriya proceeds to oppress Brāhmaṇas, the Brāhmaṇas alone are their restrainers. Kṣatriyas who, intoxicated by wealth and pride, act by violating the established order, are set back upon the right path by the Brāhmaṇas through means such as silent recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), and curses. The reason for this is: "The Kṣatra is born from the Brahman. The origin of the Kṣatriyas is from the Brāhmaṇa caste. This is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). (9.320)
"Is it not the case that whatever is the cause of something's arising cannot be its destroyer? Not so;
for fire arises from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone.
Yet the all-pervading heat of these subsides within their own respective sources. (9.321)

"From water and from plants and trees he is born"—thus fire is produced from water alone. Its all-pervading heat always burns whatever is combustible and overcomes with its brilliance. Upon reaching water, that heat of his is extinguished. From stone comes iron, swords, and the like; by it everything is pierced, and it bursts open upon impact with stone. In this way, Kṣatriyas who desire victory everywhere are victorious, but if they behave with arrogance toward Brāhmaṇas, then they perish. (9.321)
The Kṣatriya power does not prosper without the Brahmanical power; the Brahmanical power does not flourish without the Kṣatriya power.
When the Brahmanical and Kṣatriya powers are joined together, they flourish both in this world and in the next. (9.322)

Whatever kingdom lacks the *kṣatra*—that is, a kingdom devoid of Brahmins, where ministers, domestic priests, and others are not Brahmins—how can there be prosperity there? Likewise, how can even the Brahmins, when dependent upon the king, obtain success? Both, when joined together, conquer the world. The words *brahma* and *kṣatra* denote the castes of the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya respectively. (9.322)
Having bestowed upon the Brahmins all the wealth arising from fines,
and having established his son in the kingdom, he should seek his end in battle.

But when he is overcome by old age and has accomplished all his duties, then, provided wealth exists, he should give to the Brahmins the entire amount arising from fines. It has been stated that the property of those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) is to be offered to Varuṇa; it must not be seized by the king. However, other wealth from fines belongs to the king. Since there is much wealth for the sake of visible and invisible purposes, and since this is the time for departure, this is the application of all [the wealth].

Others, however, explain that the mention of "taking up the staff" (daṇḍagrahaṇa) is intended as an illustration for taxes, tolls, and so forth. If that were the case, it would mean "he should give everything," implying that everything except vehicles, weapons, land, and men should be surrendered.
But if explained in this way, the statement "having established his son in the kingdom" would not be consistent; for it is impossible for one who is without a treasury to exercise royal authority.

One should make one’s departure in battle; one should engage in combat by sacrificing one’s own life. If, for some reason, one does not encounter battle in the final stage of life, then one should abandon the body through fire, water, or other means. However, the attainment of the excellence of results occurs in battle. *Samāsañjanam* means mounting [onto the funeral pyre]. 9.323.
Acting thus and always disciplined in the duties of a king, the monarch should appoint all his servants to tasks that are beneficial for the worlds.

Acting and dwelling thus, always disciplined and devoted to the duties of a king as taught in the scriptures, he should appoint all his servants to tasks for the welfare of his own subjects throughout the world. (9.324)
This eternal rule of action for the king has been declared in its entirety;
one should likewise know this rule of action for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra in due order. (9.325)

By this first [verse], the duties of a king, ending with the removal of thorns, are summarized; by the second, they cause one to recall what was stated in [MDh 1.116]: "And the conduct toward Vaiśyas and Śūdras. 9.325.
But the Vaiśya, having undergone the purificatory rites and taken a wife, should be constantly engaged in agriculture and trade, as well as in the protection of cattle. (9.326)

Having undergone the purificatory rites, having been initiated, and having performed his marriage, he should be appointed to the occupation of *vārtā*. *Vārtā* refers to the aggregate of activities to be described in due time; he should be engaged therein, just as the science of *vārtā* has been taught in the work of Bṛhaspati. (9.326)
For Prajāpati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaiśya; and he entrusted all subjects to the Brāhmaṇa and the King. (9.327)

The protection of cattle is not merely for the livelihood of the Vaiśya, but also for his *dharma*; this is shown by means of an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). But how can the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) be mentioned when the seen (*dṛṣṭa*) is present? It is like the protection of subjects: it is an entrustment through an injunction, saying, "It must be protected by you according to the rule. The qualification of the Kṣatriya for the protection of subjects has already been established. For the Brāhmaṇa, through the instruction of penances and so forth, as well as through silent recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), and so on—and because of the [text], "From the Sun rain is born" (MDh 3.76)—there is a universal qualification. And this is for the sake of illustration; in the same way, for the Vaiśya, the protection of cattle and so forth is indeed *dharma*. (9.327)
A Vaiśya should have no desire [to think], "I shall not tend cattle";
if the Vaiśya so desires, they must by no means be tended by anyone else. (9.328)

Now, what desire is there for the sake of life? As it has been said: "Even that which is unseen is indeed dependent upon the seen, just as facing east is [dependent] upon eating. In that case, how can it be said: "A Vaiśya should not have a desire"? For one who does not wish to eat does not incur transgression.

This is true; however, it is stated [in this way] in order to indicate that animal husbandry is superior to agriculture and the like. Someone might think that all these [occupations] are restrictive in nature and yield equal results. If they yielded equal results, then even one who lacks desire for them would [be compelled to] engage in another occupation while desiring something else. But when [animal husbandry] is more excellent than others, then one should live by that alone, and there is no engagement in another occupation. Therefore, one should live supported by that very thing. (9.328)
One should know the relative value and worth of gems, pearls, corals, metals, woven fabrics, perfumes, and liquids. (9.329)

By the word *loha* (metal), he refers to copper, iron, and bell-metal. The strength and weakness of price (*arghabalābala*) refers to the deficiency or excess of price in relation to place and time: "In which place is this highly priced, or in which is it of low price? The same applies to time as well. 9.329.

One should know the method of sowing seeds, as well as the defects and virtues of the field; one should understand the application of measures and all the applications of the scales in every respect. (9.330)

"One knows this sowing: 'This seed is sown scattered; this is sown in a heap. Such are the qualities and defects [of the seeds], such as: 'This seed sprouts in this field, this does not, and this bears fruit abundantly. Droṇa, śūrpa, āḍhaka, and so forth are specific measures of capacity; their applications are those things measured by the hand. (9.330)
He [should know] the worth and worthlessness of merchandise, the merits and defects of regions, the profit and loss of trade goods, and the breeding of livestock. (9.331)

By the word *bhāṇḍa*, saleable goods such as cloth and skins are meant. In that regard, "worthiness" (*sāratā*) refers to that which does not perish even when kept for a long time; the opposite of that is "unworthiness" (*asāra*). The qualities and defects of a region include such things as: "In this region rice is abundant; in this region barley [is abundant]; in this region such is the custom; such is the disposition of the local people," and so forth. And: "By using such fodder and such salt at this time, livestock will thrive. (9.331)
He should know the wages of servants, the various languages of men, the methods of storing goods, and their purchase and sale. (9.332)

He should know the wages for servants, slaves, messengers, and the like, as well as for cowherds, shepherds, high officials, and others—specifically, how much their pay should be. He should also understand the dialects of various regions, such as Mālava, Magadha, and Draviḍa; that is, he should know that in this particular region people pronounce such a word for this meaning. Furthermore, he should know how a commodity is stored, how it is processed, how it is covered, with what it is mixed, and for how much it is sold. (9.332) He should exert the greatest effort to increase his wealth through righteous means, and he should diligently provide food for all living beings. (9.333)
The meaning is that much food must be given; otherwise, one would be punished by the king. This is stated here for that reason. And this applies to one who possesses great wealth. 9.333.
For a Śūdra, however, the service of Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, householders, and illustrious, is indeed the supreme dharma for attaining the highest bliss. (9.334)
By the term "of the illustrious," virtuous conduct is indicated; service is indeed attendance. Its practice brings about the highest good. (9.334)
Pure, devoted to the highest service, gentle in speech, free from egoism, and always taking refuge in Brahmins and the like, one attains a superior birth. (9.335)

By means of purity, cleansing with earth and water, and the restraint of the senses, and by desiring to serve the superior members of the three castes while speaking gently—meaning he does not speak harshly due to being tainted by the study of logic (tarka) and other such treatises—he attains a superior birth, such as that of a Brāhmaṇa; this is the meaning. The purpose has been clearly stated. Furthermore, because of the specific mention of "taking refuge in a Brāhmaṇa," even for one who relies on others and serves others, this [conduct] constitutes dharma provided it is not in conflict [with his primary duty]. (9.335)
This auspicious rule of action for the social classes in times of non-distress has been declared;
now learn, in due order, that which pertains to them even in times of distress. (9.336)
And the purpose has been clearly stated. 9.336.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Commentary on Manu, composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
